question: On the Irish coast of Northern Ireland, the sea cliffs end in 40,000 hexagonal stone columns packed tight like a giant honeycomb. What shaped them into six-sided columns?
choices: Cooling lava cracked into six-sided columns as it shrank, locking the shape forever
Sea waves carved the columns slowly out of one solid block of limestone
Glaciers slid down the coast and ground the rock into the column pattern
Wind-blown sand polished the cliffs into the columns over millions of years
answer: Cooling lava cracked into six-sided columns as it shrank, locking the shape forever
context: The Giant's Causeway formed ~60 million years ago. Lava cooled slowly and contracted; the most efficient pattern for contraction stress is six-sided columns. Same physics makes mud cracks hexagonal.

question: In central Turkey a region called Cappadocia has tall pointed stone towers with caps like mushrooms. People carved entire underground cities inside the soft rock. What rock makes the towers?
choices: Soft volcanic ash welded into rock, with harder caps that shield the towers
Soft limestone left behind when an ancient sea dried out and packed down
Soft sandstone laid down by an old river that flowed across the plateau
Soft chalk made from microscopic shells in a warm shallow inland lake
answer: Soft volcanic ash welded into rock, with harder caps that shield the towers
context: Cappadocia's fairy chimneys are tuff (welded volcanic ash) from Mt Erciyes and Hasan. The caps are harder basalt left when softer tuff eroded around them. Underground cities like Derinkuyu held ~20,000 people.

question: In the Karakum desert of Turkmenistan, a crater the size of a soccer field has been burning nonstop since 1971. Locals call it the Door to Hell. What keeps the flames going?
choices: Natural gas leaks up through the soil and burns as it reaches the air
A buried oil tanker keeps slowly leaking new fuel into the pit
An ancient coal seam exposed by the crater smolders beneath the floor
Volcanic vents under the desert release a constant stream of hot lava
answer: Natural gas leaks up through the soil and burns as it reaches the air
context: Soviet geologists drilling in 1971 collapsed a cavern over natural gas. They lit it off, expecting it to burn out in weeks. The Darvaza crater is still flaming — the gas field is huge.

question: On the island of Iceland, hot springs throw boiling water 20 m straight up into the air at regular times. The English word for this comes from one Icelandic spring. What is the word?
choices: Geyser, from Geysir, the great Icelandic spring people watched first
Volcano, from Vulcan, the Roman blacksmith god of fire and forges
Crater, from the Greek word for a great mixing bowl for wine
Cauldron, from a Latin word for the iron pot witches once cooked in
answer: Geyser, from Geysir, the great Icelandic spring people watched first
context: Geysir in southwest Iceland gave English the word 'geyser.' Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; hot rock below the surface boils groundwater that erupts in regular bursts.

question: In southern Mexico the limestone ground is full of round natural pools called cenotes. Maya kids swam in them; modern divers explore them. Why are these pools so common in the Yucatan?
choices: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone underground, making caves whose roofs cave in
Long-ago volcanoes left round craters that filled up with rainwater over time
Old meteor impacts pocked the peninsula with thousands of small round holes
Sea waves washed inland during storms and carved the pools out of the rock
answer: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone underground, making caves whose roofs cave in
context: Cenotes form by karst dissolution. Rainwater is slightly acidic; over thousands of years it eats limestone underground, hollows out caves, and the roofs collapse into round pools. Yucatan has ~6,000 cenotes.

question: In the New Mexico desert lies a cave system so deep and dark that a colony of half a million bats flies out every evening like smoke. What kind of rock holds Carlsbad Caverns?
choices: Limestone, hollowed out by underground water dissolving it over millions of years
Sandstone, layered down by an ancient river the cave water later cut through
Granite, slowly broken apart along cracks by water freezing in winter
Basalt, leftover from old lava tubes drained when the volcano went quiet
answer: Limestone, hollowed out by underground water dissolving it over millions of years
context: Carlsbad Caverns formed in a 250 million-year-old limestone reef. Sulfuric acid from oil-and-gas gases dissolved the rock, making chambers like the Big Room (~10 football fields).

question: Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is so big and so flat that after rain it becomes the world's largest natural mirror. Beneath the salt lies half the world's supply of one valuable metal. Which metal?
choices: Lithium — powering laptop, phone, and electric-car batteries
Gold — used in jewelry, electronics, and central-bank reserves
Silver — used in coins, photography, and electronics
Platinum — used in catalytic converters and luxury jewelry
answer: Lithium — powering laptop, phone, and electric-car batteries
context: Salar de Uyuni is ~10,500 km2 at 3,656 m elevation — world's largest salt flat. Its brine holds an estimated 50-70% of world lithium reserves. After rain, the surface mirrors the sky perfectly.

question: In southwest China, hundreds of green pointed limestone hills stick straight up from rice paddies. Boats slip between them along the Li River. Why are these karst peaks so steep and pointed?
choices: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, leaving the hardest cores standing as steep towers
Old earthquakes shoved blocks of limestone up out of the ground at sharp angles
Glaciers slid through and ground the softer rock down between harder hills
Volcanoes pushed thin spires of magma up through the limestone long ago
answer: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, leaving the hardest cores standing as steep towers
context: Guilin's karst landscape formed over millions of years of warm wet weather dissolving limestone. The hardest cores stayed standing; softer rock washed away. Same process makes haystack hills in Vietnam's Ha Long Bay.

question: Death Valley in California holds Badwater Basin — a flat white salt pan 86 m below sea level. The Pacific Ocean is just 200 km west. Why is this basin so far below sea level?
choices: Two tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart, dropping the valley floor down
An ancient meteor impact left a deep crater the sea later filled with salt
Glaciers from the last Ice Age scooped out the basin and left it dry
A long-ago volcano collapsed and the floor of the crater sank far below
answer: Two tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart, dropping the valley floor down
context: Death Valley is a graben — a valley dropped down between two parallel faults as the Basin and Range region stretches apart. Badwater (-86 m) is the lowest spot in North America.

question: Most kids picture sand as soft sliding stuff. On Hawaii's Big Island, one beach has sand that is glittering green crystals instead of yellow grains. What mineral makes the green sand?
choices: Olivine, a green crystal that forms inside cooling volcanic lava nearby
Emerald, a precious green stone the waves wash down from inland mines
Jade, the famous green stone carved into ornaments and old jewelry
Malachite, a green copper mineral washed in from underwater veins
answer: Olivine, a green crystal that forms inside cooling volcanic lava nearby
context: Papakolea Beach on Hawaii's south coast is green from olivine crystals weathered out of an old cinder cone. Olivine is a common mineral inside basalt lava — Hawaii is essentially made of basalt.

question: In Turkey near Pamukkale, white terraces look like a frozen waterfall of cotton tumbling down a hillside. Roman soldiers bathed in their warm pools. What white mineral built the terraces?
choices: Calcium carbonate, dropped out of warm spring water as it cools and steps down
Salt crystals, dried out of an old sea the springs slowly washed across
Quartz, polished by the spring water tumbling over the same spot for ages
Chalk, eroded out of cliffs above and carried down to the terrace pools
answer: Calcium carbonate, dropped out of warm spring water as it cools and steps down
context: Pamukkale (Turkish for 'cotton castle') forms when hot mineral springs deposit calcium carbonate (travertine) as the water cools and gives up CO2. The Roman city of Hierapolis sits above; the springs were a famous bath.

question: In a flat part of Australia called Karijini, water has carved deep narrow gorges through red rock — sometimes so narrow a kid can touch both walls. Why is the rock red?
choices: It is iron-rich rock that rusted slowly when oxygen reached it in air
Ancient fires burned across the plain and baked the rock a dark rusty red
Red sand blown by desert winds stuck to the cliffs and stained them deep
The rock has tiny garnet crystals scattered through it that color it red
answer: It is iron-rich rock that rusted slowly when oxygen reached it in air
context: Karijini's rocks are banded iron formations — among Earth's oldest (~2.5 billion years). Iron in the rock has slowly rusted (oxidized), giving the canyons their famous red color. Iron-rich rocks built Australia's iron-export economy.

question: Between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia, a tall cone called Krakatoa blew itself apart in 1883. The boom was heard 3,000 miles away. What name do geologists give the empty bowl such a blast leaves?
choices: A caldera — a wide sunken bowl left when the volcano's chamber emptied below
A canyon — a deep narrow valley a river has cut into a flat plateau
A crater — a small round dip dug by a meteor strike from above
A trench — a long deep dip in the ocean floor between two land plates
answer: A caldera — a wide sunken bowl left when the volcano's chamber emptied below
context: Krakatoa's 1883 eruption emptied its magma chamber catastrophically; the cone collapsed into a caldera. The blast was heard from Australia to Mauritius (4,800 km) — among the loudest sounds in recorded history.

question: In Norway long narrow arms of the sea cut deep inland between steep cliffs, sometimes more than a kilometer tall. Cruise ships sail right up the middle. What carved these long deep inlets?
choices: Glaciers that gouged out U-shaped valleys later filled by the sea
Rivers that slowly cut V-shaped valleys later flooded by the sea
Earthquakes that cracked open the coast and let the sea rush in
Lava flows that left long channels the sea poured into long ago
answer: Glaciers that gouged out U-shaped valleys later filled by the sea
context: Norwegian fjords are flooded glacial valleys. During the last Ice Age, glaciers scoured the coast into deep U-shaped troughs. When the ice melted, the sea filled them. Sognefjord runs 205 km inland.

question: Beneath Vietnam's jungle hides a cave called Son Doong — so big a 40-story skyscraper would fit inside, with clouds forming under its own roof. What kind of rock holds this giant cave?
choices: Limestone, slowly hollowed out by a river running through it for millions of years
Granite, broken open along cracks by water that froze and split the rock
Sandstone, sandblasted by river water carrying coarse grit through the gap
Basalt, drained out as a hollow tube when long-ago lava ran through it
answer: Limestone, slowly hollowed out by a river running through it for millions of years
context: Son Doong cave in Quang Binh, Vietnam, is among the world's largest cave passages. A river dissolved limestone for ~3 million years. Some chambers are so big they have their own clouds and jungle inside.

question: Off the coast of Scotland, an entire island called Staffa is made of stone columns standing in tidy rows. Inside Fingal's Cave the columns rise like organ pipes. Why columns at all?
choices: Lava cooled slowly and contracted, cracking into tidy six-sided columns
Sea waves wore the cliff away between harder vertical rock seams of basalt
Roman builders quarried the rock long ago and left the columns standing
Ancient earthquakes shook the island until cracks formed in straight lines
answer: Lava cooled slowly and contracted, cracking into tidy six-sided columns
context: Fingal's Cave (Staffa, Inner Hebrides) shows columnar jointing in basalt — same physics as the Giant's Causeway across the sea in Ireland. Both come from the same lava field ~60 million years ago.

question: In Mexico's Naica Mine, deep underground in Chihuahua, miners broke into a cave full of clear crystals as long as a city bus. Workers had to wear cooling suits inside. What mineral are the crystals?
choices: Selenite, a clear form of gypsum that grew slowly in warm mineral water
Quartz, the hard rocky crystal that makes up most beach sand worldwide
Diamond, the hardest of natural minerals, formed deep below in old times
Ruby, the red corundum crystal famous in jewelry and watch parts today
answer: Selenite, a clear form of gypsum that grew slowly in warm mineral water
context: The Cave of Crystals at Naica holds selenite (gypsum) crystals up to 11 m long. Warm mineral water sat at ~58°C for ~500,000 years; the slow steady conditions grew crystals to incredible size. The cave is closed now.

question: The Atacama desert in northern Chile is so dry that some weather stations have never recorded rain. Bone-dry mummies older than the Egyptian ones still rest there. Why is Atacama so extra-dry?
choices: Tall Andes mountains block all rain from one side; cold ocean blocks it from the other
It sits at the exact pole of cold, so any moisture there freezes before it can fall
It is the deepest desert valley on Earth, and rain rises off it before it lands
An invisible wall of warm air over the desert traps moisture above and pulls it away
answer: Tall Andes mountains block all rain from one side; cold ocean blocks it from the other
context: Atacama is squeezed between the Andes (blocking Atlantic moisture) and the cold Humboldt Current (cooling Pacific air so it can't carry rain inland). Some spots may have gone centuries without rain.

question: On the lonely volcanic island of Surtsey south of Iceland, scientists watched an entire island rise out of the sea in one year in 1963. How did the island appear so fast?
choices: Hot magma from below the seafloor erupted underwater and stacked rock above the waves
Hot water rising in a vent cooked the seabed into hard rock that pushed upward
Sea ice scraped sediment together off the floor and packed it into a small island
Fish bones and sand piled around an underwater rock formed a reef that grew up
answer: Hot magma from below the seafloor erupted underwater and stacked rock above the waves
context: Surtsey appeared November 14, 1963, when a submarine eruption built basalt above sea level. The island is a protected science laboratory; only researchers may land. It is slowly being eroded by Atlantic waves.

question: In the dry red center of Australia near Yulara, one huge red rock named Uluru rises 348 m straight up from a flat plain. Kids and elders both call it a sacred place. What kind of rock is Uluru?
choices: Sandstone, hard old layers tilted nearly vertical and worn smooth around them
Granite, a hard igneous rock that cooled deep below and was uncovered
Limestone, made from old shellbeds packed and lifted up out of a sea
Basalt, a dark lava rock left over from an ancient buried volcano
answer: Sandstone, hard old layers tilted nearly vertical and worn smooth around them
context: Uluru (Ayers Rock) is arkose sandstone, ~550 million years old. Its layers stand nearly vertical because the entire block was tilted ~90°; what looks like horizontal weathering banding is actually the original sediment layering on end.

question: Around the edges of Russia and Alaska, the ground is permanently frozen — sometimes hundreds of meters deep. Houses must stand on stilts or they sink. Why must houses sit on stilts?
choices: Heat from the house would melt the frozen ground and the house would tilt and sink
Wild winds at ground level need open space below to blow under and miss the walls
Spring floods rise high every year and would soak the floors of low buildings
Small earthquakes shake the frozen ground often and stilts let buildings sway safely
answer: Heat from the house would melt the frozen ground and the house would tilt and sink
context: Permafrost is rock-hard until heat reaches it. A house built on it melts the upper layer; the building sinks lopsided. Stilts keep the floor up; cold air below preserves the frozen ground.

question: Argentina's Perito Moreno glacier in Patagonia is one of the few ice rivers on Earth still advancing. Big chunks fall off the front into a lake with a boom. What is the falling-off called?
choices: Calving — when chunks of ice break off a glacier's front into water below
Plowing — when a glacier scrapes rocks and dirt forward as it advances
Crevassing — when deep cracks open in the surface of a moving ice sheet
Sluicing — when meltwater carves long channels down a glacier's edge
answer: Calving — when chunks of ice break off a glacier's front into water below
context: Perito Moreno (Los Glaciares National Park, Argentina) advances ~2 m/day. When it crosses Lago Argentino it dams an arm; pressure builds, then a tunnel breaks through and ice arches collapse spectacularly every few years.

question: Off England's southwest coast cliffs hold ammonites — coiled stone shells of long-extinct sea animals. A girl named Mary Anning sold them from her beach shop. What does an ammonite tell us?
choices: That this dry rocky cliff was once the floor of a warm shallow sea
That a tropical jungle once grew on the spot where the cliff now stands
That a hot desert once covered the land before the cliff slowly rose
That a deep glacier once carved out the cliff during the last ice age
answer: That this dry rocky cliff was once the floor of a warm shallow sea
context: Mary Anning (1799-1847) of Lyme Regis sold fossils from the Jurassic cliffs of Dorset, making major discoveries (the first ichthyosaur, plesiosaur). Ammonites lived in warm shallow seas; finding their fossils inland marks where seas once were.

question: In the high Atacama desert of Chile, geysers at El Tatio shoot steam at sunrise from holes in bare ground. White crust around each vent is built by minerals. Why do they only burst at dawn?
choices: Cold morning air condenses steam from underground vents into visible white columns
Magma below pulses just before sunrise on a steady daily geological cycle
Sunlight heats the rock instantly each morning, making it shoot steam up at once
Earth's daily rotation pulls water down each night and pushes it up at dawn
answer: Cold morning air condenses steam from underground vents into visible white columns
context: El Tatio sits at ~4,300 m. The geysers vent year-round, but cold pre-dawn air (-15°C) condenses the steam into the tall white plumes that draw tourists. By midday the steam is invisible.

question: Where Africa is slowly splitting in two, a stripe of land from Mozambique through Kenya to Ethiopia is dotted with deep lakes, hot springs, and volcanoes. What is this stripe called?
choices: The Great Rift Valley — where two tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart
The African Trench — a long deep cut left where two plates collided long ago
The Equator Belt — where Africa straddles the line and weather is always wet
The Sahel Strip — the dry edge of the Sahara where farming barely works
answer: The Great Rift Valley — where two tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart
context: The East African Rift is splitting the continent. In a few million years the Horn of Africa will separate from the mainland and a new ocean basin will fill the gap. Olduvai Gorge, Mt Kilimanjaro, Lake Victoria, Mt Kenya all sit in or near the rift.

question: On the Pacific island of Tonga in 2022, an underwater volcano blew so hard the wave rang the Earth. People in California felt small surges from the blast. What is such a giant ocean wave called?
choices: A tsunami — a huge fast water wave kicked up by a quake, blast, or landslide
A typhoon — a strong tropical storm whose winds push water onto the shore
A whirlpool — a swirling sea current that pulls floating things downward
A riptide — a current pulling away from the beach that swims people out
answer: A tsunami — a huge fast water wave kicked up by a quake, blast, or landslide
context: The Hunga Tonga eruption (Jan 15, 2022) sent tsunamis across the Pacific, ash 58 km up into the mesosphere, and shock waves around the planet twice. Tsunami means 'harbor wave' in Japanese.

question: The Black Hills of South Dakota stand alone on the plains. The famous faces on Mt Rushmore are carved into a special hard rock. What kind of rock holds those four presidents?
choices: Granite — slow-cooled deep magma that hardened into a strong even crystal mix
Sandstone — old sand layers packed and cemented into a flaky brown rock
Limestone — old shells packed into a chalky white rock that dissolves in rain
Shale — fine mud packed flat into a layer that splits along its old bed lines
answer: Granite — slow-cooled deep magma that hardened into a strong even crystal mix
context: Mt Rushmore is granite — durable enough to hold detail for thousands of years and resist freeze-thaw. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum chose it deliberately. Granite erodes only about 1 inch per 10,000 years.

question: Most kids think of glaciers as white ice. On Argentina's Perito Moreno and other glaciers the inside ice glows bright sky blue when sun shines through it. Why is glacier ice blue?
choices: Dense ice absorbs warm reds and yellows from sunlight, letting blue light pass through
Tiny algae living in the ice color the inner layers a brilliant pale blue
Dissolved copper minerals in old snow gradually tint the buried ice blue
Sky reflects off the smooth ice surface and the underlayers pick up the color
answer: Dense ice absorbs warm reds and yellows from sunlight, letting blue light pass through
context: Glacier ice is dense and bubble-free in its deep layers. Long red wavelengths get absorbed; only short blue ones pass through and reflect. Pile snow is white because air bubbles scatter all colors equally.

question: In the Cape Verde islands a volcano named Pico do Fogo rises out of the Atlantic west of Senegal. People live and farm grapes inside its old caldera. Why farm inside a volcano?
choices: Volcanic ash makes some of the most fertile soil on Earth for crops
The caldera floor is the only spot on the island flat enough to plow
Old lava blocks make windbreaks that shield the crops from coastal storms
Hot springs inside the caldera keep the grapevines from freezing at night
answer: Volcanic ash makes some of the most fertile soil on Earth for crops
context: Volcanic soils are rich in minerals (potassium, phosphorus, magnesium). Many famous wine regions (Sicily near Etna, Santorini, Mendoza) sit on volcanic ground. Fogo's eruptions in 1995 and 2014 forced villages to rebuild.

question: Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming has more hot springs and geysers than the rest of the world combined. Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes. Why this much hot water in one place?
choices: A giant blob of hot rock sits close below the surface, heating groundwater fast
The park sits where five rivers meet, and friction from flowing water heats the ground
Old coal seams buried below the park are slowly burning and warming the rocks
Sunshine at the park's high altitude warms the rocks far more than at sea level
answer: A giant blob of hot rock sits close below the surface, heating groundwater fast
context: Yellowstone sits over a continental hotspot — a plume of hot mantle rock close to the surface. Groundwater seeps down, gets superheated, returns as geysers and hot springs. The park has ~10,000 hydrothermal features.

question: The Pacific Ring of Fire is a horseshoe-shaped zone tracing the rim of the Pacific Ocean. Why do so many of Earth's volcanoes and earthquakes happen along this single curve?
choices: The Pacific plate is sinking under surrounding plates; friction and melting drive the volcanism
Earth's crust is thinnest under the Pacific, so magma escapes easily anywhere along the ocean's edge
Ocean weight on the seafloor presses the crust down, cracking the rim and releasing pressure outward
The Pacific is the planet's oldest ocean basin, so its rim has had the longest time to develop weak zones
answer: The Pacific plate is sinking under surrounding plates; friction and melting drive the volcanism
context: The Ring of Fire holds about 75% of active volcanoes and 90% of earthquakes. It traces subduction zones where the Pacific plate dives under surrounding plates. Friction melts rock; the melt rises as volcanoes.

question: The Himalaya mountains in Asia rise about 1 cm per year — still growing. The range holds Earth's tallest peaks; Mt Everest sits at 8,849 m on the Nepal-Tibet border. What collision is pushing the Himalaya skyward?
choices: The Indian plate is ramming northward into the Eurasian plate, crumpling crust upward
A mantle plume under Tibet is pushing the surface above it into a high plateau
The Pacific plate's western edge is buckling Asia where it crashes underneath
Wind and rain over millions of years stacked Asian sediment into the high range
answer: The Indian plate is ramming northward into the Eurasian plate, crumpling crust upward
context: India broke from Africa ~140 mya, drifted north, and slammed into Asia ~50 mya. The collision continues at ~5 cm/year. Tibet sits ~5,000 m above sea level — thickest crust on Earth. The Himalaya block monsoon rains, drying out central Asia.

question: Iceland sits directly on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the North American and Eurasian plates are spreading apart. The country gains about 2 cm of width per year. What does this mean for Iceland's volcanism?
choices: Magma rises into the spreading gap continuously; Iceland has frequent eruptions from many vents
Once-active volcanoes are slowly cooling because new crust forms between them and stops eruptions
Eruptions happen only at the island's center where the two plates meet underground
Volcanic activity has shifted offshore; mainland Iceland is now mostly geologically quiet
answer: Magma rises into the spreading gap continuously; Iceland has frequent eruptions from many vents
context: Iceland is one of the few places where a mid-ocean ridge surfaces. New basalt erupts as plates pull apart — about 30 active volcanic systems on the island. Eyjafjallajökull (2010) and Fagradalsfjall (2021-23) are recent examples.

question: On Sicily in the Mediterranean, Mt Etna is Europe's most active volcano. Local farms grow grapes and pistachios on its lower slopes despite frequent eruptions. Why farm under a working volcano?
choices: Volcanic ash weathers into mineral-rich soil; the crops grow faster and richer than elsewhere on Sicily
Frequent eruptions sterilize the soil of plant diseases that ruin crops in unburned regions
Heat from below keeps the soil at growing temperature year-round, extending the harvest season
Lava flows divert rainwater into natural irrigation channels that water the vineyards for free
answer: Volcanic ash weathers into mineral-rich soil; the crops grow faster and richer than elsewhere on Sicily
context: Etna's slopes (Sicily, ~3,357 m) are among Italy's richest agricultural regions. Volcanic ash supplies potassium, phosphorus, and trace minerals. The Nerello Mascalese grape produces sought-after Etna Rosso wine on its eastern slopes.

question: The Grand Canyon in Arizona is about 1.8 km deep and 446 km long. Africa's Blue Nile gorge is roughly 1.6 km deep and 800 km long. Both are river canyons, but the Grand Canyon's age is much greater. What carved the Grand Canyon so deep?
choices: The Colorado River cutting downward while the Colorado Plateau itself rose under it
An ancient inland sea draining westward in one catastrophic flood across the plateau
Glaciers scouring out a wide canyon, then a small river running down the bottom later
An earthquake fault dropping the canyon floor while the river kept its flat surface course
answer: The Colorado River cutting downward while the Colorado Plateau itself rose under it
context: The Grand Canyon (Arizona) cuts ~1.8 km into rock as old as 1.8 billion years. The Colorado Plateau uplifted slowly; the river kept pace by cutting down. Canyons need either rapid uplift, drop in sea level, or steepening of a river's path.

question: 'Orogeny' is the word for the slow building of a mountain range. The Appalachian orogeny in eastern North America ran from ~480 to 250 million years ago, once rivaling the Himalaya in height. Why are the Appalachians so much lower today?
choices: Hundreds of millions of years of erosion by rain, rivers, and freeze-thaw wore them down
An ancient asteroid impact in the eastern US flattened the high peaks in one geological event
The Atlantic Ocean rising over the past million years has slowly submerged the highest summits
Glaciers from the last Ice Age ground them flat from northern Maine all the way south to Georgia
answer: Hundreds of millions of years of erosion by rain, rivers, and freeze-thaw wore them down
context: The Appalachians formed in three major orogenies (Taconic, Acadian, Alleghanian) ending ~250 mya when Pangaea assembled. Erosion since then has lowered them from Himalayan-scale to today's gentle range. Mt Mitchell tops out at 2,037 m.

question: In southern Utah a fragile sandstone arch named Delicate Arch stands free in the open desert. Hundreds of similar arches dot the same park. Why so many natural arches in this one place?
choices: Thick sandstone over a layer of salt; the salt shifts and cracks the sandstone into fins that wear into arches
An ancient inland sea retreating drilled holes through the sandstone with whirlpool currents
Frequent earthquakes have cracked open Utah's sandstone in arch-shaped fracture patterns
Wind-blown sand has carved each arch by sandblasting around their bases over millions of years
answer: Thick sandstone over a layer of salt; the salt shifts and cracks the sandstone into fins that wear into arches
context: Arches National Park sits on the Paradox Basin. A buried salt layer rises like dough as the rocks above shift, fracturing sandstone into parallel fins. Weathering of the fins opens windows that grow into arches. Most arches collapse eventually (Wall Arch fell in 2008).

question: The Dead Sea between Jordan and Israel is the lowest land point on Earth at about 430 m below sea level. People float so easily that swimming is almost impossible. What makes the water so dense?
choices: Salt content around 10 times the ocean's; the dense brine lifts a person almost effortlessly
Dissolved minerals from nearby hot springs make the water heavier than ordinary seawater
Geologically old water has slowly thickened over time, holding more dissolved material than seas
Cold deep water from below the surface mixes upward and gives the sea its unusual density
answer: Salt content around 10 times the ocean's; the dense brine lifts a person almost effortlessly
context: The Dead Sea is ~34% salinity (Atlantic is ~3.5%). Water flows in but only evaporates out, concentrating salts and minerals. The high density makes humans naturally buoyant — newspaper photos of floating readers are easy to stage.

question: An igneous rock called pumice is so full of tiny air bubbles that it floats on water. After the 2022 Tonga eruption a raft of pumice the size of Manhattan drifted across the Pacific Ocean. How does pumice form bubbly?
choices: Dissolved gases in magma expand suddenly when pressure drops in a violent eruption
Air mixed into hot lava as it fell down a volcano's slope and trapped bubbles inside
Seawater met hot lava on impact and rapidly boiled into bubbles within the cooling rock
Rain falling into a hot lava flow boiled instantly and left bubble holes in the new rock
answer: Dissolved gases in magma expand suddenly when pressure drops in a violent eruption
context: Pumice forms when frothy magma — rich in dissolved gas under pressure — erupts violently. Gas expansion is so fast the lava cools into a foam-like rock before bubbles escape. Pumice rafts from 1883 Krakatoa drifted for years and ferried marine life across oceans.

question: The San Andreas Fault in California runs about 1,200 km from the Salton Sea to north of San Francisco. Los Angeles and San Francisco sit on opposite sides. Why does California get so many earthquakes along this single line?
choices: Two tectonic plates are sliding past each other; built-up friction releases as sudden quakes
A subduction zone runs along it and the Pacific plate dives under California releasing energy
The fault marks where an old continental rift is slowly pulling California into two pieces
It is a deep volcanic fissure connecting many magma chambers that pulse and shake the rock
answer: Two tectonic plates are sliding past each other; built-up friction releases as sudden quakes
context: The San Andreas is a transform boundary — the Pacific plate slides northwest past the North American plate at ~5 cm/year. In ~16 million years Los Angeles will be next to San Francisco. The 1906 San Francisco quake slipped ~6 m in seconds.

question: In Tanzania near the Olduvai Gorge stands Ol Doinyo Lengai — the only active volcano on Earth that erupts black lava that turns chalky white within days. What unusual chemistry produces this lava?
choices: Carbonatite — lava rich in sodium carbonate that cools cool, runs fast, and weathers quickly to white
Obsidian — black glassy lava that breaks apart into chips of clear and white shards as it cools
Basalt — common dark lava that loses its iron oxide tint quickly when exposed to dry desert air
Andesite — sticky gray lava that turns lighter as the silica content settles out near the surface
answer: Carbonatite — lava rich in sodium carbonate that cools cool, runs fast, and weathers quickly to white
context: Ol Doinyo Lengai ('Mountain of God' in Maasai) erupts natrocarbonatite lava at just ~540°C — half the temperature of most lava. It hardens black, then absorbs water and turns white within hours-to-days. The Maasai consider the volcano sacred.

question: Mt Fuji in Japan and Mt St Helens in Washington are both stratovolcanoes — cone-shaped peaks built up by layers of lava and ash. Both sit on the Pacific Ring of Fire. What kind of plate boundary creates such cone-shaped peaks?
choices: Subduction zones — where an ocean plate dives under a continental plate, melting and rising as sticky lava
Spreading ridges — where two plates pull apart and runny lava flows out building tall stacked cones
Transform faults — where two plates slide past each other and friction creates magma deep below
Continental collisions — where two land plates ram each other and folded crust builds the cones
answer: Subduction zones — where an ocean plate dives under a continental plate, melting and rising as sticky lava
context: Stratovolcanoes form above subduction zones where wet sinking plates release water that melts rock. The melt is silica-rich, sticky, and explosive — building steep cones from alternating lava and ash. Examples: Fuji, St Helens, Vesuvius, Pinatubo, Mt Rainier.

question: In southwest Africa the Namib desert ends at the Atlantic in a wall of orange sand dunes hundreds of meters tall. The dunes have stood roughly where they are for ~5 million years. Why hasn't the Atlantic washed them away?
choices: The cold Benguela Current cools coastal air, blocking rain; without river outflow the sand keeps stacking
Wind blows steadily inland from the sea, packing the dunes hard against an inland mountain range
Underground bedrock just below the sand holds the dunes in place against ocean wave erosion
Dunes regenerate quickly from sand swept along the coast by the Benguela ocean current itself
answer: The cold Benguela Current cools coastal air, blocking rain; without river outflow the sand keeps stacking
context: The Namib is fed by sand the Orange River carries to the sea; the Benguela Current sweeps it north along the coast. Cold-current coastal deserts (Namib, Atacama, Baja California) get almost no rain — air over cold water can't carry much moisture inland.

question: Slovenia's Postojna Cave system holds an animal called the olm — a pale, eyeless salamander that lives only in underground rivers. It can survive a decade without eating. What kind of rock forms these cave-rich karst landscapes?
choices: Limestone — slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves it underground, hollowing out cave networks
Sandstone — rivers carry away loose sand grains over millions of years to leave caves behind
Granite — water freezing and thawing in cracks splits the rock and forms underground galleries
Basalt — drained-out lava tubes leave long hollow caves under old volcanic flow fields
answer: Limestone — slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves it underground, hollowing out cave networks
context: Karst landscapes (Slovenia's term, kras, gave the name) form where carbonate rock — usually limestone — dissolves in mildly acidic groundwater. Postojna's system runs over 24 km. The olm (Proteus anguinus) has lived in lightless caves for so long it lost both pigment and eyes.

question: The Atacama and the Gobi are both cold deserts that get little rain. The Atacama in Chile is squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific. The Gobi in Mongolia sits north of the Himalaya. What blocks the Gobi from rain?
choices: The Himalaya wall stops monsoon rains from reaching Mongolia; rain falls south of the range
Mongolia is too far north for atmospheric moisture; only polar air masses reach the Gobi
Cold winds from Siberia dry out the air before any moisture from the south can reach it
The Pacific Ocean is so distant from Mongolia that no oceanic moisture can travel inland that far
answer: The Himalaya wall stops monsoon rains from reaching Mongolia; rain falls south of the range
context: The Himalaya cast a rain shadow over the Tibetan Plateau and the Gobi beyond. Indian Ocean monsoon moisture dumps rain on Bangladesh, Nepal, and the Indian plains. By the time air crosses the range it is wrung dry. Cherrapunji (south side) gets ~11,000 mm/year; Lhasa (north side) gets ~430 mm.

question: Off the southwest coast of New Zealand a chain of fjords called Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound cut deep inland from the Tasman Sea. Glaciers carved them during ice ages. Why does the water look almost black?
choices: Tannin-stained freshwater from rainforest streams sits on top of denser saltwater below
Volcanic mud from ancient eruptions still tints the sound waters dark across the surface
Deep shadows from steep cliff walls keep sunlight off the surface most of the daylight hours
Underwater plant life is so thick it covers the sound waters in a dark green cloak
answer: Tannin-stained freshwater from rainforest streams sits on top of denser saltwater below
context: Milford and Doubtful Sounds in Fiordland have a freshwater layer 1-10 m thick — heavy rainforest runoff (Milford gets ~7,000 mm/year) sits on saltwater. The freshwater carries plant tannins that stain it dark, mimicking deep water and letting deep-sea creatures live shallow.

question: Crater Lake in Oregon sits inside a perfect bowl 8 km wide. The water is stunningly blue. The bowl was once a tall mountain that vanished in a single eruption 7,700 years ago. What name do geologists give such a bowl?
choices: A caldera — formed when a magma chamber emptied and the volcano's roof collapsed inward
A crater — formed by the explosion at the throat of a volcano during an eruption above ground
A maar — formed by a single steam blast where groundwater met rising magma near the surface
A cirque — formed by glacier ice scooping a round bowl out of a mountain's high side
answer: A caldera — formed when a magma chamber emptied and the volcano's roof collapsed inward
context: Mt Mazama erupted ~7,700 years ago, ejecting ~50 km3 of magma. The emptied chamber collapsed, leaving a 1,200 m deep caldera that filled with rain and snow. Klamath oral tradition records the eruption. Crater Lake is the US's deepest lake (594 m).

question: In Hawaii the Big Island grows by lava flow each year as Kilauea erupts. Kilauea's lava is runny and fast; Mt St Helens in Washington blew up explosively in 1980. What chemistry makes these volcanoes behave so differently?
choices: Silica content — Hawaiian basalt is low-silica and runny, while St Helens magma is silica-rich and sticky
Iron content — Hawaiian magma is iron-rich and runs easy, while St Helens magma is iron-poor and explosive
Water content — Hawaiian magma is wet and quiet, while St Helens magma is dry and blows out hard
Temperature — Hawaiian magma is cool and creeps, while St Helens magma is much hotter and bursts out
answer: Silica content — Hawaiian basalt is low-silica and runny, while St Helens magma is silica-rich and sticky
context: Magma viscosity tracks silica content. Basalt (~50% silica) flows easily, so gases escape gently — Hawaii. Andesite/dacite (60-70% silica) is sticky; gas builds pressure until it erupts explosively — Mt St Helens, Pinatubo, Vesuvius.

question: Climbing Mt Kilimanjaro in Tanzania feels like walking from equator to Arctic — rainforest at base, cloud forest higher, alpine grass above, glacier on top. What name fits this stacking pattern of climate zones up a slope?
choices: Altitudinal zonation — climate and thus vegetation bands change with elevation up a mountain's slope
Latitudinal zonation — climate bands change as one moves north or south away from the equator
Tropical inversion — a temperate climate sits above a tropical zone on certain rare mountains
Trophic stacking — predators living in one band feed on prey in the band just below them
answer: Altitudinal zonation — climate and thus vegetation bands change with elevation up a mountain's slope
context: Kilimanjaro (5,895 m, Tanzania) crosses ~5 climate zones in ~25 km of trail. Each ~1,000 m gain is roughly equivalent to 1,000 km of latitude shift. Alexander von Humboldt documented this on Mt Chimborazo (Ecuador) in 1802, founding modern biogeography.

question: On a Russian peninsula sticking into the Pacific, the Kamchatka region holds 29 active volcanoes in a single line. Wild brown bears outnumber people in some districts. What plate boundary lines them up like that?
choices: The Pacific plate dives under Kamchatka in a subduction zone, and rising melt builds a volcano chain
A mantle plume under Kamchatka melts the crust, and the plate slides over it forming the chain
Two plates pull apart along Kamchatka and lava rises straight up into a clean north-south line
An ancient meteor strike chain dropped impacts along the peninsula and each became a volcano
answer: The Pacific plate dives under Kamchatka in a subduction zone, and rising melt builds a volcano chain
context: Kamchatka sits on a subduction zone where the Pacific plate slides under the Okhotsk plate at ~8 cm/year. Klyuchevskaya (4,750 m) is one of Eurasia's tallest active volcanoes. UNESCO calls Kamchatka one of the world's most outstanding volcanic regions.

question: Along the Mediterranean coast of Israel and Lebanon are sea caves so polished smooth that boats can glide inside. The Rosh HaNikra grottoes on Israel's northern border show off this work. How do sea caves form along a coast?
choices: Waves attack weak cracks in the cliff for thousands of years, widening them into deep open caves
Underground rivers exit at the cliff face and have carved out long horizontal cave openings
Ancient buried glaciers melted out, leaving long horizontal tunnels at the modern shoreline
Earthquakes cracked the cliff open and the sea later carved the cracks into smooth caves
answer: Waves attack weak cracks in the cliff for thousands of years, widening them into deep open caves
context: Sea caves form by hydraulic action — waves compress air in cliff cracks, slowly enlarging them. Rosh HaNikra's chalk cliffs at the Israel-Lebanon border show 100 m of grotto tunnels carved over millennia. Common worldwide where wave-exposed cliffs hold soft rock.

question: On Stromboli north of Sicily, a small volcano has erupted little blasts of glowing rock every 10-20 minutes for over 2,000 years. Sailors used it as a natural lighthouse. Why steady mild eruptions instead of long quiet then big blast?
choices: Gas bubbles rise through low-viscosity magma and burst at the top every few minutes
A small magma chamber refills quickly enough to release pressure in many small pulses
Steady seawater leaking into the vent boils, blowing small puffs at regular intervals
Trade winds shake the cone, jarring loose enough rock to trigger frequent small spillover
answer: Gas bubbles rise through low-viscosity magma and burst at the top every few minutes
context: Stromboli's mildly explosive eruption style — short bursts of glowing scoria — became the type for 'Strombolian' volcanic activity. Low-silica magma lets gas bubbles rise and burst at the surface. Pliny the Elder noted the steady fireworks ~1,900 years ago.

question: The Andes and Rockies both run north-south. The Andes formed by oceanic subduction at the coast; modern Rockies formed when ocean crust slid almost flat under North America. How does flat subduction differ from steeper subduction?
choices: Mountain building happens hundreds of km inland instead of right at the coast as in steeper cases
Mountain building happens right at the coast more sharply than usual instead of farther inland
Volcanoes form right at the trench in long lines instead of in arcs a few hundred km inland
Crust melting stops entirely so no mountains form and a flat low plateau remains in its place
answer: Mountain building happens hundreds of km inland instead of right at the coast as in steeper cases
context: The Laramide orogeny (~80-35 mya) built the modern Rockies far inland — the Farallon plate slid almost flat under western North America, pushing crust up across Wyoming and Colorado. Normal subduction (Andes today) builds coastal mountain arcs with active volcanoes.

question: Brazil's Pao de Acucar (Sugarloaf Mountain) and similar bare granite domes around Rio de Janeiro rise straight out of the jungle without soil or trees. They are made of granite that cooled deep underground. Why does the surface granite look so smooth and round?
choices: Exfoliation — layers of granite flake off in curved sheets as pressure from above is lost
Wind sandblasting — offshore winds blew dust for millions of years and polished the granite round
Volcanic heating — magma from below smoothed the granite surface in past geological epochs
Acid weathering — coastal-rainforest rain slowly etched and rounded the granite into domes
answer: Exfoliation — layers of granite flake off in curved sheets as pressure from above is lost
context: Sugarloaf Mountain (Rio, Brazil) and Yosemite's Half Dome (California) and Stone Mountain (Georgia) all show exfoliation. Buried granite was under huge pressure; when erosion removes the cover, the rock expands and sheds curved sheets — like an onion peeling.

question: In Saskatchewan, a buried meteor impact crater 39 km wide named Carswell shows up only as a faint ring on geologic maps. Most ancient impact craters look like nothing from ground level. Why do they erode so completely?
choices: Earth's surface is constantly remade by weathering, plate motion, and erosion that wipes out craters
Most meteorite impacts happen at sea, so the crater records sink to the seabed and dissolve away
Earth's atmosphere absorbs most meteorites before they can dig deep craters in the surface
Volcanic activity buries every impact crater under fresh lava within a few million years
answer: Earth's surface is constantly remade by weathering, plate motion, and erosion that wipes out craters
context: Earth's active surface (erosion, tectonics, volcanism, oceans) erases craters fast in geological time. The Moon — no atmosphere, no plates, no weather — preserves billions of years of impacts. Earth has ~200 known craters; the Moon has millions.

question: In southwest Iceland a dramatic crack in the ground called Silfra holds water so clear that divers can see 100 m through it. The crack runs along the meeting of two tectonic plates. Why is the water inside so unusually clear?
choices: Glacial meltwater filters through porous lava for decades before reaching the crack
Cold polar air keeps algae and plankton growth too slow to cloud the water there
Strong tides flush silt out of the crack faster than runoff can carry new mud in
Volcanic salts in the water bond to silt and pull it out of suspension into the floor
answer: Glacial meltwater filters through porous lava for decades before reaching the crack
context: Silfra is filled by water from the Langjökull glacier that filters slowly through porous basalt for 30-100 years before emerging in the crack. The filtration removes essentially all particles; visibility reaches 100+ m. The crack itself is between the North American and Eurasian plates.

question: Australia's Twelve Apostles — tall limestone sea stacks lining the coast of Victoria — are still being chipped down by ocean waves. Several have collapsed in living memory. What erosion process creates such isolated sea stacks?
choices: Waves erode cliff caves into arches; arches collapse, leaving the outer pillars as stacks
Volcanic spires were left standing as softer surrounding rock washed into the Southern Ocean
Underwater earthquakes broke a continuous cliff into pieces with deep cracks between each stack
Glaciers carved the cliffs into vertical columns during the last Ice Age along the Victoria coast
answer: Waves erode cliff caves into arches; arches collapse, leaving the outer pillars as stacks
context: Coastal erosion sequence: cliff → cave (wave attack on weak rock) → arch (caves meet through a headland) → stack (arch collapses) → stump (stack erodes). The Twelve Apostles are at stack stage; one fell in 2005, another in 2009.

question: Off Madagascar's east coast, a coral atoll called Aldabra holds the world's second-largest population of giant tortoises. The atoll itself is a fossilized coral reef risen out of the ocean. How does a ring-shaped atoll form?
choices: Coral grew around a volcanic island; the volcano sank, leaving the reef as a ring
Storms repeatedly pile coral sand into ring-shaped beaches above a shallow bank
Two tectonic plates pull apart underwater and coral colonizes the rim of the resulting gap
A meteor crater in the seafloor was colonized by coral that grew up along the round rim
answer: Coral grew around a volcanic island; the volcano sank, leaving the reef as a ring
context: Darwin proposed the atoll-formation theory in 1842. Coral grows up as a volcanic island subsides; eventually the cone sinks below sea level, leaving a ring (atoll) around an inner lagoon. Bikini, Eniwetok, Tuvalu, and the Maldives all formed this way.

question: Across northern Canada, Finland, and Russia the land is dotted with thousands of round lakes. Some are nearly perfect circles. They didn't form from impacts. Why does this region have so many round lakes?
choices: Glaciers from the last Ice Age plucked round chunks of bedrock loose, leaving round basins
Permafrost melt creates round pools called thermokarst lakes when frozen ground sags down
Heavy snow loads pressed round depressions into soft soil for thousands of winters in a row
Cold tundra winds slowly carved out round hollows from sandy soil over many millennia
answer: Glaciers from the last Ice Age plucked round chunks of bedrock loose, leaving round basins
context: Both glacial plucking AND thermokarst contribute. Glacial kettles form when blocks of buried ice melt and the ground above sinks. Thermokarst lakes form when permafrost thaws unevenly. Boreal landscapes (Canada, Finland, Siberia) hold millions of these lakes — among the world's largest freshwater reserves.

question: Diamond and graphite are both made entirely of carbon atoms. Diamond is the hardest natural substance; graphite is so soft it works as pencil lead. Where do diamonds form to become so different from soft graphite?
choices: Deep in Earth's mantle far down at very high pressure and temperature for billions of years
On the seafloor where pressure crushes graphite layers into diamond shape and form
Inside volcanoes near the surface where eruption forge heat crystallizes the carbon
On glaciers where extreme cold restructures carbon atoms into a hard crystal pattern
answer: Deep in Earth's mantle far down at very high pressure and temperature for billions of years
context: Diamonds crystallize at ~150-200 km depth, pressures ~5 GPa, temperatures ~1,000-1,300°C. Kimberlite pipes (volcanic intrusions, e.g., South Africa, Russia, Canada) carry them rapidly to the surface — slow rise lets diamond revert to graphite, the stable form at low pressure.

question: The Hawaiian island chain stretches northwest across the Pacific — Kauai (oldest, ~5 million years) to the Big Island (youngest, still erupting). The islands sit in the middle of a tectonic plate, not at a plate edge. What mechanism produces this age-gradient chain?
choices: A fixed mantle plume melts the crust above it; the Pacific plate slides over the plume, leaving a trail of volcanoes
A spreading ridge under the Pacific is laying down new crust island by island as it propagates northwestward
An old subduction zone is releasing magma in pulses, each pulse forming a new island on the same line
A series of meteor impacts spaced over millions of years happened to fall along a straight Pacific track
answer: A fixed mantle plume melts the crust above it; the Pacific plate slides over the plume, leaving a trail of volcanoes
context: The Hawaiian hotspot is a stationary mantle plume under the moving Pacific plate. The Big Island sits over the plume now; the plate carries old volcanoes (Maui, Oahu, Kauai) progressively northwest. Beyond Kauai the chain continues underwater as the Emperor Seamounts.

question: The Marianas Trench in the western Pacific reaches 11 km below sea level — Earth's deepest spot. The Atacama Trench off Chile reaches 8 km. Such trenches run parallel to volcanic island arcs and coasts. What plate-tectonic feature creates such deep ocean trenches?
choices: Subduction zones — one oceanic plate bends and dives steeply under another, forming a long V-shaped trench
Spreading ridges — two oceanic plates pull apart, leaving a deep central rift between fresh crust on each side
Transform faults — two plates slide past each other and pull the seabed downward in a long groove
Mantle convection cells — descending convection currents pull seafloor down into long narrow basins
answer: Subduction zones — one oceanic plate bends and dives steeply under another, forming a long V-shaped trench
context: Trenches mark subduction zones. The denser oceanic plate bends and dives at 30-60°, pulling the seafloor down. The Marianas (where the Pacific dives under the Philippine plate) reaches 11,034 m at the Challenger Deep. Trenches and volcanic arcs come paired.

question: South America's Andes formed largely from oceanic subduction at the coast; Asia's Himalaya formed from continental collision. Both ranges hold massive peaks. Why do continental collisions like India-Eurasia build thicker, taller ranges than ocean-continent subduction?
choices: Two continental plates can't sink against each other; both crumple upward into a doubled crust
Continental crust melts faster than oceanic crust, building taller volcanic cones from the molten rise
Collision releases more earthquake energy that physically lifts the surface higher than subduction
Faster plate speeds at continental collisions push the crust upward more sharply than at coasts
answer: Two continental plates can't sink against each other; both crumple upward into a doubled crust
context: Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct — when India hit Asia, neither sank. The crust thickened to ~70 km under Tibet (twice the global average), lifting the surface to the world's highest plateau. Subduction zones (Andes) lift one plate over the other; no doubling of crust.

question: The continents we know fit together like puzzle pieces around the Atlantic — Brazil's bulge slots into West Africa's hollow. Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that all continents once joined into a single landmass. What name did he give that ancient supercontinent?
choices: Pangaea — the Greek-named supercontinent that began breaking apart around 200 million years ago
Eurasia — the joined modern landmass of Europe and Asia, which Wegener also named in the same proposal
Gondwana — the southern half of the proposed supercontinent including Australia and Antarctica
Laurasia — the northern half of the supercontinent including North America and northern Europe
answer: Pangaea — the Greek-named supercontinent that began breaking apart around 200 million years ago
context: Wegener named the assembled continent Pangaea in 1912; the southern half Gondwana, the northern Laurasia. Geologists rejected it for decades — no mechanism. Mid-ocean spreading discoveries (1960s) confirmed the drift. Pangaea broke ~175 mya, opening the Atlantic.

question: Across central France lies the Massif Central. It holds dormant volcanoes — the Chaîne des Puys, a row of 80 young cones — but no plate boundary runs nearby. Geologists call such isolated continental volcanism by a specific name. What mechanism is at work?
choices: A continental hotspot — a deep mantle plume melting crust away from any plate edge
A buried subduction zone — an old plate boundary still releasing magma far underground
A spreading ridge inland — two pieces of European crust slowly pulling apart on land
A meteor-impact zone — a meteor strike chain whose craters reactivated into volcanoes
answer: A continental hotspot — a deep mantle plume melting crust away from any plate edge
context: The Chaîne des Puys (Auvergne, France) erupted as recently as 4040 BC. The Massif Central sits over a small mantle plume, like Yellowstone's. Continental hotspots also drive volcanism at Cameroon's Mt Cameroon and the Eifel district of Germany.

question: On Sicily, Mt Etna erupts often but mostly with quiet lava flows. Mt Vesuvius near Naples erupts rarely but catastrophically — its 79 AD blast buried Pompeii. Both sit near subduction zones in Italy. What chemical difference makes Vesuvius more explosive than Etna?
choices: Vesuvius's magma is more silica-rich, trapping gas; Etna's lower-silica magma lets gas escape calmly
Vesuvius has less water in its magma, building more pressure than Etna's wetter magma releases easily
Vesuvius's chamber sits deeper, building higher pressure before eruptions than Etna's shallower one
Vesuvius lacks the side vents that let Etna release magma without building to large blasts
answer: Vesuvius's magma is more silica-rich, trapping gas; Etna's lower-silica magma lets gas escape calmly
context: Vesuvius erupts more silica-rich tephrite-phonolite magma than Etna's relatively basaltic flows. Higher silica means stickier melt; dissolved gas can't escape until pressure exceeds the rock above. The 79 AD eruption killed ~16,000 in Pompeii and Herculaneum.

question: In southeast Utah a series of canyons holds Anasazi cliff dwellings tucked into alcoves — perfect overhangs in solid sandstone. The famous Mesa Verde dwellings in Colorado sit in similar alcoves. What weathering process carves such large alcoves into sandstone cliffs?
choices: Spalling from freeze-thaw cycles along bedding planes pops out slabs above a softer rock layer below
Wind erosion sandblasts the lower cliff face faster than the upper, hollowing out alcove shelters
Cliff-face dissolution by acidic rain etches the lower cliff faster than the upper near the cap
Ground vibration from earthquakes loosens lower rock that falls away faster than upper rock
answer: Spalling from freeze-thaw cycles along bedding planes pops out slabs above a softer rock layer below
context: Sandstone alcoves form where water seeping along a bedding plane (or above a less-permeable layer below) freezes, expands, and spalls flakes outward. Mesa Verde, Bandelier, Canyon de Chelly, and Betatakin alcoves all formed this way. Ancestral Puebloans built into them ~1100-1300 AD for the natural shelter.

question: Africa's Mt Kilimanjaro is a stratovolcano rising 5,895 m from a flat Tanzanian plain, near no plate boundary. Mt St Helens in Washington sits on the Ring of Fire above a subduction zone. Both are stratovolcanoes — yet only one is plate-edge-driven. What drives Kilimanjaro?
choices: The East African Rift — continental crust pulling apart releases magma far from any subduction edge
Continental hotspot — a mantle plume below Tanzania melts crust independently of plate boundaries
Buried subduction — an ancient slab still beneath East Africa releases magma to the surface
Meteor impact — Kilimanjaro grew in an old impact crater that opened up to mantle below
answer: The East African Rift — continental crust pulling apart releases magma far from any subduction edge
context: Kilimanjaro sits on the East African Rift system — Africa is slowly tearing in two along ~6,000 km of rift. The Somali plate is splitting from the larger Nubian plate. Rifting thins the crust and releases magma, building rift-zone volcanoes (Kilimanjaro, Kenya, Meru, Nyiragongo).

question: In northern Arizona near Flagstaff, a perfectly round, 1.2 km wide hole called Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater) sits in the desert. Around 50,000 years ago a chunk of iron from space struck at ~20 km/sec. Why is the crater so much wider than the meteorite that made it?
choices: Kinetic energy at impact vaporizes the meteor and excavates a crater ~10-20x the meteor's diameter
The shock wave from impact spreads outward, slowly enlarging the crater for thousands of years
Wind and water erosion over 50,000 years has gradually widened the original small impact crater
The meteor broke into fragments above the surface; each piece carved part of the wide crater rim
answer: Kinetic energy at impact vaporizes the meteor and excavates a crater ~10-20x the meteor's diameter
context: Meteor Crater's iron-nickel impactor was ~50 m across; the crater is 1,200 m wide and 170 m deep. Energy at hypervelocity impact vaporizes both the meteor and target rock; the explosion (~10 megatons TNT-equivalent) excavates the hole. The same scaling explains lunar craters.

question: Across the Andes, the Himalayas, the Alps, and the Rockies, dark folded stripes of rock cut horizontally through cliff faces — once-flat layers now bent into waves. Climbers call them folds. What kind of stress turns flat sedimentary layers into such folded patterns?
choices: Compression — squeezing stress from converging plates folds rock layers like a stack of paper pressed end-on
Tension — pulling stress from rifting stretches the rock layers thin and bends them into folds
Shear — sliding stress from transform faults twists rock layers into corkscrew patterns
Heat — magma intrusion melts rock layers slightly and rearranges them into folded shapes
answer: Compression — squeezing stress from converging plates folds rock layers like a stack of paper pressed end-on
context: Folding requires ductile compression — slow horizontal squeezing of layered rock at depth where pressure prevents brittle fracture. Anticlines fold up; synclines fold down. The Swiss Jura, the Appalachians, and the Zagros (Iran) show classic fold belts. Brittle compression near the surface produces thrust faults instead.

question: In the Karoo Basin of South Africa, a single rock layer holds fossils of a reptile called Lystrosaurus from ~250 million years ago. The same Lystrosaurus fossils show up in identical rock layers in India, Antarctica, and Australia. What does this scatter prove?
choices: Those continents were once joined as Gondwana; Lystrosaurus walked across before they drifted apart
Lystrosaurus could swim across oceans, colonizing new continents in a single radiation event
Birds carried Lystrosaurus seeds across the ancient Tethys Sea between separate continents
Lystrosaurus's bone shape was so common it evolved independently on each modern continent
answer: Those continents were once joined as Gondwana; Lystrosaurus walked across before they drifted apart
context: Lystrosaurus is a key continental-drift fossil. Its presence in South Africa, India, Antarctica, and Australia shows those landmasses were joined ~250 mya. Glossopteris plants and Mesosaurus reptiles show the same pattern — strong evidence Wegener's drift hypothesis was right.

question: On Earth's continents granite is everywhere — most mountain cores, most stable bedrock. On the ocean floor, granite is essentially absent; the seabed is basalt. Why this sharp continental-vs-oceanic chemical divide?
choices: Continental crust is silica-rich granite; oceanic crust forms by spreading-ridge basalt eruptions which are silica-poor
Granite is denser than basalt and sank to make continents; basalt floats so it pooled in ocean basins
Continental volcanoes erupted granite over millions of years; oceanic volcanoes erupted only basalt instead
Erosion concentrated granite on land while ocean waves washed it off the seabed into the trenches
answer: Continental crust is silica-rich granite; oceanic crust forms by spreading-ridge basalt eruptions which are silica-poor
context: Continental crust averages ~60% silica (granitic) and ~35 km thick; oceanic crust ~50% silica (basaltic) and ~7 km thick. Less-dense continental crust floats higher on the mantle (isostasy). New oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges from basaltic mantle melt; continental crust grows by complex magmatic-tectonic processes over billions of years.

question: At the meeting of the Indian and Eurasian plates the Himalaya holds 10 of the 14 peaks above 8,000 m on Earth. Geologists found fossils of sea creatures near Mt Everest's summit. What do those summit-area marine fossils prove?
choices: Rock now atop the Himalaya was once seafloor, lifted ~9 km by continental collision over millions of years
Ancient flying sea-birds carried mollusks high enough to leave shells on the mountain summit ridges
A sudden meteor impact splashed seafloor up onto the summit during the early Himalayan formation
Glaciers carried marine fossils from coastal beaches up to the summit during repeated Ice Ages
answer: Rock now atop the Himalaya was once seafloor, lifted ~9 km by continental collision over millions of years
context: Ammonites, sea-lily fossils, and other marine sediments at Himalaya summits prove the Tethys Sea floor was lifted by India's collision with Asia. The Tethys closed as India drifted north (~140-50 mya). The crumpled seabed now sits at >8,000 m, including parts of Everest's summit pyramid.

question: In western Iceland the Thingvellir valley splits along visible cracks where Earth's surface is pulling apart. Vikings held the world's first parliament here in 930 AD. Geologists call such a valley a rift. What two plate-boundary features distinguish a true rift?
choices: Spreading plates and a central down-dropped block — magma rises through it and the floor sinks between faults
Colliding plates and an uplifted central block — pressure pushes the floor up between two faults
Sliding plates and a twisted central block — the floor rotates between two horizontal faults
Subduction and a thinned central crust — the upper plate stretches above the descending slab below
answer: Spreading plates and a central down-dropped block — magma rises through it and the floor sinks between faults
context: A rift valley forms at divergent boundaries: two plates pull apart and a central graben drops between parallel normal faults. Magma may rise into the gap. Thingvellir (Iceland) and the East African Rift are textbook examples. The Vikings' Althing parliament met here from 930 AD.

question: The Black Hills of South Dakota and the Adirondacks of New York stand alone, far from plate boundaries. The Black Hills are uplifted Precambrian granite; the Adirondacks are a recent dome of similar old crust. What raises such interior dome ranges far from any plate boundary?
choices: Vertical uplift by mantle warming or far-field plate stress; the crust bulges into a broad dome without folding
Active rifting beneath the dome that has not yet broken through the surface to create a real rift valley
Buried hotspots still active that push the crust upward without erupting any lava to the surface above
Crustal thickening by erosion redistributing eroded material that piles up under the existing range
answer: Vertical uplift by mantle warming or far-field plate stress; the crust bulges into a broad dome without folding
context: Both the Black Hills and the Adirondacks are crustal domes — large broad uplifts of old crystalline rock without folding. Possible causes include mantle warming, far-field plate stresses, or isostatic rebound. The Adirondacks are still rising ~3 mm/year — geologically active, far from any plate boundary.

question: In Indonesia the Tambora volcano on Sumbawa erupted in 1815. Crops failed across Europe and New England the next year — 1816 was known as 'the year without a summer.' How did a single eruption in the southern hemisphere chill the northern world a year later?
choices: Sulfate aerosols from the eruption stayed in the stratosphere for years, reflecting sunlight back to space
Volcanic ash blocked sunlight directly across the Pacific and Atlantic for the whole 1816 growing season
Tambora's CO2 created a temporary greenhouse effect that disrupted normal weather patterns globally
Ash falling into the ocean cooled surface waters globally and changed currents that delivered heat
answer: Sulfate aerosols from the eruption stayed in the stratosphere for years, reflecting sunlight back to space
context: Tambora's 1815 eruption (VEI 7, ~150 km3 ejecta) injected ~60 Mt of sulfur into the stratosphere. The sulfate aerosols circled the globe for ~3 years, reducing solar input by ~1 W/m2. Global temperatures dropped ~1°C in 1816. Snow fell in New England in June; crops failed across Europe.

question: The Galápagos Islands sit on the equator ~1,000 km west of Ecuador. Each island has slightly different rock chemistry; older islands northwest, younger southeast. A hotspot builds new islands. What chemistry distinguishes hotspot basalt from spreading-ridge basalt?
choices: Hotspot magma is enriched in incompatible elements, hinting at deeper mantle origin than ridge basalts
Hotspot magma is silica-rich, while spreading-ridge basalt is consistently silica-poor across the planet
Hotspot magma is iron-poor, while spreading-ridge basalt is iron-rich in every comparable example
Hotspot magma cools so fast it has no crystals, unlike the slow-cooled crystalline ridge basalts
answer: Hotspot magma is enriched in incompatible elements, hinting at deeper mantle origin than ridge basalts
context: Hotspot (OIB — Ocean Island Basalt) magmas are slightly enriched in trace elements (K, Ti, P, rare earths) compared to MORB (Mid-Ocean Ridge Basalt). The enrichment is read as evidence that hotspot melts come from deeper, less-depleted mantle. The Galápagos hotspot lies under the Nazca plate.

question: The phrase 'isostasy' describes how Earth's crust floats on the mantle like a wooden raft on water — thicker crust floats higher; if you load weight on top, it sinks deeper. Scandinavia is still rising after glaciers melted ~10,000 years ago. What is this rebound called?
choices: Isostatic rebound — the crust slowly springs back up as the heavy ice load it once carried disappears
Tectonic uplift — collision pushing crust up at a plate boundary far away from the rebounding zone
Sea-level fall — the ocean dropping relative to the land as the land remains stationary in absolute terms
Mantle convection — slow currents in the mantle pushing the crust up locally from far below
answer: Isostatic rebound — the crust slowly springs back up as the heavy ice load it once carried disappears
context: Scandinavia sank under ~3 km of Pleistocene ice; since deglaciation it has risen ~250 m and continues at ~9 mm/year in Bothnian areas. Hudson Bay shows the same rebound. The Baltic Sea is shrinking on the Swedish side; islands emerge. Same mechanism in Glacier Bay (Alaska) and parts of Canada.

question: On Iceland's Surtsey island, born in 1963 from underwater eruption, scientists have watched soil form, plants colonize, birds arrive, and seabirds nest — primary succession in fast-forward. How does brand-new volcanic rock become soil capable of holding plants?
choices: Lichens and mosses colonize first, chemically weather rock, and trap windblown dust to build soil
Rain dissolves volcanic rock into clay quickly, allowing the first plants to root within months
Buried organic seeds inside the lava sprout once cooling permits, establishing the first plant cover
Volcanic rock contains all nutrients plants need, so plants colonize bare rock immediately
answer: Lichens and mosses colonize first, chemically weather rock, and trap windblown dust to build soil
context: Primary succession on bare volcanic rock: lichens and crusty algae arrive first, secreting acids that pit the rock. Their dead matter plus windblown dust builds millimeter-deep proto-soil. Mosses follow, then grasses, then shrubs. Surtsey reached 91 plant species and 16 nesting bird species by ~50 years of age.

question: Earthquakes happen along three plate-boundary types: subduction zones, transform faults like San Andreas, and spreading ridges. Megathrust quakes off Japan and Sumatra reach magnitude 9+; transform quakes max ~8; ridge quakes rarely exceed 6. Why the hierarchy?
choices: Megathrust faults can rupture for hundreds of km along a wide locked surface, releasing the most energy in one event
Megathrust faults sit deeper than transform faults, so their quakes release more pressure as they break upward
Megathrust faults move faster than transform faults, accumulating more energy between major earthquakes
Megathrust faults are wetter than transform faults, so they slip more easily and release more energy
answer: Megathrust faults can rupture for hundreds of km along a wide locked surface, releasing the most energy in one event
context: Magnitude scales with rupture area times slip. Megathrust subduction faults can rupture along 1,000+ km and 100+ km wide, slipping tens of meters — Sumatra 2004 was M9.1, Tohoku 2011 was M9.1. Transform faults are narrower (~20 km wide). Ridge quakes are limited by hot, thin spreading zones.

question: On Sumatra in 2004 a megathrust quake released enough energy to slip the seafloor ~15 m vertically along a 1,200 km rupture. The displaced water generated a tsunami that killed ~228,000 people across 14 countries. Why are subduction earthquakes the worst tsunami sources?
choices: Vertical seafloor displacement bulk-shifts the ocean column, generating large waves that radiate across whole oceans
Transform faults shift the seafloor horizontally instead of vertically, generating much smaller tsunami waves
Subduction zones lie under deeper water, so quakes there create taller tsunamis than shallow-water quakes do
Subduction quakes are more frequent than transform quakes, increasing the chance of any single tsunami event
answer: Vertical seafloor displacement bulk-shifts the ocean column, generating large waves that radiate across whole oceans
context: Tsunamis are driven by vertical seafloor displacement — only subduction (megathrust) faults bulk-shift the water column efficiently. Transform faults slip horizontally; ridge quakes are too small. The 2004 Sumatra quake (M9.1) raised the seafloor ~15 m vertically along a 1,200 km rupture. Waves crossed the Indian Ocean in hours.

question: On the seafloor of the Pacific, basalt rocks show alternating bands of magnetic orientation — one band lined up with Earth's current magnetic field, the next band reversed, then back again. The bands are symmetric across mid-ocean ridges. What does this magnetic striping prove?
choices: Seafloor spreading — new basalt at the ridge records the magnetic field, then drifts outward as more rises
Polar wandering — Earth's magnetic poles have drifted across the seafloor leaving stripes behind them
Iron deposition — magnetic iron settled out of seawater in periodic bands across the ocean floor over time
Mantle convection — convection cells under the Pacific magnetize the basalt as it cools above them slowly
answer: Seafloor spreading — new basalt at the ridge records the magnetic field, then drifts outward as more rises
context: Magnetic seafloor stripes — discovered by Vine and Matthews (1963) — confirmed seafloor spreading. New basalt at mid-ocean ridges cools and locks in Earth's magnetic orientation. As spreading continues, older bands drift away symmetrically. Earth's field flips polarity every ~200-300 ky; the bands record the history.

question: The Rocky Mountains in western North America hold few active volcanoes today; the Andes in South America hold over 200. Both ranges run along subduction zones where an oceanic plate dives under a continent. What difference in those subduction zones explains the volcanic gap?
choices: The Farallon plate broke up under North America; only fragments remain to drive western US volcanism
The North American climate is too cold for volcanic activity, while the Andean climate favors eruption
Rocky Mountain basement rock is too thick for magma to penetrate, unlike the thinner Andean crust
The Rockies stopped subducting millions of years ago, while Andean subduction has continued steadily
answer: The Farallon plate broke up under North America; only fragments remain to drive western US volcanism
context: The Farallon plate once subducted under North America (driving Sierra Nevada and Cascade volcanism). It has mostly been consumed; only remnants (Juan de Fuca, Cocos, Nazca) survive. The Cascades' active arc (St Helens, Rainier, Mt Hood) is what's left. South America still subducts the Nazca plate; its Andes hold the world's longest active volcanic chain.

question: On Hawaii, fresh basalt flows from Kilauea reach 1,100°C and run up to 30 km/h on steep slopes. The same volcano can produce a'a (rough jagged blocks) and pahoehoe (smooth ropy surface) meters apart. What controls which type a flow becomes?
choices: Cooling rate and slope — faster cooling or steeper slope tends toward a'a, slower cooling on gentler slope yields pahoehoe
Source vent — separate vents on Kilauea reliably produce one or the other; the surface form tracks vent chemistry
Gas content — gas-rich lava forms pahoehoe, while gas-poor lava forms a'a regardless of the cooling rate observed
Distance from ocean — flows that reach the ocean become pahoehoe, flows that stop inland become rough-jagged a'a
answer: Cooling rate and slope — faster cooling or steeper slope tends toward a'a, slower cooling on gentler slope yields pahoehoe
context: 'Pahoehoe' (Hawaiian for 'smooth') and 'a'a (rough) are end-members of basaltic lava texture. As lava advances, it cools and degasses; viscosity rises. A flow can transition from 'pahoehoe' to 'a'a' downstream as it cools. Slope steepness, cooling rate, and shear stress all contribute. Same lava chemistry; different surface form.

question: Below the western Pacific, geologists detect a slab of crust descending into the mantle — material that subducted millions of years ago and is still sinking.
