context: The astrolabe (Greek astron + lambanein, star-taker) was perfected by Al-Battani, Al-Sufi, and the school of Maragheh. It solved latitude, time, prayer times (qibla direction toward Mecca), star identification. European Renaissance astronomers learned it via translated Arabic texts.

question: Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972 landed humans on the Moon — Apollo 11 at Mare Tranquillitatis, Apollo 17 at Taurus-Littrow. They left scientific instruments still working today. What did the landings establish in the new field of lunar geography?
choices: Six site-specific maps of mare and highland terrain, with rock samples returned for laboratory dating
A grid of Apollo seismometers covering the lunar far side, transmitting moonquakes daily back to Earth
A complete photo-mosaic of the Moon's south polar craters, with confirmed deep ice deposits at the south
A global lunar magnetic field map, proving the Moon has a molten metallic core like Earth and Mars
answer: Six site-specific maps of mare and highland terrain, with rock samples returned for laboratory dating
context: Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17 landed at six different sites — three mare, three highland. 382 kg of rock samples enabled radiometric dating. The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (ALSEPs) ran 1969-77. Far-side mapping came from orbital flights; ice at the poles from later missions.

question: Landsat 1 launched in 1972 began continuous Earth-from-orbit imaging — the longest-running civilian remote-sensing program. Its multispectral scanner sees what human eyes cannot, in seven wavelength bands. What did Landsat reveal that ground surveys had missed?
choices: Continent-scale deforestation patterns, dust storms, lake expansion and contraction year on year
Live time-lapse of magnetic field fluctuations and the daily auroral oval shape changes
Direct subsurface mapping of underground rivers and aquifers across the world's deserts
Real-time tracking of individual whales, polar bears, and migratory bird flocks at sea
answer: Continent-scale deforestation patterns, dust storms, lake expansion and contraction year on year
context: Landsat 1 (ERTS, 1972) launched a 50-year civilian satellite imaging program. Its 30m-resolution multispectral images revealed Aral Sea shrinkage, Brazilian deforestation, urban sprawl. The archive is free and downloadable — the world's most-used remote-sensing dataset.

question: In 1873 a British naval expedition under George Nares began a three-year scientific voyage in HMS Challenger — a refitted steam corvette circling the world to sound depths, sample seabeds, and catalog deep-ocean life. What field of science did it found?
choices: Oceanography — systematic sea science with 50 published volumes of physical and biological data
Meteorology — systematic atmospheric science with the first global wind and temperature charts
Volcanology — systematic ocean-floor volcano mapping with the first hot-vent sample collection
Climatology — systematic global temperature tracking with the first ocean surface heat distribution
answer: Oceanography — systematic sea science with 50 published volumes of physical and biological data
context: The Challenger expedition (1872-76) sailed ~127,000 km, sounded 492 deep stations, identified 4,717 new species. The 50-volume Challenger Reports (1885) is the founding work of oceanography. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is named for it.

question: The Northwest Passage threads through the Canadian Arctic archipelago — Lancaster Sound, Barrow Strait, Peel Sound, Franklin Strait, Victoria Strait, Coronation Gulf, and out via the Beaufort Sea to the Bering. Why did this route prove so deadly to 19th-century British expeditions?
choices: Multi-year sea ice clogged the channels, trapping wooden hulls and dooming crews to scurvy and starvation
Magnetic anomalies near the North Magnetic Pole disabled all the British compass equipment immediately
Native Inuit hostility prevented all British expeditions from re-supplying with local meat and fish stocks
Underwater shoals known only to Russian whalers wrecked British ships before they could reach the open sea
answer: Multi-year sea ice clogged the channels, trapping wooden hulls and dooming crews to scurvy and starvation
context: Pre-Amundsen British expeditions (Franklin 1845, lost with 129; Parry, Ross, M'Clure) were trapped by multi-year sea ice. Scurvy, lead poisoning from tinned food, and starvation killed crews. Amundsen's small Gjøa (1903-06) overwintered for years and slipped through during summer melt windows.

question: Marine biologist Sylvia Earle has spent over 7,000 hours underwater. In 1979 she set an untethered record by walking the seafloor at 381 m off Hawaii in a JIM suit — a pressurized one-person hard armor. What does the JIM suit make possible?
choices: It keeps a diver at one atmosphere of internal pressure, so no decompression is needed on the way back up
It cools the diver to ocean temperature, so no shivering blocks the work at very deep operating sites
It transmits the diver's voice directly via sonar to surface ships hundreds of kilometers away from the dive
It folds compactly into a backpack form for descent, then inflates to body-fitting size on reaching the seabed
answer: It keeps a diver at one atmosphere of internal pressure, so no decompression is needed on the way back up
context: The JIM suit (named for diver Jim Jarrett) is an atmospheric diving suit — articulated armor holding internal pressure at one atmosphere. The diver decompresses zero on ascent. Earle's 1979 dive was the deepest untethered seafloor walk. She founded Mission Blue (ocean conservation) in 2009.

question: Cartographers describe a method called dead reckoning, used at sea before satellites. The navigator records course, speed, and elapsed time since the last known fix, plotting forward step by step. What is dead reckoning's fatal weakness over a long voyage?
choices: Errors compound — each estimate adds to the previous, so the calculated position drifts further from the real one
Iron parts deflect — every hull rivet pulls the compass slightly, accumulating bias on long voyages
Salt-spray fading — log-book ink fades in spray and old entries become unreadable after several weeks
Magnetic dip — at high latitudes the compass needle tilts and the bearings become impossible to read at sea
answer: Errors compound — each estimate adds to the previous, so the calculated position drifts further from the real one
context: Dead reckoning (a corruption of deduced reckoning) plots forward from the last known fix using estimated course and speed. Without a celestial fix, errors compound; a few percent per day drift means hundreds of miles error in a month. Celestial fixes (or GPS) reset the cumulative error.

question: In 1909 a Norwegian named Roald Amundsen had planned a try for the North Pole. When word came that Peary had claimed it, he secretly switched targets — and his Fram sailed south to Antarctica instead. What strategy did he use that beat Scott to the South Pole?
choices: Dog teams, a coastal base camp closer to the pole, ski technique, and a Norse-style food cache strategy
British naval ponies, well-funded coastal base, motor sledges, and large man-hauling support teams
Air reconnaissance balloons, a Russian-style winter base, ski technique, and aerial dropped resupply
Submarine landings under sea ice, a Russian-style winter base, ski technique, and overland tractors
answer: Dog teams, a coastal base camp closer to the pole, ski technique, and a Norse-style food cache strategy
context: Amundsen wintered at the Bay of Whales (Ross Ice Shelf), 100 km closer to the pole than Scott's Cape Evans. He used Greenland dogs in relays, Inuit-style clothing, and Norwegian ski technique. Five men reached the pole 14 Dec 1911 and returned with no losses.

question: Aerial photography came of age in WWI — photo planes mapped trench lines daily. Between the wars, aerial mapping replaced ground survey for many large regions. What advantage of aerial photography enabled the change?
choices: Wide-area coverage at uniform scale — a single image can replace weeks of triangulation across difficult terrain
X-ray penetration through cloud cover — photo planes could map any region in any weather conditions year-round
Underwater clarity from low altitude — photo planes could chart coastal seabeds to 200 m of depth at low tide
Auto-rectification of mountain shadow — photo planes returned undistorted images regardless of terrain shadowing
answer: Wide-area coverage at uniform scale — a single image can replace weeks of triangulation across difficult terrain
context: Aerial photography from a flying camera covers in one frame what ground survey teams would triangulate in weeks — and at uniform scale. Photogrammetry (Laussedat, Pulfrich, Hugershoff) developed the math. WWII pushed aerial mapping into mass production; satellites took over from the 1970s.

question: Vinland — the Norse name for the North American coast Leif Erikson landed on ~1000 AD — was confirmed by the discovery of a Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in northern Newfoundland in 1960. What distinctive feature at the site convinced archaeologists?
choices: Sod-walled longhouses built in classic Greenland Norse style, plus a Norse-style iron-smelting smithy
Carved Norse runestones with detailed dates and the names of Erik the Red and Leif Erikson at the site
Walls of stacked Norse-cut limestone blocks identical to those at the Erik the Red Greenland farms
Wooden Norse longships preserved in coastal peat bogs, intact with Norse iron rivets and ash benches
answer: Sod-walled longhouses built in classic Greenland Norse style, plus a Norse-style iron-smelting smithy
context: Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad excavated L'Anse aux Meadows (1960-68). Eight sod-walled buildings on Greenland Norse plans, plus a smithy, plus Norse iron nails and ringed pin established Norse occupation ~1000. UNESCO site 1978. Vinland's wild grapes likely lay farther south.

question: Ferdinand Magellan named the calm sea west of South America Mar Pacifico — the peaceful sea — because his crossing in 1520-21 met no major storms. The name stuck. What is misleading about calling the world's largest ocean peaceful?
choices: Pacific typhoons among the world's most violent storms; the basin holds the deepest trenches and most active volcanoes
Pacific waves are the steepest of any ocean; commercial ships routinely break in half during summer storms
Pacific currents move only in tight gyres; ships drift sideways for weeks without making real progress to ports
Pacific surface temperatures change so rapidly that sudden ice patches form during summer storms in the tropics
answer: Pacific typhoons among the world's most violent storms; the basin holds the deepest trenches and most active volcanoes
context: The Pacific holds the western Pacific typhoon belt (the most intense tropical cyclones), the Ring of Fire (90% of earthquakes, 75% of volcanoes), the deepest trenches (Mariana, Tonga, Kuril). Magellan's calm crossing was a fluke. The basin is more violent than any other ocean.

question: A French explorer led three expeditions up the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s and 1540s, claiming the region for France. His ships were stuck in winter ice at Stadacona; scurvy nearly killed his men until local Iroquoians showed them a remedy. Who?
choices: Jacques Cartier, whose voyages laid the basis for the New France colony and the city of Quebec
Samuel de Champlain, whose later voyages founded Quebec City and pushed deep into the Great Lakes
La Salle, whose later voyages descended the Mississippi River from the Great Lakes to its mouth
Marquette, whose later voyages with Jolliet first mapped the upper Mississippi for the French crown
answer: Jacques Cartier, whose voyages laid the basis for the New France colony and the city of Quebec
context: Jacques Cartier (1491-1557) made three St. Lawrence voyages (1534, 1535-36, 1541-42). His men were saved from scurvy at Stadacona (modern Quebec) by Iroquoian thuja (annedda) tea, rich in vitamin C. Champlain founded Quebec City (1608) on the same site.

question: In 1819 the British Admiralty offered £5,000 for the first ship to reach 110° W longitude north of 77° N — pushing for the Northwest Passage. Edward Parry's 1819-20 voyage broke through to 113° W and won the prize. Why was longitude rather than latitude the prize target?
choices: Reaching far west through the Arctic islands was the breakthrough that proved a passage might exist at all
Reaching far north of any prior expedition was easy; reaching far west was much harder due to ice motion
Reaching past 110° W meant crossing into the Russian-claimed eastern Bering Sea sector at that time
Reaching past 110° W meant entering open polar water that earlier explorers had thought was solid ice
answer: Reaching far west through the Arctic islands was the breakthrough that proved a passage might exist at all
context: Parry pushed through Lancaster Sound and Barrow Strait (1819) to Melville Island — proving open water existed deep into the archipelago. The £5,000 westward-longitude prize captured the geography: the question wasn't whether to reach the pole, but whether a westward channel could be found.

question: James Rennell, a British naval officer in Bengal, surveyed the Ganges and Brahmaputra in the 1760s — work that earned him the title Father of Indian Geography. He later mapped the Indian Ocean and African interior. What survey technique gave his maps unusual accuracy?
choices: Triangulation from a measured baseline, with chained distances locked into a network of geometric figures
Open-circuit traverse with a single magnetic compass and pacing, then drawing the route from memory
Reconnaissance from elephant back, with bearings called out by mahouts to a riding clerk in the howdah
Aerial sketching from kite-borne cameras, then plotted by tracing onto a flat surface in the survey tent
answer: Triangulation from a measured baseline, with chained distances locked into a network of geometric figures
context: James Rennell (1742-1830) applied trigonometric triangulation to the Ganges-Brahmaputra. A measured baseline gave true distance; chained angles built a rigid network. The Great Trigonometrical Survey of India (1802) extended the method to the subcontinent — naming Everest along the way.

question: A Prussian naturalist explored equatorial America from 1799 to 1804 with botanist Aimé Bonpland. He climbed Chimborazo in Ecuador, traced the Casiquiare canal linking the Orinoco and Amazon, and laid the foundations of biogeography. Who?
choices: Alexander von Humboldt, German polymath whose Cosmos and many monographs founded the discipline
Charles Darwin, English naturalist whose Beagle voyage decades later focused on Galápagos finches
Alfred Russel Wallace, English naturalist whose Malay Archipelago decades later defined the Wallace Line
Joseph Banks, English botanist whose Endeavour voyage with Cook focused on Tahiti and Australia
answer: Alexander von Humboldt, German polymath whose Cosmos and many monographs founded the discipline
context: Alexander von Humboldt (1769-1859) traveled the Americas with Bonpland 1799-1804. His isothermal maps, Chimborazo plant-zone diagram, and Cosmos synthesis founded biogeography. Darwin called Humboldt his pattern. Bolívar said Humboldt was the true discoverer of South America.

question: A French explorer in the 1760s led the first French circumnavigation (1766-69) with two ships, taking botanists and astronomers. He gave the world the name Bougainvillea (the flower his botanist Commerson identified in Brazil) and the name Bougainville Island (Solomon archipelago). Who was he?
choices: Louis Antoine de Bougainville, whose Boudeuse and Étoile voyage was France's answer to British Pacific exploration
Jean-François de La Pérouse, whose later Boussole and Astrolabe voyage vanished in the Solomon Islands at Vanikoro
Charles de Brosses, whose Histoire des navigations aux terres australes inspired French Pacific exploration but who never himself sailed
Alexander Dalrymple, whose maps for the East India Company inspired British Pacific exploration but who never himself led a Pacific voyage
answer: Louis Antoine de Bougainville, whose Boudeuse and Étoile voyage was France's answer to British Pacific exploration
context: Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1729-1811) led the French circumnavigation 1766-69 in Boudeuse and Étoile. He returned via Tahiti, the Solomons, Java, the Cape. His Voyage autour du monde (1771) helped seed European fascination with Tahiti. Bougainvillea, Bougainville Island, and the Bougainville Strait bear his name.

question: Captain Cook's first Pacific voyage (1768-71) had a secret Admiralty mission, but its public mission was a scientific one: sailing to Tahiti to observe a rare astronomical event of June 1769 from the Pacific. What were Cook's astronomers measuring, and why send a ship?
choices: The transit of Venus across the Sun, timed from widely separated longitudes to compute the Earth-Sun distance
The lunar eclipse of June 1769, timed against Greenwich to test the lunar-distance method for longitude at sea
The opposition of Mars during 1769, timed against European observatories to refine the planet's orbital ellipse
The conjunction of Jupiter's moons, timed at multiple longitudes to refine the Galilean satellite clock method
answer: The transit of Venus across the Sun, timed from widely separated longitudes to compute the Earth-Sun distance
context: The 1769 transit of Venus (a rare ~8-year-paired event; the prior was 1761, the next 1874-82) let astronomers compute the astronomical unit (Earth-Sun distance) by timing Venus's silhouette crossing the Sun from widely separated locations and using parallax. The Royal Society's expedition sent Cook in HMS Endeavour to Tahiti, where Charles Green and Cook observed from Point Venus. Results were combined with European data; Encke's 1824 analysis gave ~153M km (modern value ~149.6M). The sealed Admiralty orders Cook opened after Tahiti directed him to search for Terra Australis.

question: In August 1805 Lewis and Clark approached the Continental Divide on horseback. Their Shoshone interpreter Sacagawea recognized the country — and the chief who met them turned out to be her brother Cameahwait. What geographic crossing did this Shoshone alliance unlock at Lemhi Pass on the Idaho-Montana border?
choices: Horses to cross the Bitterroots; the Shoshone supplied 29 mounts that let the expedition leave the Missouri's headwaters for the Pacific drainage
Boats to descend the Snake River; the Shoshone built dugout canoes that let the expedition leave the Missouri's headwaters for the Pacific drainage
Maps of the Bitterroots; the Shoshone drew route diagrams that let the expedition leave the Missouri's headwaters for the Pacific drainage
Guides through the Bitterroots; the Shoshone led the party that let the expedition leave the Missouri's headwaters for the Pacific drainage
answer: Horses to cross the Bitterroots; the Shoshone supplied 29 mounts that let the expedition leave the Missouri's headwaters for the Pacific drainage
context: Sacagawea (Lemhi Shoshone, captured by Hidatsa as a girl, then sold to French-Canadian trader Toussaint Charbonneau) was hired at Fort Mandan. At Lemhi Pass (Idaho-Montana border) on 17 August 1805 the expedition met her birth band; Cameahwait was her brother. The Shoshone traded ~29 horses essential for the Bitterroot crossing — without them the expedition would have been stranded. They later picked up Nez Perce guide Old Toby. Without Sacagawea's recognition and family link, no horses; without horses, the Pacific never reached.

question: John Harrison's first marine timekeeper H1 (1735) used a 4-foot grasshopper escapement and counter-balanced springs to stay accurate at sea. His H4 (1759), shipped to Jamaica in 1761, fit in a 5-inch case and lost only 5 seconds across 81 days. What did Harrison's design evolution from H1 to H4 abandon?
choices: The pendulum-substitute spring balance for a high-frequency oscillator with diamond pallets and bimetallic temperature compensation
The wood-frame internal mounting for a brass-frame chassis able to withstand the temperature and humidity changes encountered at sea
The marine spring drive for a fusee-and-mainspring approach matching land clocks of the period and the standard escapement of land clocks
The face-up display for a compass-mount gimbal that kept the dial level despite the ship's roll and pitch in heavy weather at sea
answer: The pendulum-substitute spring balance for a high-frequency oscillator with diamond pallets and bimetallic temperature compensation
context: Harrison's H1 (1735), H2 (1741), and H3 (1759) were all large, used pendulum-substitute oscillators and elaborate temperature compensation built into the balance itself. H4 (1759) was a radical departure: a 5-inch pocket-watch-shaped chronometer with a small high-frequency oscillator using diamond pallets in the escapement and a bimetallic temperature compensator. The H4 design (and Kendall's K1 copy that Cook carried) became the production pattern. Parliament's £20,000 Longitude Prize (1714) was paid in stages; Harrison received the full balance by 1773 with George III's intervention. Dava Sobel's Longitude (1995) is the popular account.

question: Magellan's 1519-22 voyage took 270 men in five ships from Spain. Eighteen returned in one ship. The voyage broke into three deadly legs: an Atlantic-and-South-American passage; a Pacific crossing; and a homeward Indian-Ocean run. Which leg killed the most men and why?
choices: Pacific crossing — 99 days without fresh food in late 1520; scurvy killed roughly 30 in the longest open-sea passage anyone had attempted before
Atlantic-and-South-American leg — overwintering at Port San Julián in 1520; cold and a mutiny killed roughly 30 before the Strait of Magellan was even found
Magellan's death at Mactan in 1521 — the Philippine ambush of April 1521 cost the expedition's captain and many of his armed retainers in a single afternoon battle
Homeward Indian-Ocean leg — running from Portuguese fleets through the Cape of Good Hope in 1522 cost roughly 30 men to dysentery and the lack of food rations near the end
answer: Pacific crossing — 99 days without fresh food in late 1520; scurvy killed roughly 30 in the longest open-sea passage anyone had attempted before
context: The Pacific crossing (late November 1520 to March 1521) was the killing leg. Magellan's crew had no idea how vast the Pacific was — Ptolemy's geography vastly underestimated its width. 99 days without fresh food: scurvy, thirst, and starvation killed ~30. Pigafetta wrote that men ate sawdust and rats. Magellan died at Mactan in the Philippines (27 April 1521) in a skirmish with chief Lapu-Lapu. Juan Sebastián Elcano sailed Victoria home via the Indian Ocean and Cape of Good Hope, dodging Portuguese fleets. The voyage proved the Earth round, the Pacific vast, and Earth's circumference far larger than Columbus had hoped.

question: A small Norwegian-flagged herring sloop with a 13-horsepower engine left Christiania in 1903 with seven men aboard. She overwintered twice with Netsilik Inuit, who taught the crew Arctic survival, and broke into the Beaufort Sea in August 1906. What had this ship accomplished that Franklin's 129 men had failed to do?
choices: First complete sea passage through the Northwest Passage; her captain went on to South Pole and circumnavigated airships over both poles
First complete sea passage through the Northeast Passage; her captain went on to South Pole and circumnavigated airships over both poles
First sailing along the open polar sea above 88° N; her captain went on to South Pole and circumnavigated airships over both poles
First steaming around Wrangel Island into the Beaufort; her captain went on to South Pole and circumnavigated airships over both poles
answer: First complete sea passage through the Northwest Passage; her captain went on to South Pole and circumnavigated airships over both poles
context: Roald Amundsen's Gjøa (47 tons, originally a herring sloop, refitted with a small auxiliary engine) made the first complete sea passage of the Northwest Passage 1903-06 — three years where Franklin's 1845 expedition (HMS Erebus + Terror, 129 men) had vanished. Amundsen wintered at Gjøa Haven (King William Island) and learned dog-handling, igloo-building, and skin-clothing from the Netsilik Inuit. Those skills underwrote his 1911 South Pole victory over Scott. He later flew the Norge airship over the North Pole (1926) and disappeared in 1928 on a rescue flight for Nobile.

question: In the early 1950s Marie Tharp was forbidden to go to sea (women were considered bad luck). She plotted by hand the sonar soundings Bruce Heezen brought back. Her drawings of the Atlantic floor revealed a feature so striking that she changed her mind on a fringe debate. Which?
choices: A central rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Tharp realized the ocean floor was spreading apart, vindicating Wegener's continental drift theory
A continuous abyssal plain east of the ridge; Tharp realized the ocean floor was uniformly old, contradicting Wegener's continental drift theory definitively
A series of north-south fracture zones in the South Atlantic; Tharp realized the ocean floor was being compressed, supporting the expanding-earth hypothesis
A meandering mid-ocean channel similar to a continental river; Tharp realized the ocean floor was eroded by currents, confirming a steady-state earth model
answer: A central rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Tharp realized the ocean floor was spreading apart, vindicating Wegener's continental drift theory
context: Marie Tharp (1920-2006), working at Lamont Geological Observatory with Bruce Heezen, plotted bathymetric profiles of the Atlantic basin from sonar data ~1952. She spotted a continuous central rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge — a feature inconsistent with a stable seafloor. Heezen initially called it 'girl talk' but the pattern repeated on every ocean basin. Combined with Vine-Matthews magnetic stripe analysis (1963), Tharp's mapping forced the geological mainstream to accept seafloor spreading and plate tectonics, vindicating Alfred Wegener's 1912 continental-drift hypothesis. Her 1977 World Ocean Floor map (with Heezen and Berann) is the definitive image.

question: In 1569 the Flemish mathematician Gerardus Mercator published Nova et aucta orbis terrae descriptio — a world map on 18 sheets. The projection has been the standard for marine charts ever since. Its breakthrough was a single mathematical property; severe area distortion at the poles is the price. What property does Mercator preserve?
choices: A straight line on the map is a constant-compass course (rhumb line), so navigators can steer one bearing without recalculating along the route
A straight line on the map is a great-circle route (geodesic), so navigators can steer one bearing along the shortest possible Earth-surface path
A straight line on the map is a constant-latitude line (parallel), so navigators steer one bearing along a true east-west path across longitudes
A straight line on the map is a constant-bearing-from-pole arc, so navigators can steer one bearing along a true magnetic-north convergent path
answer: A straight line on the map is a constant-compass course (rhumb line), so navigators can steer one bearing without recalculating along the route
context: Mercator's 1569 cylindrical conformal projection mathematically preserves angles locally — so a straight line on the map (a 'loxodrome' or rhumb line) corresponds to a course of constant compass bearing on the Earth. A navigator who follows that bearing can sail directly between two points on the map without recalculating. The cost is area distortion: latitudes are stretched in proportion to sec(latitude). Greenland (2.2M km²) appears larger than Africa (30M km²). Great-circle routes (the actual shortest paths) appear as curves on Mercator. The projection's navigational utility kept it dominant on sea charts; its area distortion drew the late-20th-century Peters polemic.

question: Captain Cook was killed at Kealakekua Bay on Hawaii's Big Island on 14 February 1779. His January arrival had coincided with the Makahiki festival of Lono; his February return came outside it. Sahlins and Obeyesekere debated this timing geography. What is Sahlins's anthropological reading?
choices: Hawaiian calendar made Cook's first visit Lono-coded and the second a transgression; the structural mismatch shaped the deadly response when he returned
Hawaiian calendar made both Cook's visits Lono-coded; the second was even more sacralized than the first and the killing was a deliberate ritual sacrifice
Hawaiian calendar had nothing to do with Cook's killing; the dispute was a quarrel over a stolen cutter and hostages, with no religious framing whatsoever
Hawaiian calendar made Cook's first visit a transgression and the second Lono-coded; the killing on the second visit was a defensive accident, not religious
answer: Hawaiian calendar made Cook's first visit Lono-coded and the second a transgression; the structural mismatch shaped the deadly response when he returned
context: Cook arrived at Kealakekua Bay in January 1779 — during the Makahiki, the four-month festival honoring Lono (god of agriculture and peace). He left in early February. A storm damaged HMS Resolution and forced his return on 11 February — outside the Makahiki, in the season of Ku (war). Cook was killed 14 February in a confrontation over a stolen cutter. Marshall Sahlins (Islands of History, 1985; How 'Natives' Think, 1995) argued the Hawaiian ritual calendar shaped the response; Gananath Obeyesekere (The Apotheosis of Captain Cook, 1992) argued this was Western myth-making and Hawaiians acted on practical grievance. The debate became a touchstone in anthropological method.

question: Vitus Bering, Danish-born officer in Russian service, was leading his St Peter back from the Alaskan coast in November 1741 when the ship wrecked on a small treeless island in the Aleutians. Bering and 30 men died of scurvy that winter. The 46 survivors then did something extraordinary in spring. What did they do?
answer: Built a smaller boat from the wreckage of the St Peter and sailed her 1,200 km to Kamchatka
choices: Built a smaller boat from the wreckage of the St Peter and sailed her 1,200 km to Kamchatka
Walked across the sea ice to the Aleutian chain mainland and trekked overland to Kamchatka
Lit signal fires nightly until a passing Russian whaler spotted them and rescued the survivors
Sent two volunteers across the open Pacific by lifeboat to bring back a rescue ship from Russia
context: Vitus Bering (1681-1741), Danish-born officer in the Russian Navy from 1704. The Great Northern Expedition (1733-43) was Russia's largest scientific project to date — 3,000 men over a decade. Bering's St Peter sighted Alaska's Mt St Elias 16 July 1741. On the return the ship was driven onto Bering Island in the Commander Islands; Bering and ~30 crew died of scurvy that winter. The survivors broke up the wreck of the St Peter, used her timbers and fittings to build a smaller two-masted boat (~12 m long), and sailed her 1,200 km west to Kamchatka in summer 1742. They brought back the sea-otter pelts that started the Russian-American fur trade (Russian-American Company, 1799). Alaska sold to the US in 1867 (Seward's 'icebox').

question: Zheng He's Ming treasure voyages (1405-33) sent fleets of ~300 ships and 28,000 men across the Indian Ocean — reaching Hormuz, Malindi, and Mecca. The expeditions stopped abruptly after his seventh voyage. What political-cultural shift in the Ming court ended them?
choices: Confucian retrenchment favored agricultural-tax revenue over maritime commerce; the Hongxi and Xuande emperors banned ocean voyaging and the fleets were burned
Mongol invasions on the northern frontier demanded all Ming naval resources by 1433; ships and crews were redeployed to the Manchurian and Korean frontiers
The Hongxi emperor's Buddhist conversion ruled out contact with non-Buddhist civilizations; the Ming court redirected revenue to monastery construction at home
A succession war between the Hongxi and Xuande factions consumed naval revenue 1424-30; both emperors banned long voyaging to prevent fleet seizure by rivals
answer: Confucian retrenchment favored agricultural-tax revenue over maritime commerce; the Hongxi and Xuande emperors banned ocean voyaging and the fleets were burned
context: Zheng He's seven voyages (1405-33) under Yongle (r. 1402-24) and Xuande (r. 1425-35) reached Calicut, Hormuz, the Swahili coast (Malindi), and possibly Madagascar. The voyages were extravagantly expensive. After Yongle's death, Confucian-traditional officials at court (long opposed to the eunuch-led naval program) gained influence under his successors. By 1433 voyaging stopped. By 1500 ocean-going construction was banned, ships destroyed, records burned. Mainstream explanation (Levathes, When China Ruled the Seas, 1994; Finlay, 2008) emphasizes Confucian-versus-eunuch court politics + agricultural-economy preferences. The geographic consequence: Europe filled the Indian Ocean trade vacuum within 60 years.

question: In 1976 the Polynesian Voyaging Society's double-hulled canoe Hokule'a sailed from Maui to Tahiti — 2,400 miles using only traditional wayfinding. The navigator Mau Piailug came from Satawal in the Caroline Islands, where the tradition had survived. What did the voyage settle scientifically?
choices: Polynesian colonization of the Pacific was deliberate two-way navigation, not lucky drift; the wayfinding system was a working technology, not a reconstruction
Polynesian colonization of the Pacific used only one-man outrigger canoes; the double-hulled canoe was a late post-contact development used for ceremonial purposes
Polynesian colonization of the Pacific followed Antarctic currents; the wayfinding system was a working technology but used southern ocean currents, not star paths
Polynesian colonization of the Pacific was one-way; the wayfinding tradition was deliberate but no return voyages were ever attempted in the pre-contact period
answer: Polynesian colonization of the Pacific was deliberate two-way navigation, not lucky drift; the wayfinding system was a working technology, not a reconstruction
context: Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki (1947) had argued accidental drift colonization. The Hokule'a voyage (1976), with Mau Piailug (1932-2010) from Satawal navigating to Tahiti without instruments, proved deliberate Polynesian wayfinding worked. Mau's tradition (etak) integrated star paths (rising and setting positions of named stars), wave patterns (especially reflected swells from unseen islands), bird species (the etak-of-birds), cloud formations over land, and dead-reckoning by remembered course-and-speed. Subsequent voyages reached New Zealand, Easter Island, Rapa Nui, and the Marquesas — the entire Polynesian triangle. Genetic and linguistic evidence confirms the same picture: a deliberate Austronesian expansion from Taiwan to Polynesia over ~3,000 years.

question: John Hadley (England) and Thomas Godfrey (Philadelphia) independently invented a navigation instrument around 1731, replacing the cross-staff and back-staff used since ~1500. The cross-staff required staring at the sun; many navigators went blind. What did the 1731 instrument fix?
choices: Twin mirrors bring sun and horizon into one optical field; the navigator never looks at the sun, and the doubled angle lets smaller arcs read finer
A hand-cranked clockwork tracks the sun's motion automatically; the navigator sets the start position and the dial reads the noon altitude on its own
A magnifying telescope over the cross-staff sighting bar; the navigator reads solar limb position from a smaller field at greater apparent distance
A heliographic filter over the cross-staff sighting bar; the navigator can safely look at the sun even at midday without any retinal damage to the eye
answer: Twin mirrors bring sun and horizon into one optical field; the navigator never looks at the sun, and the doubled angle lets smaller arcs read finer
context: Hadley's and Godfrey's octant (1731), refined into the sextant (Bird, 1757; reads up to 120° on a 60° arc due to the reflection doubling), used twin mirrors to superimpose images of the sun (or a star) and the horizon. The observer measures the angle between by adjusting the index mirror until the two images touch. Looking through the telescope, you see the horizon directly through the unsilvered half of the horizon glass and the sun reflected off the index mirror via the silvered half. Solar damage to the eye is avoided by shade glasses in front of the mirrors. The sextant became standard naval kit by 1800 and remained essential until satellite positioning.

question: Amundsen's December 1911 South Pole party was five men. They left Framheim on the Ross Ice Shelf 19 October with four sledges, 52 dogs, and ~800 miles to pole and back. Cull-and-eat: weak dogs were shot and fed to the rest. Why dogs over ponies, motors, or man-hauling?
choices: Dogs pull on snow, eat snow for water, survive subzero cold without shelter, and can be eaten when no longer needed; no other transport choice had all four traits
Dogs pull on snow, eat snow for water, but require imported feed; the Norwegian government pre-positioned ten tons of pemmican at Framheim before Amundsen left
Dogs pull faster than ponies on hard snow but cannot survive subzero nights without stabling; Amundsen built portable kennels his team carried up the polar plateau
Dogs pull slower than ponies on hard snow but are easier to manage; Amundsen accepted slower pace for simpler logistics and ate his ponies for emergency food
answer: Dogs pull on snow, eat snow for water, survive subzero cold without shelter, and can be eaten when no longer needed; no other transport choice had all four traits
context: Amundsen's choice of dogs reflected systematic study of Inuit and Sami practice (he had wintered with Netsilik on the Northwest Passage). Dogs: pull well on snow; metabolize snow for water; survive temperatures below -50°C without shelter; and the weaker ones can be killed to feed stronger ones — making the food cache self-extending. Scott's British party tried motorized sledges (broke down), ponies (had to be shot at the foot of the Beardmore Glacier), and man-hauling (exhausted men in 30,000-foot total altitude gain). Amundsen reached the pole 14 December 1911 with five men and 11 dogs; returned with all five men and 11 dogs. Scott reached the pole 17 January 1912; all five returned and died.

question: In May 1869 John Wesley Powell — a Union Major who had lost his right arm at Shiloh — left Green River, Wyoming with ten men in four oar-powered wooden boats. Three months and 1,000 river-miles later six men emerged at the Grand Wash Cliffs. What did Powell resolve about Grand Canyon geology?
choices: Antecedent erosion — the Colorado cut downward as fast as the Colorado Plateau rose around it; the canyon is millions of years of steady cutting, not catastrophic
Catastrophic flood erosion — the Colorado carved the canyon in a single Pleistocene ice-dam burst over a few thousand years; the canyon is brief, not gradual
Marine erosion — the Colorado channel had been submerged beneath an inland sea then exposed; the canyon walls are an exhumed marine basin, not steady cutting
Tectonic faulting — the canyon is a rift valley formed by Colorado Plateau pulling apart; the Colorado merely cleaned out the fault zone, not steady cutting
answer: Antecedent erosion — the Colorado cut downward as fast as the Colorado Plateau rose around it; the canyon is millions of years of steady cutting, not catastrophic
context: John Wesley Powell (1834-1902, lost right arm at Shiloh April 1862, retired Major) led the 1869 Colorado River Expedition through the Grand Canyon. Three months, 1,000 miles, three men quit at Separation Canyon (killed by Shivwits Paiutes or possibly Mormons — disputed). His 1875 Exploration of the Colorado River of the West laid out the antecedent-erosion model: river cuts downward as plateau rises around it. He founded the US Geological Survey direction (1881-94) and the Bureau of American Ethnology. His Report on the Lands of the Arid Region (1878) anticipated 20th-century western water disputes — recommending settlement organized by watershed; ignored at the time.

question: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ninth emperor of Mali, passed through Cairo on his way to Mecca with a Hajj caravan of 60,000 men, 12,000 slaves carrying 4 pounds of gold each, and 80 camels with up to 300 lbs of gold dust each. His generous spending wrecked Cairo's economy for over a decade. What did he then do on the way home that historians find most striking?
answer: Borrowed gold back from Cairo merchants at high interest, trying to slow the inflation he had caused
choices: Borrowed gold back from Cairo merchants at high interest, trying to slow the inflation he had caused
Confiscated all gold from the Cairo treasury to refill his own caravan stores
Banned Mali subjects from carrying gold abroad to prevent further damage to foreign markets
Refused to leave Cairo until the price returned to normal, waiting for over six months there
context: Mansa Musa I (r. 1312-37) is regularly cited as the wealthiest individual in human history (modern estimates of his wealth are largely speculative but contemporary Arabic and European sources are vivid). The 1324 Hajj passed through Cairo and Mecca; Al-Umari (writing 1340s) reported the gold dump crashed Cairo's gold price for about 12 years. On the return journey, Musa attempted to borrow gold back from Cairo lenders at high interest — historians cite this as the first recorded large-scale market-stabilization intervention, an effort to slow the inflation he had caused. The geography behind the wealth: Mali controlled the Niger bend and trade routes south to the Bambuk and Bure goldfields (modern Senegal-Mali border zone) — the source of perhaps two-thirds of medieval Old World gold. The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows Mansa Musa on his throne holding a gold nugget.

question: Four generations of one Italian-French astronomer family ran the Paris Observatory and the first scientific national survey 1668-1793. Their century-long project produced the first accurate map of any large country — 182 sheets at 1:86,400 scale. Which family?
choices: Cassini — Giovanni Domenico, Jacques, César-François, and Jean-Dominique mapped France over four generations using triangulation from a measured baseline
Picard — Jean, his son Philippe, his grandson, and great-grandson mapped France over four generations using triangulation from a measured baseline at Sourdon
La Caille — Nicolas-Louis, his nephew, grandnephew, and great-grandnephew mapped France over four generations using triangulation from a baseline at the Cape
Lalande — Jérôme, his son Michel, his grandson, and great-grandson mapped France over four generations using triangulation from a measured Bourges baseline
answer: Cassini — Giovanni Domenico, Jacques, César-François, and Jean-Dominique mapped France over four generations using triangulation from a measured baseline
context: The Cassini family — Giovanni Domenico (Cassini I, 1625-1712, Italian, recruited by Louis XIV to direct the Paris Observatory 1671); Jacques Cassini (Cassini II, 1677-1756); César-François Cassini de Thury (Cassini III, 1714-84); and Jean-Dominique Cassini (Cassini IV, 1748-1845) — ran the Paris Observatory across four generations. The Carte de Cassini (Carte de l'Académie, 1747-1793) used triangulation from a measured Picard-baseline. 182 sheets at 1:86,400. The Revolutionary government finished the project. Cassini IV was imprisoned during the Terror. The map influenced national-survey projects across Europe (Ordnance Survey 1791 in Britain, US Coast Survey 1807 under Hassler).

question: Vasco da Gama's 1497-99 voyage opened the all-water spice route to Calicut. The crucial leg from Malindi (Kenya) across the Indian Ocean depended on a local pilot whose monsoon and coastal knowledge far exceeded any Portuguese chart. Who guided da Gama's crossing?
choices: Ahmad ibn Majid — the Arab navigator from Najd whose Kitab al-Fawa'id codified monsoon timing and Indian Ocean coastal pilotage
Wang Dayuan — the Chinese maritime trader whose Daoyi Zhilue codified monsoon timing and Indian Ocean coastal pilotage from Yuan-era voyages
Giovanni Polo — Marco Polo's son, the Venetian whose Indian Ocean pilotage knowledge had been preserved in Venice from his father's 13th-century journey
Ibn Battuta IV — the Moroccan jurist whose Indian Ocean pilotage knowledge derived from his grandfather's 14th-century travels through the region
answer: Ahmad ibn Majid — the Arab navigator from Najd whose Kitab al-Fawa'id codified monsoon timing and Indian Ocean coastal pilotage
context: Ahmad ibn Majid (c. 1432-c. 1500), known as the Lion of the Sea, was the most celebrated Arab navigator of his era. His Kitab al-Fawa'id (Book of Useful Information on the Principles and Rules of Navigation) and ~40 other works codified Indian Ocean pilotage — monsoon timing (southwest April-September, northeast October-March), Indian and East African coastal landmarks, star-altitude latitude (using the qiyas — a knotted rope system). Da Gama hired him at Malindi in 1498 (some Arab sources name a different pilot; the identification is disputed by modern scholars including Ibrahim Khoury). The crossing to Calicut took 23 days using the southwest monsoon. The Indian Ocean had been an Arab-Persian-Indian-Chinese trade network for centuries before Europeans 'discovered' it.

question: Amundsen sited his Antarctic base at the Bay of Whales on the Ross Ice Shelf — 60 nautical miles closer to the pole than Scott's base at Cape Evans on Ross Island. Scott considered the bay risky (ice shelf, not bedrock). What did Amundsen's risk calculation get right?
choices: The bay's ice shelf had been stable for a century of recorded sightings; the 60-mile saving was decisive against the marginal ice-shelf risk
The bay's ice shelf was structurally firmer than the bedrock at Cape Evans; ice gave better foundation for permanent buildings than volcanic rock
The bay offered better wildlife access than Cape Evans; the seals and penguins around Framheim gave abundant fresh meat for the sledge dogs
The bay had a sheltered harbor unlike Cape Evans; the Fram's anchorage was safer at Framheim than at any other point along the Ross Sea coast
answer: The bay's ice shelf had been stable for a century of recorded sightings; the 60-mile saving was decisive against the marginal ice-shelf risk
context: Amundsen sited Framheim on the Bay of Whales (Ross Ice Shelf) — a calculated risk Scott had explicitly considered and rejected. The ice shelf could in principle calve away with the base on it. Amundsen judged the bay had been stable for ~70 years of recorded sightings; he was right (the bay was stable until the 1980s). The 60-nautical-mile saving on the pole leg saved roughly 10 days of dog-sledge time round-trip — a substantial margin in a survival situation. Scott chose the safer Cape Evans (Ross Island bedrock) and accepted the extra distance. The geography choice — combined with dogs, skis, the cull-and-eat food strategy, and Norwegian winter mountaineering experience — gave Amundsen his decisive edge.

question: Two methods solved the longitude problem in the late 18th century. Harrison's chronometer gave one. The other, refined by Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne, was published as annual Nautical Almanac tables (1767 onward). Why did the lunar-distance method work?
choices: Moon moves against background stars about half a degree per hour; measure the Moon-star angle at sea, compare to Greenwich tables, solve for time
Moon's libration produces a small wobble visible from Earth; measure the wobble amplitude at sea, compare to Greenwich predictions, solve for longitude
Moon's apparent diameter varies with its orbital position; measure the disc size at sea precisely, compare to Greenwich tables, solve for longitude
Moon's phase shadow shifts measurably hour by hour; measure the terminator angle at sea precisely, compare to Greenwich tables, solve for longitude
answer: Moon moves against background stars about half a degree per hour; measure the Moon-star angle at sea, compare to Greenwich tables, solve for time
context: The lunar-distance method exploited the Moon's relatively fast apparent motion against the background stars (~0.5°/hour). Tobias Mayer's improved lunar tables (~1755) finally made it accurate enough for navigation. Procedure: measure the angle between the Moon and a chosen star or the Sun with a sextant, correct for parallax and refraction, compare to the Nautical Almanac (Maskelyne, from 1767 onward) which gave precomputed Greenwich predictions, and solve for GMT — hence longitude. Demanding observation and ~3-4 hours of calculation per fix, but it required no expensive chronometer. Cook carried both Kendall's K1 chronometer AND the Almanac. By 1850 chronometers became cheap enough to replace lunars; both methods continued in use as cross-checks.

question: An English navigator's fourth voyage (1610) pushed into a vast bay south of Hudson Strait, hoping for a Northwest Passage. The Discovery iced in over winter; food ran short; the crew mutinied in June 1611 and set him adrift with his teenage son and seven sick men. Whose bay?
choices: Henry Hudson — English explorer whose Dutch-funded 1609 voyage also gave his name to a North American river that the Manhattan harbor opens onto
Martin Frobisher — English explorer whose Elizabethan voyages gave his name to a Baffin Island bay where his 1577 expedition mined worthless pyrite as fool's gold
John Davis — English explorer whose Elizabethan voyages gave his name to a strait between Greenland and Baffin Island that he charted in 1585-87 expeditions
William Baffin — English explorer whose Elizabethan voyages gave his name to an island in the Canadian Arctic that his expeditions charted in 1612-16 voyages
answer: Henry Hudson — English explorer whose Dutch-funded 1609 voyage also gave his name to a North American river that the Manhattan harbor opens onto
context: Henry Hudson (c.1565-1611) made four documented voyages searching for a northern passage to Asia. Voyages 1 & 2 (1607, 1608) tried for a polar route over Spitsbergen, both turned by ice. Voyage 3 (1609, Dutch-funded) found the Hudson River — Manhattan's first European map. Voyage 4 (1610, English-funded) reached Hudson Strait, then the enormous Hudson Bay, which Hudson believed was the Pacific. The Discovery wintered at James Bay (south end); food was short. On 22 June 1611 the crew mutinied, set Hudson, his son John, and seven men adrift in a small shallop. None survived. The mutineers reached London but most died en route; the survivors faced trial but were acquitted. The Hudson's Bay Company (1670) made the bay England's gateway to the fur trade.

question: Arthur Robinson was commissioned by Rand McNally in 1961 to design a world projection optimized not for a single property (angle, area, distance) but for general appeal — distortion spread broadly. National Geographic adopted it in 1988. Where does Robinson's distortion concentrate?
choices: Polar regions look horizontally stretched and tropics look slightly compressed; the projection compromises between Mercator's poles and Mollweide's equator
Polar regions look correct and tropics look horizontally stretched; the projection prioritizes high-latitude accuracy over equatorial accuracy worldwide
Polar regions look vertically compressed and tropics look vertically stretched; the projection prioritizes equatorial accuracy over high-latitude accuracy
Polar regions look correct in shape and area but tropics look skewed; the projection trades east-west accuracy against north-south accuracy worldwide
answer: Polar regions look horizontally stretched and tropics look slightly compressed; the projection compromises between Mercator's poles and Mollweide's equator
context: Arthur Robinson's 1963 projection (often called Robinson, sometimes orthophanic 'right-appearing') was designed by visual judgment rather than a single mathematical optimization — Robinson tested several variations on viewers and settled on the parameters that looked best overall. The projection is neither conformal (Mercator) nor equal-area (Mollweide, Peters); it's a compromise. Polar regions appear horizontally stretched and slightly tall; tropical regions appear nearly correct. The projection became the National Geographic Society standard 1988-1998. Winkel Tripel (Winkel, 1921) replaced it as NGS standard in 1998 — Winkel achieves a slightly better numerical-distortion profile by a different formula. The Peters polemic (1973) about Mercator's area distortion accelerated cartographic interest in equal-area alternatives, but most professional cartographers preferred Robinson-class compromises.

question: George Vancouver, who had sailed under Cook, returned to the Pacific Northwest in HMS Discovery (1792-94) to settle the British-Spanish Nootka Crisis and survey the coast. He produced charts so accurate they were used into the 20th century. What geographic question did his survey close?
choices: Whether a Northwest Passage opened to Asia through the Pacific Northwest fjord system; his crews rowed every major inlet to its head and ruled it out
Whether the Columbia River was navigable inland for ocean shipping to the Rocky Mountains; his crews sounded the bar and the lower channel and ruled it out
Whether Mt St Helens was active or dormant; his crews recorded no eruption signs during 1792-94 anywhere on the slopes and ruled out ongoing activity
Whether the Salish Sea linked to the Strait of Juan de Fuca; his crews traced the islands and confirmed the strait was a closed inlet and ruled it out
answer: Whether a Northwest Passage opened to Asia through the Pacific Northwest fjord system; his crews rowed every major inlet to its head and ruled it out
context: George Vancouver (1757-98) had sailed under Cook on the second and third voyages. He commanded HMS Discovery 1791-95. His Pacific Northwest survey 1792-94 charted the coast from southern Oregon (just south of the Columbia) to Cook Inlet in Alaska, with the Boundary Strait, Puget Sound, Vancouver Island, and the Inland Passage all traced. The boats' crews rowed and sailed every major inlet to its head, definitively closing the question of a Northwest Passage through the region (Juan de Fuca's 1592 claim had implied a continent-spanning sea). Vancouver met Spanish surveyors at Nootka Sound (Quadra). His 1798 Voyage of Discovery (published posthumously) was the standard reference. Vancouver Island, Vancouver (city), Vancouver (Washington), Mount Rainier, and Mount Baker all bear names he assigned.

question: Francis Beaufort, Royal Navy hydrographer, devised in 1805 a 13-point wind scale based not on instruments but on what a fully-rigged sloop could carry. The Royal Navy adopted it in 1838 and the scale remains in use. What problem did Beaufort's scale solve for ship logs?
choices: Standardizing wind reports across ships and observers; anemometers were rare in 1805 and judgments varied wildly between captains in their daily logs
Measuring wind speed precisely in m/s; anemometer instruments were unreliable below 5 knots in 1805 and could not capture light-air conditions in logs
Calibrating barometers across ships; mercury-tube instruments were unreliable in 1805 and could not hold calibration across the temperature ranges at sea
Predicting weather 48 hours ahead; wind direction was reliable in 1805 but speed forecasts were unreliable and ships' daily logs needed a way to estimate
answer: Standardizing wind reports across ships and observers; anemometers were rare in 1805 and judgments varied wildly between captains in their daily logs
context: Francis Beaufort (1774-1857) joined the Royal Navy at 13. As hydrographer to the navy (1829-55) he reorganized chart production. The 1805 wind scale he originated keyed wind force to what canvas a man-of-war could carry: Force 0 (calm, no canvas action) through Force 12 (hurricane, no canvas survives). Adopted Royal Navy 1838, civilian use thereafter. Anemometers (Robinson cup anemometer, 1845) eventually allowed numerical wind speed measurement; the Beaufort scale was recalibrated against velocity in 1906. Modern Beaufort scale extends 0-17. The scale remains common in marine forecasts because it captures sea state (wave height, foam, spindrift) along with wind — easier to estimate visually than wind speed alone.

question: On 21 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St Louis from Long Island to Le Bourget — 3,600 miles, 33.5 hours, solo, no radio. The first solo nonstop transatlantic flight. The Orteig Prize ($25,000) had stood since 1919. What technical innovation made the solo crossing possible where prior attempts had failed?
choices: Range — auxiliary fuel tanks gave the Ryan NYP 425 gallons of fuel and roughly 4,000 miles of still-air range with reserves for headwinds
Range — supercharged engine doubled the Ryan NYP's altitude ceiling and roughly 2,000 miles of still-air range with reserves for headwinds and weather diversions
Range — variable-pitch propeller gave the Ryan NYP a fuel efficiency at altitude that effectively doubled range vs the fixed-pitch competition at the time
Range — retractable landing gear gave the Ryan NYP a reduction in drag worth an estimated 30% more range vs the fixed-gear competition at the time
answer: Range — auxiliary fuel tanks gave the Ryan NYP 425 gallons of fuel and roughly 4,000 miles of still-air range with reserves for headwinds
context: Lindbergh's Ryan NYP Spirit of St Louis was custom-built to maximize fuel capacity: five tanks (forward 88 gal, three nose 56 gal each, wing 145 gal — total 425 gallons giving ~4,210 mile range in still air). To make room Lindbergh sat behind the main tank with no forward view (he used a periscope). He used a sealed Earth-inductor compass and a Pioneer drift meter. Solo flight saved weight. Wright Whirlwind J-5C engine. No radio (weight saving). The Orteig Prize ($25,000, 1919) had cost lives: Nungesser and Coli's L'Oiseau Blanc disappeared 8 May 1927 over the Atlantic; Chamberlin and Acosta crossed 4-6 June 1927 (two weeks after Lindbergh). The 1927-29 aviation boom that followed made transoceanic geography a regular fact rather than a one-time stunt.

question: On 12 May 1926 Amundsen, American Lincoln Ellsworth, and Italian Umberto Nobile flew the airship Norge from Spitsbergen to Teller, Alaska — via the North Pole. 72 hours, 5,200 km. What specific geographic question did the transpolar route settle that Peary's 1909 and Cook's 1908 claims had not?
choices: Whether any unknown land or large island existed between Spitsbergen, the Pole, and Alaska; Norge confirmed empty Arctic Ocean for the whole route
Whether sea ice extended continuously across the Arctic Ocean; Norge confirmed unbroken ice with no open polynyas anywhere across the whole route
Whether Atlantic and Pacific currents converged at the pole; Norge confirmed converging currents created surface eddies across the whole route
Whether magnetic compass readings were reliable at the geographic pole; Norge confirmed bearings stayed consistent across the whole route with no loss
answer: Whether any unknown land or large island existed between Spitsbergen, the Pole, and Alaska; Norge confirmed empty Arctic Ocean for the whole route
context: The Norge expedition (12-14 May 1926) was Amundsen's third major polar first (after the Northwest Passage 1903-06 and South Pole 1911). Built by Italian engineer Umberto Nobile, the semi-rigid airship Norge (106m, hydrogen) carried 16 men 5,200 km from Ny-Ålesund (Spitsbergen) over the North Pole to Teller, Alaska. The transpolar route definitively confirmed no large unknown landmass existed between Eurasia and North America across the Arctic Basin — the Pole was a frozen ocean. Earlier theorists (Harris, Peary) had hypothesized continents that didn't exist. Richard Byrd's flight 9 May 1926 (three days before Norge) claimed first overflight of the Pole; his navigation logs are now disputed. Nobile returned in the Italia (1928), which crashed; Amundsen vanished on a rescue flight 18 June 1928.

question: Roald Amundsen's career compiled polar firsts: the Northwest Passage; the South Pole; an airship overflight of the North Pole. By his 1928 disappearance he was the most accomplished polar explorer of any nation. Which of these did Amundsen NOT do first?
choices: Reach the geographic North Pole by surface travel; the Cook-Peary 1908-09 claims remain disputed and the surface route was never confirmed in his lifetime
Reach the geographic South Pole; his five-man party with 52 dogs reached the pole 14 December 1911, beating Scott's British party by 35 days from a closer base
Traverse the Northwest Passage by sea; his Gjøa expedition 1903-06 took three years to cross from Atlantic to Pacific through the Canadian Arctic archipelago
Fly across the Arctic Ocean; with Nobile and Ellsworth, the airship Norge crossed Spitsbergen to Alaska via the North Pole 11-14 May 1926 in a 72-hour flight
answer: Reach the geographic North Pole by surface travel; the Cook-Peary 1908-09 claims remain disputed and the surface route was never confirmed in his lifetime
context: Amundsen reached the South Pole (14 December 1911); first to traverse the Northwest Passage by sea (Gjøa, 1903-06); first confirmed person at both Poles (the Norge overflight 12 May 1926 reaching the geographic North Pole from Spitsbergen). He did NOT make a confirmed surface trek to the geographic North Pole — that claim is contested between Cook (1908) and Peary (1909); modern analysis (Henderson, True North; Bryce, Cook & Peary) doubts both. Amundsen vanished 18 June 1928 in a Latham 47 seaplane searching for Nobile's wrecked Italia airship north of Bear Island. Wreckage was found; no bodies. His memoir My Life as an Explorer (1927) is the standard source.

question: In 1796 Scottish doctor Mungo Park reached the Niger at Ségou and confirmed a long-disputed fact: that the river flowed east, not west. Park returned in 1805 with 44 men; he died at the Bussa rapids in 1806. What had ancient Greek and Arab geographers gotten wrong about the Niger?
choices: Identified the Niger with the Senegal — both seem to reach the Atlantic, but the Niger turns south to the Gulf of Guinea, not the Atlantic west coast
Identified the Niger with the Nile — both flow east, but the Niger turns south to the Gulf of Guinea, not north into the Mediterranean Sea coast
Identified the Niger with the Zambezi — both turn south, but the Niger reaches the Gulf of Guinea, not the Mozambique Channel on Africa's east coast
Identified the Niger with the Congo — both reach the Atlantic, but the Niger drains the West African Sahel, not the southern equatorial rainforest
answer: Identified the Niger with the Senegal — both seem to reach the Atlantic, but the Niger turns south to the Gulf of Guinea, not the Atlantic west coast
context: Mungo Park (1771-1806) made two expeditions for the African Association. First (1795-97): he reached the Niger at Ségou 20 July 1796, proved it flowed eastward (contradicting Pliny, Ptolemy, and Leo Africanus who had identified it with the Senegal). Second (1805-06): a 44-man military-style expedition pushed downriver from Bamako; disease, hostile encounters, and rapids killed all but Park and three others. They died at Bussa Rapids (modern Nigeria) ~early 1806 in a fight with local people defending their territory. The Lander brothers (1830) finally traced the Niger to its Gulf of Guinea delta — closing a 2,000-year geographic puzzle. Park's Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa (1799) became a classic of exploration literature.

question: GPS satellites orbit at ~20,200 km, traveling ~14,000 km/h. Without an Einsteinian correction they'd accumulate ~11 km of position error per day. Special relativity slows satellite clocks (~7 microseconds/day); general relativity speeds them up (~45). Net correction +38 microseconds/day. Which other GPS error source is the LARGEST civilian-grade budget?
choices: Ionospheric refraction — Earth's ionosphere bends GPS signals; single-frequency receivers correct via the Klobuchar model with meter-class residual error
Selective Availability dithering — US DoD intentionally degraded civilian signals 1990 to 2 May 2000, then turned dithering off; receivers now get the clean signal
Lunar tidal acceleration — Moon's gravitational pull on GPS satellites perturbs orbits; receivers correct via standard tables with meter-class residual error per fix
Solar radiation pressure — sunlight pushes lightly on the satellites; receivers correct via standard ephemeris models with meter-class residual error per fix
answer: Ionospheric refraction — Earth's ionosphere bends GPS signals; single-frequency receivers correct via the Klobuchar model with meter-class residual error
context: GPS (US Department of Defense, fully operational 1995; opened to civilians 1983 after KAL 007 shootdown showed civilian aviation needed it). Without relativistic correction, GPS would drift ~11 km/day. Largest remaining civilian-grade error: ionospheric refraction (multi-meter without correction; meter-class with Klobuchar model on single-frequency receivers). Dual-frequency receivers cancel ionospheric error directly. Selective Availability (intentional civilian-signal dithering, ~100m horizontal accuracy) operated 1990-2000; President Clinton signed the order to discontinue it 1 May 2000. Modern civilian GPS accuracy is typically 3-5 meters; differential GPS (with ground reference stations) achieves centimeter accuracy. WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) provides aviation-grade integrity over North America. Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia), BeiDou (China), QZSS (Japan), NavIC (India) are the other operational systems.

question: Jared Diamond argues geography put Europe at the western end of Eurasia's east-west axis with Atlantic harbors, enabling Iberian voyages of discovery; without geography, no Magellan. Thomas Sowell counters that geography doesn't explain WHY Iberians achieved the voyages and not Ming China (similar peninsula). Which is Sowell's move?
choices: Geography is necessary but insufficient; comparable geography produced opposite trajectories (Ming retrenchment vs Iberian expansion), so cultural variables load independently
Geography is the proximate cause; culture is a downstream effect of geographic conditions producing the observed regional differences via generational adaptation
Geography is irrelevant to long-run outcomes; cultural variables determine everything and the geographic facts Diamond cites are post-hoc rationalizations of choices
Geography determines the timing of voyaging traditions; culture determines only destinations and the technologies used, with no independent causal contribution
answer: Geography is necessary but insufficient; comparable geography produced opposite trajectories (Ming retrenchment vs Iberian expansion), so cultural variables load independently
context: Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997, Pulitzer 1998) makes geographic determinism the central claim for differential development. The Iberian case fits: Atlantic peninsula, Mediterranean entry, easy distance to West African coast. Thomas Sowell's Conquests and Cultures (1998), Migrations and Cultures (1996), and Race and Culture (1994) make the counter-move: comparable geography produces opposite trajectories. Ming China had equivalent maritime geography and superior shipbuilding in 1400, then retrenched culturally (Confucian-vs-eunuch court politics). The Arab Indian Ocean trade network was vast and stable but did not produce circumnavigation. Iberian culture (Reconquista habituation to long-range military campaigning, Henry the Navigator's school at Sagres, court patronage of cartography, Christian-vs-Islam pressure as motivation) supplied the missing variables Diamond's geography cannot reach. The pedagogical move: identify each analytical claim without declaring a verdict on which side wins.

question: The Antarctic Treaty (signed Washington 1 December 1959) was negotiated among the twelve nations active in IGY Antarctic research. It froze seven overlapping territorial claims, demilitarized the continent, opened all areas to inspection, and reserved Antarctica for peaceful science. What does the geography of overlapping claims explain?
choices: Argentine and Chilean claims collide with the British claim on the Peninsula; the treaty's claim-freeze prevented an active Cold War territorial dispute from heating
Argentine and Chilean claims collide with the Soviet claim on the Peninsula; the treaty's claim-freeze prevented Soviet political pressure from extending southward
Argentine and Chilean claims collide with the American claim on the Peninsula; the treaty's claim-freeze prevented Monroe-Doctrine logic from extending southward
Argentine and Chilean claims collide with the Norwegian claim on the Peninsula; the treaty's claim-freeze prevented NATO's framework from extending southward
answer: Argentine and Chilean claims collide with the British claim on the Peninsula; the treaty's claim-freeze prevented an active Cold War territorial dispute from heating
context: The Antarctic Treaty (1 December 1959, 12 original signatories: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Chile, France, Japan, NZ, Norway, South Africa, USSR, UK, US) is a Cold War achievement of remarkable durability. The seven territorial claimants had overlapping Peninsula claims: British claim (the Falkland Islands Dependencies, 1908); Argentine claim (1942); Chilean claim (1940). These three overlap. The treaty (Article IV) neither recognizes nor renounces claims — claims stay frozen 'as is.' Article I bans military use; Article V bans nuclear tests; Article VII gives any signatory the right to inspect any other's facilities. Madrid Protocol (1991, in force 1998) added a 50-year ban on mining. The treaty system now has 56 signatories (29 consultative parties). It's regularly cited as a model for the Outer Space Treaty (1967) and proposed lunar/Mars governance frameworks.

question: Eratosthenes (~240 BC) measured Earth's circumference at 252,000 stadia — within ~1-15% of the modern value. Two centuries later Posidonius (~85 BC) re-measured using the angle of Canopus from Rhodes and Alexandria, getting a smaller value. Ptolemy adopted Posidonius's figure. Why does this matter for the Age of Discovery?
choices: Columbus relied on Ptolemy's smaller earth and inflated Asian east-west extent; he projected Japan ~3,500 miles west of the Canaries instead of ~12,000
Columbus relied on Eratosthenes's larger earth and accurate Asian east-west extent; he projected Japan ~12,000 miles west and packed extra supplies for the crossing
Magellan relied on Ptolemy's smaller earth and inflated Pacific east-west extent; he projected Asia ~4,000 miles west of South America with adequate supplies aboard
Vasco da Gama relied on Ptolemy's smaller earth and inflated African south-north extent; he projected India ~5,000 miles south of Lisbon with adequate supplies aboard
answer: Columbus relied on Ptolemy's smaller earth and inflated Asian east-west extent; he projected Japan ~3,500 miles west of the Canaries instead of ~12,000
context: Eratosthenes's ~240 BC measurement (252,000 stadia from Syene-Alexandria shadow comparison) is famously close to the modern figure (40,075 km equatorial circumference). The exact accuracy depends on which stadion length you use — the Olympic stadion (185m) gives ~46,620 km (~16% too large); the Egyptian stadion (157m) gives ~39,564 km (~1% too small). Posidonius's later measurement (Canopus altitude from Rhodes vs Alexandria) gave a smaller value, ~180,000 stadia. Ptolemy (~150 AD) used Posidonius and also stretched Asia's east-west extent (his 'Sinae' and 'Serica' are far too long). Columbus combined Ptolemy's small Earth with Marinus of Tyre's inflated Asia and Marco Polo's exaggerated 'Cipangu' (Japan) distance to project a ~3,000-mile westward crossing — making the Atlantic voyage seem feasible. He would have run out of supplies if America hadn't intervened.

question: The Svalbard archipelago (Spitsbergen) lies between 74° and 81° N. The 1920 Spitsbergen Treaty recognized Norwegian sovereignty but reserved unusual rights for signatory nations: equal access to commercial activity (mining, fishing), no military fortifications, visa-free entry. What strategic logic shaped the arrangement?
choices: The archipelago's coal seams and Arctic position drew nations there since the 17th century; the treaty preserved access for all rather than dispute sovereignty among them
The archipelago's coal seams and Arctic position drew nations there since the 17th century; the treaty was Soviet-driven and excluded the UK, US, France from inspection rights
The archipelago's polar bear and walrus drew conservation groups there since the 17th century; the treaty was wildlife-protection-driven and excluded mining activity afterward
The archipelago's whaling stations and Arctic position drew nations there since the 17th century; the treaty was Norway-driven and explicitly excluded Russian access afterward
answer: The archipelago's coal seams and Arctic position drew nations there since the 17th century; the treaty preserved access for all rather than dispute sovereignty among them
context: Svalbard ('cold edges,' Old Norse) was used by Dutch, English, Danish-Norwegian, and Russian whalers from the 17th century. After whaling's decline, coal mining (American, Norwegian, Russian) drew renewed interest 1900-20. The 1920 Spitsbergen Treaty (9 February 1920, signed Paris during the post-WWI conference; in force 14 August 1925) is unusual: it recognizes Norwegian sovereignty (Article 1) but reserves substantial rights for the 46 signatory states — equal commercial-fishing-mining access (Article 3), no military fortifications (Article 9), visa-free entry for any signatory's citizens. Russia maintains the coal-mining town Barentsburg (~400 people); Norway runs the larger Longyearbyen (~2,400 people). The Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008) at Longyearbyen stores ~1.2 million seed samples in a permafrost-stable mine shaft. The treaty has held for over a century — a rare durable inter-war framework.

question: Selective Availability (SA) was a US DoD feature degrading civilian GPS accuracy to ~100 m from 1990 to 2 May 2000, when Clinton signed the order to discontinue it. Civilian accuracy immediately jumped to ~3-5 m. What forced the decision a decade after the Cold War ended?
choices: Civilian Differential GPS (using ground reference stations) had reached sub-meter accuracy by 1995, defeating SA's military-denial purpose; turning SA off ratified the civilian sector's work
Civilian commercial demand had outgrown SA's purpose by 1990; turning SA off ratified what dual-frequency civilian receivers had already accomplished by ground-based correction
Civilian WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation, aviation) had completed its rollout by 1995; turning SA off ratified what the aviation sector had already accomplished by ground-based correction
Civilian ionospheric correction (the Klobuchar model in single-frequency receivers) had reached sub-meter by 1995; turning SA off ratified what civilian receiver makers had already accomplished
answer: Civilian Differential GPS (using ground reference stations) had reached sub-meter accuracy by 1995, defeating SA's military-denial purpose; turning SA off ratified the civilian sector's work
context: Selective Availability (SA) used pseudo-random clock dithering and ephemeris error injection to limit civilian accuracy. From 1990 (operational) to 1 May 2000 (Clinton's announcement), civilian GPS was held to ~100m horizontal, ~140m vertical accuracy. By 1995-2000 Differential GPS (DGPS) using ground reference stations broadcasting corrections had become widespread — DGPS receivers achieved sub-meter accuracy, completely defeating SA's military-denial purpose. The cost was on civilian users without DGPS (aviation, agriculture, emergency services, consumer products) who got artificially poor accuracy. Clinton's 1 May 2000 order discontinued SA worldwide overnight. Modern civilian GPS accuracy is 3-5 meters; with WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System, 2003), sub-meter for North America aviation. The 2007 modernization of GPS made SA permanently impossible to reinstate. Clinton's decision is a clean case of a defense-purpose technology yielding to civilian utility once the defense purpose became technically obsolete.

question: Vasco da Gama (1497-99), Magellan (1519-22), and Drake (1577-80) all crossed oceans for which no chronometer existed. Cook (1768-79) carried both Kendall's K1 chronometer AND the Nautical Almanac for lunar distances. How did pre-chronometer captains estimate longitude across an ocean?
choices: Dead reckoning by chip log and compass with errors compounding daily; landfall corrections (sight known islands) reset the cumulative drift but transoceanic legs accumulated hundreds of miles of error
Lunar distance from a pre-printed almanac of Greenwich times; pre-chronometer captains used Mayer's tables and the back-staff to measure Moon-star angles and solve for Greenwich time
Magnetic-declination charts using Halley's isogonic lines; pre-chronometer captains compared compass bearing to the chart to derive longitude from regional magnetic variation
Star-occultation timing by hour-glass; pre-chronometer captains timed Jupiter's moon eclipses with hour glasses and compared to printed tables to derive longitude
answer: Dead reckoning by chip log and compass with errors compounding daily; landfall corrections (sight known islands) reset the cumulative drift but transoceanic legs accumulated hundreds of miles of error
context: Pre-chronometer longitude: dead reckoning by chip log (speed measurement using a knotted line cast astern) and compass, with errors compounding at a few percent per day. Captains relied on landfall corrections (sight a known coast, reset the position) to limit cumulative drift. Transoceanic legs without intermediate landfall accumulated hundreds of miles of east-west error — which is why Magellan's Pacific crossing was so much worse than anticipated and why Columbus thought he was near Asia. Lunar distance method (Mayer's tables 1755, Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac 1767) and Harrison's chronometer (H4, 1759) both arrived in the mid-18th century. Galileo had proposed using Jupiter's moons as a celestial clock (1610) — workable on land (Cassini's 1668 ephemeris let cartographers like the Cassini family fix observatory longitudes), but the telescope couldn't be steadied on a moving ship. Iberian and Northern European captains crossed oceans for ~250 years without solving longitude.

question: Marie Tharp's mid-Atlantic bathymetric mapping (Lamont, 1950s) revealed a central rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Bruce Heezen integrated her map with seafloor magnetic-stripe data (Vine-Matthews 1963) and earthquake-epicenter data (Wadati-Benioff zones). What picture did the three datasets establish by 1965?
choices: Seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges balanced by subduction at deep trenches; the ocean floor is recycled on a ~200 million year cycle around upper-mantle convection cells
