question: Norse sailors in the open North Atlantic, before the magnetic compass reached Scandinavia, used a flat wooden disc with a central pin and rim notches to steer by the sun even on hazy days. What is this device called?
choices: A sun compass — a wooden disc with a central pin that cast a shadow used to find south by daylight
An astrolabe — a brass disc with movable arms used to measure star angles for finding latitude at sea
A magnetic compass — a magnetized needle floating on a cork that pointed north for Norse helmsmen
A cross-staff — a long stick with a sliding crosspiece used to measure star angles above the horizon
answer: A sun compass — a wooden disc with a central pin that cast a shadow used to find south by daylight
context: A wooden disc fragment from Uunartoq, Greenland (Norse, 11th century) shows a central pin gnomon and notches. Combined with a 'sunstone' (cordierite or calcite) to polarize hazy daylight, Norse sailors could steer by the sun even when cloud covered the Atlantic.

question: Yanomami villages in the Amazonian rainforest of Venezuela and Brazil live in a single round structure called a shabono — one huge donut-shaped house with an open central courtyard. Why this layout in the rainforest?
choices: Central plaza is shared cooking and ceremony ground; the ring roof shields each family hammock from rain
Central plaza is sacred burial ground; each family lives in a separate small palm-leaf hut some distance off
Round shape resists Amazonian flood waters better when the nearby river rises several meters in wet season
Donut shape lets fire travel evenly between sections when a tribe burns the village and rebuilds a new one
answer: Central plaza is shared cooking and ceremony ground; the ring roof shields each family hammock from rain
context: The Yanomami shabono is a large communal structure — palm-leaf roof on a wooden frame, open central plaza. Each extended family hangs hammocks under its section of the ring. The plaza is shared social, ceremonial, and play space.

question: Sami winter herders of Arctic Scandinavia eat large amounts of reindeer meat, fish, and reindeer milk; almost no grain. Their bodies run on this near-zero-carbohydrate diet. What body process supplies most of their energy?
choices: Ketosis — the body switches to burning fat and protein for fuel instead of carbohydrates from grain
Glycolysis — the body breaks down sugar molecules from reindeer milk for energy through the day
Photosynthesis — the body uses Arctic summer sunlight to convert plant chemicals into stored energy
Fermentation — gut microbes ferment plant fibers, producing all the sugars the body needs each day
answer: Ketosis — the body switches to burning fat and protein for fuel instead of carbohydrates from grain
context: On a near-zero-carbohydrate diet, the human body enters ketosis: liver converts fat into ketone bodies as the primary fuel for muscles and brain. The Sami, Inuit, and Maasai diets (high fat, high protein, low or zero plant carbohydrate) all rely on this metabolic flexibility.

question: Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest stacked adobe rooms many levels high, accessed only by wooden ladders that could be pulled up onto the roof. Why pull the ladders up at night?
choices: Defense — raiders could not climb a smooth adobe wall without ladders; pulling them up sealed the village
Cold — sealing the ladder-hole at the top kept warm air from escaping the top floor during winter nights
Sand — open ladders let blowing desert sand fill the rooms; sealing the door kept out the dust storms
Snakes — ladders pulled in stopped rattlesnakes from climbing the walls into the upper Pueblo rooms
answer: Defense — raiders could not climb a smooth adobe wall without ladders; pulling them up sealed the village
context: Taos Pueblo and others (e.g., Acoma Pueblo on its mesa) used pull-up ladders as defense. The smooth adobe wall is hard to climb without one; rooftop access meant raiders had to fight uphill into prepared defenders. Acoma resisted Spanish attacks for a century.

question: Tuareg salt caravans crossed the Sahara from oasis to oasis, sometimes hundreds of kilometers between water sources. Caravans moved only at night, slept by day under cover. Why move at night in the desert?
choices: Sahara day-night temperature can swing 40°C; nightwork avoids the worst heat and saves the camels
Sahara is patrolled by daylight by rival tribes who could not see the caravan by night and could not attack
Camels' eyes are evolved for night vision and they cannot find a desert path in the harsh daylight glare
Tuareg religious tradition forbids salt caravans under the desert sun by day during summer crossings only
answer: Sahara day-night temperature can swing 40°C; nightwork avoids the worst heat and saves the camels
context: Saharan caravans, including the Tuareg salt traders to Taghaza and Bilma, moved at night to avoid 45°C+ midday heat. Day-night swing in the central Sahara can be 30-40°C. Nighttime travel saves water, eases on camels, and reduces evaporation from waterskins.

question: Inuit caribou-skin winter parkas at -40°C use the hide with the hair still attached, worn fur-side out. Underneath is a second parka of the same hide worn fur-side in. Why two parkas with fur facing opposite ways?
choices: Outer fur sheds wind and snow; inner fur traps a layer of warm still air, doubling the insulation effect
Outer fur shows the family pattern in the village; inner fur is a religious symbol against winter spirits
Outer fur comes from old caribou for toughness; inner fur from young caribou for softness in long wear
Outer fur is bleached white as snow camouflage; inner fur is brown to absorb body heat through the day
answer: Outer fur sheds wind and snow; inner fur traps a layer of warm still air, doubling the insulation effect
context: Traditional Inuit winter dress uses two caribou-hide parkas (atigi inside, qulittaq outside). Caribou hollow hair traps air; double-layer with fur facing opposite directions doubles insulation. Without the double parka, -40°C cold would defeat any single layer.

question: In the rainforest of Borneo, the Iban people built one long communal house — sometimes 150+ meters long — on stilts above the forest floor, with one room per family along the length. Why this strung-out longhouse design?
choices: One shared roof was efficient to build and maintain; stilts kept the floors above floods and crawling pests
Iban religious tradition required all families of a clan to share a single long unbroken roof of palm thatch
Longhouse design helped families call for help; an enemy attack could be heard along the building at once
A long single roof captured more rainwater than separate houses, stored in giant pots under the floor boards
answer: One shared roof was efficient to build and maintain; stilts kept the floors above floods and crawling pests
context: The Iban longhouse (rumah panjai) of Sarawak (Borneo) is a single shared-roof multi-family building on stilts. The verandah (ruai) runs the length and is shared social space; each family has its own apartment (bilik). Common in many SE Asian forest cultures.

question: On Cambodia's great Tonle Sap lake, entire villages float on the water — schools, shops, homes — moving as the lake rises and falls 10 meters with the monsoon. Why floating instead of fixed stilts on this lake?
choices: The lake's 10-meter seasonal swing is too large for fixed stilts; floating houses simply rise with the water
Floating villages were a religious tradition long predating the Khmer Empire on the lake's western bank
Floating houses are cheaper to build than fixed stilts; bamboo rafts cost less than long hardwood posts
Fixed stilts would tip over in the monsoon current; floating houses ride the flow with no risk of tipping
answer: The lake's 10-meter seasonal swing is too large for fixed stilts; floating houses simply rise with the water
context: The Tonle Sap reverses direction each year: monsoon pushes the Mekong into the lake, which swells from ~2,500 to ~16,000 km². Floating villages (predominantly Vietnamese and Cham communities) rise and fall with the water. Mobile schools, churches, markets, even basketball courts.

question: Polynesian wayfinders crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific without compass, map, or written language. One key tool was the pattern of ocean waves wrapping around a distant island. How did they read these waves?
choices: By feel — a wayfinder lying in the hull sensed the canoe's rocking, deducing island direction from the swell
By color — a wayfinder spotted a green tint in the waves reflected from a distant lagoon over the horizon
By sound — a wayfinder heard waves slapping against a coral reef on a calm night from many miles away
By taste — a wayfinder tasted slight saltwater changes from an island river outflow drifting on the current
answer: By feel — a wayfinder lying in the hull sensed the canoe's rocking, deducing island direction from the swell
context: Marshallese wave-pilots used 'stick charts' (rebbelib) showing how swell wrapped islands. At sea a wayfinder lay in the bottom of the hull to feel the dominant swell and any island-reflected swell — the boat's rocking pattern revealed island position. Pacific wave navigation is a unique human skill.

question: Bedouin tents of the Saharan and Arabian deserts are woven from black goat wool in long narrow strips, 60-80 cm wide, sewn together. Why such narrow strips, not one big sheet?
choices: Narrow strips fit the portable horizontal loom Bedouin women use; a wider loom will not pack onto a camel
Narrow strips block desert wind better than a single sheet, with seams catching the gusts and bleeding off
Narrow strips are easier to dye black at home; a wide piece would not soak up the dye evenly across the cloth
Narrow strips are a Bedouin religious tradition with no real effect on the tent's behavior in the desert wind
answer: Narrow strips fit the portable horizontal loom Bedouin women use; a wider loom will not pack onto a camel
context: The Bedouin bayt al-sha'r ('house of hair') is built from narrow strips of black-goat-wool (fala'if). The portable horizontal loom limits strip width. Worn strips can also be replaced one at a time, extending the tent's useful life by decades — efficient design for nomads.

question: Inuit kayaks were skin-on-frame boats built around the paddler's body, sealed at the waist by a tight skirt. A capsized hunter could right himself with a single paddle stroke without leaving the boat. What is this self-rescue move called?
choices: An Eskimo roll — a sweeping paddle plus a hip-snap that rotates the kayak back upright in one motion
A reverse paddle — a back-stroke that drags the kayak through the water in the opposite forward direction
A bow rudder — a paddle held vertical at the front of the kayak used to turn a sharp corner at slow speed
A draw stroke — a sideways paddle pull used to move the kayak directly sideways without forward motion
answer: An Eskimo roll — a sweeping paddle plus a hip-snap that rotates the kayak back upright in one motion
context: The 'Eskimo roll' (also called a Greenland roll, kayak roll) is a self-rescue technique central to Inuit hunting kayaks. Falling into ice water without rolling back up meant death in minutes. Greenland-style rolls remain a paddling tradition with many named variations.

question: Inca khipu — knotted-string records — encoded numbers in colored knotted cords. The Inca had no paper, papyrus, or clay tablet. Why might a mountain civilization develop string-based records?
choices: Cords rolled small for runners on Inca mountain roads, faster to carry than clay or stone tablets
String was the only material in the Andes; the high mountains had no clay or papyrus reed at all
Inca religion forbade marks on stone or paper; only knotted cords were proper by the sun-priests
Khipu was a poor substitute; the Inca were planning to develop a real script when Spain arrived
answer: Cords rolled small for runners on Inca mountain roads, faster to carry than clay or stone tablets
context: Inca khipu (Quechua: 'knot') encoded numerical records — taxation, population, herds — and possibly narrative. The Inca Qhapaq Ñan road network depended on chasqui runners; khipu was small, light, portable, weather-resistant. The mountain's geography shaped the record-keeping.

question: Bajau Sea Nomads of the Coral Triangle (Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia) free-dive 20+ meters for fish, sometimes for 5+ minutes without surface gear. Their spleens are larger than the human average. Why?
choices: Bajau bodies have adapted over generations of free-diving; a larger spleen releases more oxygen-rich blood
Bajau spleens grow large from a sea-only diet; ocean fish provide a chemical no land population gets at all
Larger spleens run in all Pacific peoples regardless of how often they dive in the open sea each year
Spleen size has no link to free-diving ability; the Bajau record times are explained by simple practice alone
answer: Bajau bodies have adapted over generations of free-diving; a larger spleen releases more oxygen-rich blood
context: Ilardo et al. (2018, *Cell*) found Bajau spleens ~50% larger on average than nearby non-diving Saluan; a PDE10A gene variant is implicated. Spleen contraction during dives releases oxygenated red blood cells. A real human population adaptation to a marine niche, shaped over generations.

question: On the Iranian plateau, gently sloping tunnels up to 50 km long bring water from mountain aquifers (underground water layers) to desert villages entirely by gravity. Lines of small wellheads mark each tunnel's path on the surface. What is this ancient system called?
choices: A qanat — a gravity-fed underground aqueduct from mountain water tables to lowland villages with minimal evaporation loss
A wadi — a desert valley that floods seasonally with flash rains and holds no surface water in the rest of the year
A badgir — a tall windcatcher tower that funnels cool desert breeze down into a building's cellar through long shafts
A cistern — a sealed underground tank that collects winter rainfall for storage and use during the dry desert summer
answer: A qanat — a gravity-fed underground aqueduct from mountain water tables to lowland villages with minimal evaporation loss
context: The qanat (Persian: kariz) is an ancient innovation, possibly Achaemenid (~600 BC). A mother well taps the aquifer at the mountain foot; the tunnel descends just under the water-table gradient. Evaporation losses are near zero. UNESCO recognized.

question: Inca terraces (andenes) line the steepest slopes of the Peruvian Andes — some still in use 500+ years after construction. Each terrace has a built-in subsurface drainage layer of gravel and sand under the topsoil. Why the drainage layer?
choices: Andean rains can saturate a slope and trigger landslides; gravel drainage carries excess water away beneath the soil
Drainage layers warm the soil through capillary action, raising root-zone temperature several degrees in the wet season
Gravel acts as a fertilizer source, slowly releasing minerals into the topsoil and feeding the potato roots above
Drainage layers store summer water for winter use, releasing moisture upward through dry months of the highland year
answer: Andean rains can saturate a slope and trigger landslides; gravel drainage carries excess water away beneath the soil
context: Inca terrace engineering at Machu Picchu, Moray, and Ollantaytambo includes layered drainage: coarse gravel below, sand above, topsoil on top. The slope and the drainage stratum together prevent saturated-soil failure on slopes too steep for unterraced farming. Brilliant geotechnical design.

question: On the Tibetan plateau at 4,000+ m, oxygen partial pressure is ~60% of sea level. Tibetan populations live and work easily here while lowland visitors suffer altitude sickness. Genetic studies trace this tolerance to a variant of one gene. Which gene?
choices: EPAS1 — a hypoxia response regulator; the Tibetan variant blunts excessive red-blood-cell thickening at low oxygen
EGLN1 — a kidney filtration regulator; the Tibetan variant changes how the kidneys filter blood proteins each day
TYR — a skin pigment regulator; the Tibetan variant produces darker skin to filter intense ultraviolet exposure
LCT — a lactase persistence regulator; the Tibetan variant lets adults digest the lactose in fresh dairy
answer: EPAS1 — a hypoxia response regulator; the Tibetan variant blunts excessive red-blood-cell thickening at low oxygen
context: Yi et al. (2010, *Science*) identified an EPAS1 variant in Tibetan populations under the strongest recent selection in any human genome. The variant prevents the hemoglobin overshoot that gives lowlanders blood-clot risk at altitude. Likely introgressed from a related Denisovan population.

question: Cappadocia, in central Anatolia (Turkey), has soft volcanic-ash tuff that erodes into 'fairy chimneys.' Early Christians carved multi-story homes, churches, and underground cities into the rock. What feature enabled the underground cities?
choices: Tuff is soft enough to carve with hand tools yet stable enough to hold roof spans without collapse in dry climate
Tuff contains a natural anti-fungal mineral that prevented mold from ruining underground walls and ceilings inside
Tuff contains pockets of natural light-emitting phosphor, dimly illuminating Cappadocia's underground city corridors
Tuff has an unusually high water content, releasing moisture into the carved chambers to keep the air comfortable
answer: Tuff is soft enough to carve with hand tools yet stable enough to hold roof spans without collapse in dry climate
context: Cappadocian tuff (welded volcanic ash from Erciyes and Hasan Dağı) is one of Earth's most carvable yet self-supporting rocks. Derinkuyu and Kaymaklı are 8-11 story underground cities (~200 BC onward), some housing 20,000+ during raids. Byzantine Christians used Cappadocia as a refuge for centuries.

question: Persian badgirs (windcatchers) are mud-brick towers that rise several stories above a desert house, open at the top with shafts running down. Many sit above an underground water channel. How does the badgir + water combination cool a desert house?
choices: Wind enters the tower, sinks past the cool water surface (evaporative cooling), and delivers chilled air to the rooms below
Wind enters the tower, compresses against the dome, releases stored heat, and the cooled air sinks into the rooms below
The tower captures solar heat at the top, drawing hot air up out of the house and pulling cool air in through windows
Both wind-driven evaporation and solar-chimney effects work; the badgir uses each in different rooms of the same house
answer: Both wind-driven evaporation and solar-chimney effects work; the badgir uses each in different rooms of the same house
context: The badgir (Persian: bâdgir, 'wind-catcher') uses two effects together. By day, the sun-heated tower acts as a solar chimney drawing hot indoor air up and out. By night, prevailing wind enters the catch face, sinks past the basement qanat water channel (evaporative cooling), and delivers chilled air to the rooms.

question: On the high Andean altiplano (~4,000 m), farmers freeze-dry potatoes outdoors using only the weather. They spread the tubers on cold nights, tread the thawed potatoes by foot to expel water, then dry them in the intense sun. What is this freeze-dried product called?
choices: Chuño — Andean freeze-dried potato made of nighttime freeze plus foot-trampling plus dry-sun drying repeated for days
Quinoa — a high-altitude grain crop of the Andes, harvested in autumn and used for soups and porridges across the region
Tarwi — a high-altitude legume crop of the Andes whose seeds are soaked for days to remove a bitter alkaloid taste
Maca — a high-altitude root crop of the Peruvian Andes, dried whole and ground into flour or used in herbal medicine
answer: Chuño — Andean freeze-dried potato made of nighttime freeze plus foot-trampling plus dry-sun drying repeated for days
context: Chuño (Quechua and Aymara) is altiplano-specific freeze-dried potato. Inca-era storehouses (qollqas) stockpiled it against famine. Nightly freeze + intense dry daytime sun + thin air is a rare combination. White chuño (tunta) is fermented in cold water first; black chuño (chuño negro) is not.

question: Inuit traditional winter diet runs heavy in seal, walrus, whale meat and blubber, raw fish — almost no plants, except some seaweed. Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) plagued European Arctic explorers eating salt pork and biscuit. Why didn't scurvy plague Inuit hunters?
choices: Raw and fresh-frozen seal, whale, and fish organs hold vitamin C; the European cooking and salting destroyed it
Inuit traded vitamin-C-rich preserved berries from Greenland's coast with every hunting band each spring season
Inuit have a genetic adaptation that internally synthesizes vitamin C, unlike European populations who must eat it
Inuit drink reindeer-milk yogurt every morning; the fermentation generates vitamin C from milk fats during storage
answer: Raw and fresh-frozen seal, whale, and fish organs hold vitamin C; the European cooking and salting destroyed it
context: Raw fresh meat (organ tissue: adrenal, kidney, brain) and raw fish retain vitamin C. Cooking destroys it. Inuit preparation kept much meat raw or near-raw (qisuk, kiviak). European Arctic crews cooked and salted everything, losing all vitamin C — diet preparation, not biology.

question: Petra, in southern Jordan, is a Nabatean city carved into pink sandstone cliffs ~300 BC. It sits in a near-rainless desert; the only access is a narrow slot canyon (the Siq) over a kilometer long. Yet Petra supported a population of ~30,000. What water adaptation enabled this?
choices: Cisterns plus dam-and-channel networks captured every flash flood from the canyon walls, storing winter rain for year-round use
Deep wells reached fossil groundwater hundreds of meters below the city's plaza, drawn up by camel-driven mechanical pulleys
Imported water from the Jordan River was carried 200 km by cattle-drawn carts twice a week in the cooler months only
Springs at the city's center fed a constant stream of fresh water; Petra was unique among desert sites in this regard
answer: Cisterns plus dam-and-channel networks captured every flash flood from the canyon walls, storing winter rain for year-round use
context: The Nabateans engineered Petra's water with cisterns, dams, settling basins, ceramic pipe networks, and channels in the Siq that caught flash floods (which would otherwise have flooded the city). Petra's water tech is still studied by engineers. The city flourished as a Roman-era caravan hub.

question: Sami winter herders work outside in -30°C cold for hours; ungloved hands manipulate harness, leather, knot work. Bare-hand frostbite risk is real. Yet the Sami often work bare-handed for short periods. What physiological adaptation enables this in cold-acclimated hands?
choices: The hunting reflex — periodic cold-induced vasodilation in the fingers cycles warm blood back to prevent frostbite
The shivering reflex — strong rapid muscle contractions in the hand warm the fingers enough to resume fine work
The diving reflex — slowed pulse and reduced peripheral blood flow conserve energy during cold-water immersion
The startle reflex — rapid adrenaline surge during exposure releases warming chemicals to the hands and feet alike
answer: The hunting reflex — periodic cold-induced vasodilation in the fingers cycles warm blood back to prevent frostbite
context: Cold-induced vasodilation (CIVD), the 'hunting reflex,' is a cycle of vasoconstriction then sudden vasodilation in cold-exposed extremities. Sami, Inuit, and some Tibetan populations show stronger CIVD than unacclimated lowlanders. Finger blood returns in waves, preventing frostbite.

question: On the Mongolian steppe, herders preserve mare's milk in a leather bag, slung from the door of the ger and stirred a thousand times a day. Wild yeast ferments the milk into a slightly fizzy, mildly alcoholic drink (~2% ABV) — a steppe staple for centuries. What is it called?
choices: Airag (Mongolian) or kumis (Turkic) — fermented mare's milk, the traditional steppe nomad drink
Tarag (Mongolian) or kefir (Turkic) — fermented cow's milk, sometimes mixed with whey starter cultures
Aaruul (Mongolian) — sun-dried curds of milk, used as portable food across the seasonal migrations
Suutei tsai (Mongolian) — salted milk tea, drunk with breakfast and after every long workday on the steppe
answer: Airag (Mongolian) or kumis (Turkic) — fermented mare's milk, the traditional steppe nomad drink
context: Airag (Mongolian), or kumis among Turkic peoples (Kazakh, Kyrgyz), is fermented mare's milk. Leather-bag fermentation introduces lactobacilli and wild yeasts. The result preserves nutrient-dense milk through the season and ferments lactose, so even lactose-intolerant adults can digest it.

question: On Indonesia and the Philippines, traditional bahay-kubo and rumah-adat houses stand on tall stilts with wide overhanging palm-thatch roofs. The roof drops at a steep ~45° pitch. Tropical climate (long-term weather pattern) shapes the design. Why the steep pitch on a tropical roof?
choices: Heavy monsoon rain runs off a steep pitch instead of pooling on the roof and rotting the thatch underneath
Steep pitch reflects more midday sun than a flat roof, keeping the interior cooler in tropical summer heat
Steep pitch lets the upstairs sleeping platform be taller, with more headroom under the roof in monsoon season
Steep pitch makes the house look bigger and more imposing to neighbors and visitors in the village square
answer: Heavy monsoon rain runs off a steep pitch instead of pooling on the roof and rotting the thatch underneath
context: Tropical monsoon climate (Köppen Am) delivers intense rain — sometimes 100+ mm in an afternoon storm. A steep pitch (>30°) sheds water faster than a flat roof can drain. Thatch lasts decades when dry between rains but rots within months if water pools. The same logic shapes traditional roofs from Borneo to Bali.

question: Inuit kayaks of the Greenland coast were sewn from 4-7 seal skins stretched over a driftwood frame, then sealed at the cockpit by a tightly fitted skin spray skirt. The whole boat weighed under 14 kg. Why so light?
choices: A hunter portaged the kayak across ice between leads of open water; weight constrained how far he could carry it
Light hulls float higher in waves, letting the hunter sneak silently on the seal at the breathing hole without splashing
Greenland driftwood was scarce; using as little wood as possible was a regional supply constraint of the trees
Heavy hulls froze faster when pulled from the water, so light hulls were preferred to lighten the freezing problem
answer: A hunter portaged the kayak across ice between leads of open water; weight constrained how far he could carry it
context: Inuit kayaks were portage-tools as much as boats. A hunter moving along the ice edge would carry the kayak across solid ice between open-water leads — sometimes for hours, sometimes for kilometers. A 14 kg load on his head let him keep up with the seal hunt; a 30 kg load would have stopped him cold.

question: Easter Island (Rapa Nui), in the southeast Pacific, lies 3,500 km from inhabited land. Polynesians reached it ~AD 1200 and built ~900 moai over 500 years. By 1722 the population had collapsed and the island was largely treeless. Two competing theories explain it. Which?
choices: Diamond: islanders cut palms for moai transport. Hunt-Lipo: Polynesian rats ate seedlings, plus later slave raids
Diamond: a Polynesian civil war over moai placement caused collapse. Hunt-Lipo: a volcanic eruption killed all plants
Diamond: European disease arrived before 1722 and killed most. Hunt-Lipo: an extreme El Niño drought destroyed crops
Diamond: moai ritual required human sacrifice. Hunt-Lipo: original Polynesian settlers never numbered many to begin
answer: Diamond: islanders cut palms for moai transport. Hunt-Lipo: Polynesian rats ate seedlings, plus later slave raids
context: Jared Diamond (*Collapse*, 2005) argues over-deforestation for moai transport drove collapse. Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo (*The Statues That Walked*, 2011) argue Polynesian rats ate seedlings, while population stayed stable until European slave raids (1862-3) and smallpox struck. Debate continues.

question: On the cold Mongolian steppe at -40°C, herders wear several layers of long-haired sheepskin coat (deel) with a wide cloth sash. Wide leather boots (gutal) come up over the calf. Why does the wide sash matter for warmth?
choices: The sash compresses layered air inside the deel, eliminating drafts that would otherwise rob body heat away
The sash supports the back when lifting heavy weights, reducing the energy spent fighting muscle fatigue in cold
The sash is purely decorative; Mongol cold-protection is from the wool layers and from the wide felt boots only
The sash holds a small fire-starter kit at the waist; the herder can light a quick fire at any pasture stop in winter
answer: The sash compresses layered air inside the deel, eliminating drafts that would otherwise rob body heat away
context: The Mongolian deel is belted with a long fabric sash (büs) that compresses the wool layers against the body, eliminating wind-driven convective heat loss between layers. The sash also supports the lower back during horseback riding and holds tools (knife, fire-striker, snuff bottle) close at hand.

question: Pre-Columbian Aztec farmers in the lake basin of central Mexico built raised garden beds in the shallow lake itself — long narrow strips of mud and cane, with canals between for canoes. The technique fed Tenochtitlan's 200,000+ people. What are these gardens called?
choices: Chinampas — long narrow raised farm-beds rising just above lake level, watered by capillary uptake from the canal water below
Andenes — stone-walled stepped terraces cut into Andean mountainsides, irrigated by gravity-fed mountain stream channels
Milpas — slash-and-burn forest clearings rotated every few years, planted with corn, beans, and squash together
Waru waru — raised soil ridges with water-filled trenches on the high Bolivian altiplano grasslands, preventing frost damage
answer: Chinampas — long narrow raised farm-beds rising just above lake level, watered by capillary uptake from the canal water below
context: Aztec chinampas in the Xochimilco basin (central Mexico) are rectangular raised garden plots, separated by canals, anchored in shallow lake mud. Water rises by capillary action. Productivity per hectare exceeds modern intensive farms in many crops. Xochimilco chinampas survive today.

question: Norwegian Lofoten fisherman drying cod on outdoor wooden racks ('hjell') leave the fish exposed to wind and freezing temperatures for 3 months. The result is stockfish, which keeps for years without salt. What climate combination enables stockfish-making in the Lofoten?
choices: Cold winter wind keeps the flesh below the temperature where bacterial spoilage runs; sub-Arctic dryness draws water out
Warm spring sun cooks the flesh slowly, killing all bacteria over weeks of intense daylight in the northern bay
Heavy snow cover insulates the racks from temperature swings, keeping the fish at exactly 0°C through 3 months
Constant winter rain washes away bacteria from the fish; the rain water then evaporates in the cool autumn nights
answer: Cold winter wind keeps the flesh below the temperature where bacterial spoilage runs; sub-Arctic dryness draws water out
context: Lofoten stockfish drying (tørrfisk) needs cold, dry, windy weather above freezing but well below body temperature — the Lofoten's late winter weather is ideal. Stockfish has been a Norwegian export for 1,000+ years; one Norse name (raa skreid) appears in 9th-century sources. Dry fish stores indefinitely.

question: A Polynesian voyaging canoe sails into the doldrums (the windless equatorial band) and loses wind. The wayfinder reads the canoe's drift by feeling the swell pattern in the hull beneath him. Why is the swell — not the wind — what reveals the canoe's direction in the doldrums?
choices: Swell patterns propagate from distant storm systems and persist across calm zones long after the local wind has died
The doldrum band contains a hidden ocean current that always pushes the canoe due west, regardless of swell
Swell direction is set by the moon's tidal pull and reverses every 6 hours, marking time more than direction
Wave foam-color reveals the canoe's heading; the wayfinder reads the slight pinkness on the western horizon
answer: Swell patterns propagate from distant storm systems and persist across calm zones long after the local wind has died
context: Ocean swells are long-period waves generated by distant storm systems, propagating thousands of km across the ocean. They persist after the local wind dies. Polynesian wayfinders memorize the dominant swell pattern in each ocean band, deducing course when winds fail. Hokule'a navigators revived this skill.

question: Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest dug 'kivas' — round, partly underground ceremonial chambers — at the heart of each village. Inside, a small fire burned. A vertical air shaft channeled cold outside air down to the fire base. Why this exact ventilation design?
choices: The shaft delivered combustion air to the fire from outside, preventing smoke from filling the chamber on still days
The shaft delivered cool air to the ceremony in summer, making the kiva a cool refuge from the desert daytime heat
The shaft delivered cold air to chill the kiva for food storage between summer ceremonies of the calendar year
The shaft channeled rising smoke directly down into the ground, hiding the kiva from enemy raiders watching above
answer: The shaft delivered combustion air to the fire from outside, preventing smoke from filling the chamber on still days
context: Ancestral Puebloan kivas — the great kiva at Chaco Canyon, the kivas at Mesa Verde — use a vertical air shaft delivering combustion air to a deflector stone before the central hearth. The deflector splits the stream, feeding the fire while preventing it from blowing out. Sophisticated indoor combustion engineering.

question: The Banaue Rice Terraces in the Cordillera mountains of Luzon (Philippines) climb to 1,500 m on steep slopes and are 2,000+ years old, hand-built by the Ifugao people. Stone-walled paddies hold water for irrigated rice. What sustains the continuous water supply to the highest terraces?
choices: A protected upland rainforest above the terraces captures monsoon rain; gravity feeds water down through stone channels
Ifugao farmers haul water by hand from a Cordillera river each morning; the village divides the labor among the families
A regional irrigation pump operated by the Philippine government lifts groundwater into a reservoir above the terraces
The terraces collect their own monsoon rain in stone-walled paddies; no external water source is needed at the highest tier
answer: A protected upland rainforest above the terraces captures monsoon rain; gravity feeds water down through stone channels
context: The Ifugao Rice Terraces depend on the muyong — protected upland forest belts above the highest paddies. The muyong holds and slowly releases monsoon rainfall through soil and roots. Each Ifugao family inherits a muyong with its terraces — the forest IS the irrigation system. UNESCO 1995.

question: Snow blindness (photokeratitis) — sunburn of the cornea — was a major Arctic hunter risk before plastic snow goggles. Inuit slit-goggles, carved from bone or driftwood with horizontal slits ~2 mm wide, reduced incidence dramatically. Beyond just blocking glare, what optical effect did the slits add?
choices: Pinhole-aperture sharpening — narrow slits effectively shrink the eye's pupil, improving distant focus on flat snow scenes
Polarization filtering — wood-grain in the goggle aligns light waves to a single direction, the same as Polaroid lenses
Magnification — slits act as cylindrical lenses that enlarge distant prey for hunting at long range across the ice
Color filtering — bone material absorbs UV and red wavelengths, leaving only blue light through to the eye lens
answer: Pinhole-aperture sharpening — narrow slits effectively shrink the eye's pupil, improving distant focus on flat snow scenes
context: Inuit slit-goggles work two ways: dramatic glare reduction (the obvious effect) and pinhole-aperture sharpening (the subtle one). With pupils 'narrowed' by the slit, depth-of-field grows and distant details sharpen — useful when scanning featureless snow for game. Same principle as pinhole reading glasses.

question: Saharan Tuareg men wear a 4-5 m indigo veil (tagelmust) wrapped many times around head and face, leaving only the eyes visible. The veil is worn even in 45°C heat. Why isn't a thinner cloth sufficient?
choices: Multiple wrap layers create still-air microclimate against the skin and filter blowing sand from breath and eyes
Multiple layers mark the wearer's tribe and household; the count of wraps signals identity to other Tuareg riders
Multiple layers absorb the indigo dye into the skin, giving the Tuareg religious protection during desert journeys
Multiple layers anchor the head-cloth against very strong winds; a thinner cloth would blow off in the desert storms
answer: Multiple wrap layers create still-air microclimate against the skin and filter blowing sand from breath and eyes
context: The Tuareg tagelmust is at once a sand filter (eye-and-respiratory in sandstorms), a thermal regulator (still-air cooling), and a marker of male adulthood. The indigo dye rubs off onto the skin and dyes it blue — source of the European nickname 'Blue People of the Sahara.'

question: A traditional Inuit semi-permanent winter house, built into the side of a hill with whalebone or driftwood framing covered in skin, sod, and snow, with a long entrance tunnel — distinct from a snow-block igloo — is called what?
choices: A qarmaq — a Thule-tradition semi-permanent earth-and-skin winter house, built into a slope and used many seasons
A lavvu — a portable conical tent of poles plus reindeer hide of the Sami reindeer herders of Lapland
A tupiq — an Inuit summer skin tent on wooden poles, used while camped at fishing or hunting grounds in warmer months
A nalingaq — a temporary windbreak of stacked snow and ice blocks, built in minutes for a brief hunting overnight
answer: A qarmaq — a Thule-tradition semi-permanent earth-and-skin winter house, built into a slope and used many seasons
context: The qarmaq (also qammaq, karmag) is a semi-permanent winter house of the Thule tradition (ancestral Inuit). Whalebone or driftwood framing supports skin, sod, moss, and packed snow. Long entrance tunnels (cold trap, like igloos) extend out. Often dug into a slope and re-used across many winters.

question: Angkor Wat, in northwestern Cambodia, was the heart of the Khmer Empire (~9th-15th centuries). Its surrounding water system included two huge artificial reservoirs (barays) each over 5 km long, plus an elaborate canal grid. The barays held water year-round. What did the canal-and-baray network enable?
choices: Year-round rice cultivation; the network released water in the dry season, supporting two or even three rice harvests per year
Royal naval fleet operations; the canals hosted war canoes year-round for the Khmer Empire's regional defense work
Religious bathing rituals; pilgrims used the reservoirs and canals for ceremonial purification before Angkor temple visits
Cool-air convection cooling of the main temple; circulating canal water lowered the temple courtyard's daily summer temperature
answer: Year-round rice cultivation; the network released water in the dry season, supporting two or even three rice harvests per year
context: The Khmer hydraulic system at Angkor supported 750,000-1M people. Two huge barays (West Baray, East Baray) plus a fine canal grid stored monsoon water for dry-season rice — up to 3 harvests per year. The 14th-c collapse may reflect a breakdown in maintenance after political stress and climate shifts.

question: In the Sahara, Berber kasbahs (mud-brick fortress-houses) have a central open courtyard. Wide thick walls surround. Almost all rooms open onto the courtyard, not the outside. Why this courtyard-centered Berber layout in the desert?
choices: Courtyard nighttime air sinks (cold settles), reaching rooms first thing each morning and cooling the day's heat
Courtyard plants and a fountain create evaporative cooling, lowering interior temperatures several degrees daily
Both cold-air-sinking and evaporative cooling apply, with the courtyard acting as a microclimate moderator each day
Courtyards were a Berber religious tradition tied to the open sky, with no thermal effect on the room temperature
answer: Both cold-air-sinking and evaporative cooling apply, with the courtyard acting as a microclimate moderator each day
context: Courtyard architecture in hot-arid climates uses radiative night cooling (clear desert sky pulls heat up; courtyard floor cools fast) AND evaporative cooling from fountains or plants. Cold air sinks into surrounding rooms. Thick walls block solar gain. Courtyards date from Mesopotamia, spread across the arid Old World.

question: Polynesian voyaging canoes from Tahiti and Hawaii used a celestial-navigation reference frame called the 'star compass' — a mental map of the horizon divided into named segments, each named for a particular star's rising or setting point. How many points around the horizon does the traditional Hawaiian star compass divide?
choices: 32 points — like a Western mariner's compass, with named rising and setting positions of stars and the sun
12 points — corresponding to the Polynesian months and the rising positions of zodiac-style constellations
8 points — one for each major Hawaiian island, each remembered by the star path that leads to it from open sea
100 points — each remembered as the name of a Polynesian ancestor who first sailed in that direction by canoe
answer: 32 points — like a Western mariner's compass, with named rising and setting positions of stars and the sun
context: The Hawaiian star compass (Nainoa Thompson's reconstruction from Mau Piailug's Carolinian teachings) divides the horizon into 32 points (~11.25° each). Each named house corresponds to a star's rising or setting position. The wayfinder memorizes star paths, sun path, and swell — a complete reference frame in the head.

question: Indigenous Australian peoples of the central desert ('Western Desert' bands) lived for ~50,000 years in an environment that lowland visitors find unsurvivable — daytime summer above 45°C, no surface water for days at a stretch. One key adaptation was knowledge of one kind of plant. Which?
choices: Water-storing plants (mallee roots, water-tree saps, native melons) that hold drinkable moisture year-round
Salt-tolerant grasses that could be fermented into a high-energy paste for trade between desert-living groups
Hallucinogenic acacia bark used in long ceremony, reducing thirst sensation across multi-day desert walks
Insulating-fiber plants whose fibers were woven into rough capes that kept body heat in cold desert nights
answer: Water-storing plants (mallee roots, water-tree saps, native melons) that hold drinkable moisture year-round
context: Aboriginal Western Desert peoples kept extraordinary botanical knowledge: water-yielding tree roots (some mallee species), water-bearing frogs buried in dry creek beds, native melons (Citrullus), and seasonal surface-water memorized across vast country. 'Songlines' — sung map-narratives — encoded the resource geography.

question: The Skellig Michael monastery, on a rocky pyramidal island 12 km off Ireland's southwest coast, housed Celtic Christian monks from ~600 AD to ~1200 AD. The monks built dry-stone beehive cells ('clocháns') on a windswept ledge 180 m above the Atlantic. Why settle this island?
choices: Deliberate isolation for the contemplative life — a 'desert' in the green Irish sea where monks pursued ascetic prayer
Refuge from Viking raids — Skellig's cliffs and isolation made it hard for Norse longships to land and plunder
Strategic surveillance — Skellig's height gave monks a viewpoint over Atlantic shipping for the Irish High King
Fertile fishing grounds — the surrounding waters teem with Atlantic cod and made the small community wealthy
answer: Deliberate isolation for the contemplative life — a 'desert' in the green Irish sea where monks pursued ascetic prayer
context: Celtic Christian monasticism prized 'green martyrdom' — voluntary exile to harsh remote places for contemplative life. Skellig Michael (Sceilig Mhichíl, UNESCO 1996) is the most extreme surviving example. Beehive clochán cells, an oratory, and a small church survive. Vikings did raid it (~824 AD).

question: On the Pacific atolls of Tuvalu, Kiribati, and the Maldives — coral islands rising barely 2 m above sea level — traditional farming digs deep pits down to the freshwater lens beneath the limestone. Crops grow in pits below ground level. What is this Pacific atoll farming technique called?
choices: Pulaka pit — a deep excavated pit reaching the freshwater lens, planted with giant swamp taro and other crops
Padi pit — a shallow flooded rice paddy planted seasonally with rice imported from larger Pacific islands annually
Slash-and-burn — a tropical rainforest clearance technique used to clear lowland forest for short-term farming
Wet-rice terracing — a stepped hillside paddy system used in the mountain villages of the Philippines and Java
answer: Pulaka pit — a deep excavated pit reaching the freshwater lens, planted with giant swamp taro and other crops
context: The pulaka pit is a Tuvalu/Kiribati/Tokelau adaptation — a 1-3 m deep excavated pit reaching the freshwater lens under the coral island. Giant swamp taro (Cyrtosperma merkusii, pulaka) is the staple crop. The pit + lens + composting + crop rotation makes farming possible. Rising sea levels now threaten it.

question: The Inuit dwelling in semi-permanent winter villages on the Greenland coast was the qarmaq, partly dug into a slope, framed with whalebone and driftwood, covered in sod and snow. The entrance was a long passage descending to a level below the floor of the main room. Why descend on entry?
choices: Cold trap — colder air sinks and stays in the entrance, while warmer air pools in the main room above
Defense — narrow descending entries forced raiders to enter single-file, easy for the defender to fight
Hunting storage — the lowest part of the entrance was used to store frozen seal carcasses out of reach of pets
Religious symbolism — descending entries mimic the qarmaq's role as a return to the earth's womb each winter
answer: Cold trap — colder air sinks and stays in the entrance, while warmer air pools in the main room above
context: Like the igloo's tunnel entrance, the qarmaq's descending entry creates a cold trap. Cold air, denser than warm, settles in the passage and stays. The main room collects body heat and lamp heat several meters higher. The same engineering insight — cold air sinks — recurs in many cold-climate dwellings.

question: In western Norway's fjord country, traditional grass-roofed timber houses ('tørveskule') had a layer of birch bark under the sod. The sod grew grass; the birch underneath did the real work. What did the birch layer do?
choices: Birch bark is naturally water-impermeable; it kept the roof watertight while the sod above held it down by weight
Birch bark contained an insect-repelling chemical; it kept beetles and termites out of the wooden roof boards
Birch bark released a slow ethanol vapor over years; it acted as a wood preservative for the underlying boards
Birch bark was a religious requirement for Norwegian winter dwellings, with no practical effect on the rain seal
answer: Birch bark is naturally water-impermeable; it kept the roof watertight while the sod above held it down by weight
context: Norwegian and Swedish torvtak (sod roof) construction uses birch-bark as waterproof membrane (it contains betulin, a natural water-repellent). Sod above weights it down; grass roots hold the sod together; the assembly insulates effectively. Roof can last 50+ years. Common across Scandinavia and Iceland.

question: Lalibela, in Ethiopia's high northern plateau (Amhara region, 2,500+ m elevation), holds 11 medieval Christian churches carved downward into solid basalt rock — entire structures excavated from the surrounding stone, not built on it. Most date from the late 12th century. What geographic feature made this possible?
choices: Soft basalt bedrock — the plateau's volcanic rock is workable with hand tools yet self-supporting in roof spans
An abundant local wood supply — wooden scaffolding inside the rock made the excavation work practical and safe
A regional Christian iconography tradition — Ethiopian Coptic architecture required all churches to be subterranean
Heavy seasonal rainfall — Ethiopia's monsoon-fed rivers eroded the basalt slowly, exposing the churches naturally
answer: Soft basalt bedrock — the plateau's volcanic rock is workable with hand tools yet self-supporting in roof spans
context: Lalibela's 11 rock-hewn churches (Bete Giyorgis, Bete Medhane Alem, etc.) were carved during the Zagwe dynasty under King Lalibela (~1181-1221). Ethiopian highland basalt is soft enough to carve with iron tools yet self-supporting. Eight centuries on, active Ethiopian Orthodox places of worship. UNESCO 1978.

question: Across the highlands of Yemen and the Hadhramaut valley, traditional mud-brick tower houses 5-11 stories tall have stood for centuries. The mud-brick walls thicken from top to bottom — sometimes 1 m thick at the base, much thinner near the top. Why the taper?
choices: Lower walls carry more weight; thicker base resists compression; thinner top saves material and reduces total load
Thicker base stays cooler in summer heat by deeper thermal mass; thinner top heats faster for winter sun warming
Thicker base prevents groundwater rising into the wall via capillary action; thinner top is above any rain damage
Thicker base makes the building harder to climb for raiders; thinner top is invulnerable to ground attack at all
answer: Lower walls carry more weight; thicker base resists compression; thinner top saves material and reduces total load
context: Mud-brick tower houses in Shibam (Yemen) and similar Yemenite cities use a taper because compressive load stacks downward — each story adds weight to walls below. A thick base spreads the load; a thinner top saves material. Pure structural engineering, intuited over generations by Yemenite masons.

question: The Lengua-Maskoy and Wichí peoples of the Gran Chaco — a semi-arid scrub forest of Paraguay and northern Argentina — gather large amounts of carob-pod (algarrobo) from native trees in the dry season, grinding it into flour. Why the heavy reliance on carob?
choices: Carob pods store carbohydrates and protein; they ripen and dry on the tree, lasting months for gathering and storage
Carob trees are sacred to Chaco peoples; the pods are not for food but for ceremonial trade with neighboring groups
Carob is the only edible plant in the Chaco; everything else is poisonous or contains too much salt for consumption
Carob is fermented into a slightly alcoholic beverage; Chaco populations live mostly on this seasonal drink alone
answer: Carob pods store carbohydrates and protein; they ripen and dry on the tree, lasting months for gathering and storage
context: Algarrobo (Prosopis alba and P. nigra) pods are a Chaco staple — high carbohydrate, modest protein, store for months on the tree, easily gathered. Indigenous Chaco populations ground dry pods into flour (harina de algarrobo) for breads, drinks, porridges. Same Prosopis genus produces 'mesquite flour' in the US Southwest.

question: On the high Andes near Lake Titicaca, the Uros people live on floating islands made entirely of bundled totora reeds. The islands themselves are about 1-3 m thick, anchored to the lake bottom. New reeds are added on top regularly. What is the technique called?
choices: Totora-island farming — building floating settlements of bundled reeds, replenished from above as the underside rots
Polderization — reclaiming land from a lake by building dikes and pumping out the water, as in the Netherlands
Chinampas — raised garden beds built in shallow lakes; not for human habitation but for intensive vegetable farming
Stilt-house construction — building permanent houses on tall fixed posts above water, common across SE Asia
answer: Totora-island farming — building floating settlements of bundled reeds, replenished from above as the underside rots
context: The Uros of Lake Titicaca live on man-made floating islands of bundled totora reed (Schoenoplectus californicus). The Uros add fresh reed layers on top as the underside decays. Tradition holds they first built these islands to escape mainland Inca and Aymara conflict. ~40 small islands survive in the Bay of Puno.

question: Norse Greenland (985 AD, Erik the Red) sustained itself for centuries by exporting one principal commodity to Europe. By 1400 the trade had collapsed and resupply ships stopped coming. Which geographic-economic shift killed the export base?
choices: African elephant ivory returning to Europe via Portuguese West Africa routes undercut the Greenland walrus-ivory monopoly Norse hunters had supplied
Sea ice in the Denmark Strait closed every shipping season after 1350; no Norse trade ship could reach Greenland regardless of available cargo
Black Death (1349 via Bergen shipping) collapsed the European luxury market itself; walrus ivory died as a casualty of general depression
Iceland's Althing imposed crown trade monopolies after 1262; Greenland Norse were legally locked out of European markets after that point
answer: African elephant ivory returning to Europe via Portuguese West Africa routes undercut the Greenland walrus-ivory monopoly Norse hunters had supplied
context: Norse Greenland's economy depended on walrus-ivory exports (carved into chess pieces, crozier-tops, reliquaries) traded through Bergen to European luxury markets. The colony also exported polar-bear pelts, gyrfalcons, narwhal tusks (sold as 'unicorn horn'). Portuguese voyages down the African coast from the 1430s (Henry the Navigator's Sagres center) reopened cheap African elephant ivory to European markets, undercutting walrus ivory's price. Combined with Little Ice Age cooling (~1300-1850) shortening summers and expanding Denmark Strait sea ice, the trade base collapsed. McGovern, Dugmore, and Diamond have analyzed the multi-causal failure. The Western Settlement was empty by ~1350; the Eastern by ~1450.

question: Norse settlers and Inuit Thule hunters in Greenland faced the same Arctic but ate radically different foods. Norse kept cattle for milk; Inuit ate seal, whale, and walrus almost exclusively. Which genetic-cultural conjunction underlies the difference?
choices: Northern European lactase persistence (the LCT-13910 T allele) let Norse adults digest milk; Inuit lacked the allele and depended on high-fat marine prey
Inuit fish-oil adaptation developed in the 19th century; pre-contact Inuit diet was actually similar to Norse pastoralism with seal as a small supplement
Norse and Inuit diets differed only by available species; both populations had identical metabolisms and the difference reflects game distribution
Inuit lactase persistence was nearly universal; the dairy gap reflects Norse cultural preference for cattle rather than any genetic constraint on Inuit
answer: Northern European lactase persistence (the LCT-13910 T allele) let Norse adults digest milk; Inuit lacked the allele and depended on high-fat marine prey
context: Lactase persistence (continued production of lactase enzyme into adulthood) evolved independently several times in pastoral populations: Northern European (LCT-13910*T allele, ~5,000-10,000 years ago in cattle herders), East African Maasai/Tutsi (different mutation, similar selection), and a few Arabian pastoralists. Inuit lack lactase persistence; their traditional diet centered on seal, whale, walrus, and caribou. They obtained vitamin C from raw seal liver, muktuk (whale skin), and berries — preventing the scurvy that killed European Arctic explorers eating salt-cured meat. Recent work (Fumagalli et al. 2015) identified Inuit-specific FADS gene variants regulating omega-3/omega-6 fatty acid metabolism — an adaptation to the high marine-fat diet.

question: Sami herders follow reindeer across northern Scandinavia and the Kola Peninsula, crossing borders the herds ignore. The 1751 Strömstad Treaty's Lapp Codicil recognized this between Denmark-Norway and Sweden. What did the treaty acknowledge about Sami geography?
choices: Reindeer migration routes cross national borders seasonally; Sami pastoralism required cross-border movement rights that fixed state boundaries would block
Sami were a separate political nation requiring sovereign treaty recognition; the Codicil established a Sami state alongside Norway and Sweden in Finnmark
Sami had no need for cross-border movement; pre-1751 Sami were settled village farmers and the Codicil's migration clauses are later 19th-century insertions
Sami herding was a Russian innovation imported westward; the Codicil restricted migration to prevent Russian Sami from entering Swedish territory entirely
answer: Reindeer migration routes cross national borders seasonally; Sami pastoralism required cross-border movement rights that fixed state boundaries would block
context: The Strömstad Treaty (1751) between Denmark-Norway and Sweden fixed the inland border in Lapland. Attached to it, the Lapp Codicil (Lappekodicillen) gave Sami the right to cross the new border seasonally with their reindeer — recognizing that the herds' migration patterns predated the political boundary. Sami pastoralism follows altitudinal and seasonal movement: summer in coastal-highland pastures, winter in inland forests where reindeer can scrape lichen from under snow. Subsequent Finnish (1809) and Russian (1826) border changes complicated the Codicil's reach. Sami in Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia maintain partially-overlapping legal status today. The Sami Parliament (Sametinget) was established in Norway 1989, Sweden 1993, Finland 1996; Russian Kola Sami have no parallel institution.

question: Aboriginal Australians used controlled burning ('fire-stick farming') across the continent for at least 40,000 years. The landscape Europeans called 'natural' in 1788 was shaped fire-ecology. How does Stephen Pyne's analysis frame the legacy?
choices: Mosaic cool-season burning kept eucalypt woodlands open; post-1788 cessation produced today's catastrophic megafires by allowing fuel to accumulate
Pyne's fire-stick thesis is contested romanticism; Aboriginal burning was opportunistic hunting practice, not continental management, and current fires reflect climate alone
Aboriginal fire-management was confined to coastal Queensland and the Northern Territory; the continental scope is overstated and arid centers needed no human burning
European colonization actually increased burning intensity; Aboriginal practice was minimal, and post-1788 fire ecology reflects pastoralist clearance practice instead
answer: Mosaic cool-season burning kept eucalypt woodlands open; post-1788 cessation produced today's catastrophic megafires by allowing fuel to accumulate
context: Stephen Pyne (Arizona State, fire historian) developed the fire-stick farming concept in Burning Bush: A Fire History of Australia (1991), drawing on earlier ethnography by Rhys Jones (1969). Aboriginal Australians used cool-season mosaic burning to maintain open woodlands, drive game, clear travel routes, promote yam and grass tubers, and reduce fuel for hot dry-season wildfires. Bill Gammage's The Biggest Estate on Earth (2011) and Bruce Pascoe's Dark Emu (2014) argued the continent was substantively shaped land-management territory at 1788. Recent megafires (Black Saturday 2009, Black Summer 2019-20) have led to renewed interest in Aboriginal-led burning programs; the Indigenous Land and Sea Management programmes now apply these techniques in northern Australia.

question: Ancestral Pueblo (Anasazi) built monumental great-houses at Chaco Canyon (New Mexico) from ~850 to ~1150 AD — Pueblo Bonito had 600+ rooms across 4 stories. By 1150 the canyon was abandoned. Which climate-and-agriculture conjunction explains the depopulation?
choices: Dry-farming maize in a marginal precipitation zone (~220mm/year) collapsed under the prolonged 1130-1180 drought documented in Southwest tree-ring chronologies
Apache and Navajo raids from the north drove abandonment around 1150; the climate-collapse reading is a 1970s archaeological interpretation overstating environment
Chaco was abandoned because of Spanish colonial pressure; the 1150 date is wrong and the canyon was occupied until conquistador entradas of the early 1500s
Chaco was a ceremonial pilgrimage center, not residential; the 1150 'abandonment' meant the ritual cycle ended and surrounding villages were unaffected by drought
answer: Dry-farming maize in a marginal precipitation zone (~220mm/year) collapsed under the prolonged 1130-1180 drought documented in Southwest tree-ring chronologies
context: Chaco Canyon (UNESCO 1987) was the center of a regional Ancestral Pueblo (Anasazi) society from ~850 to ~1150 AD. Pueblo Bonito (begun ~850) reached 600+ rooms and 4 stories — the largest dwelling in North America until 1882. The 'Chaco Phenomenon' included a road network radiating 250+ km, astronomical alignments (the Sun Dagger at Fajada Butte), and great kivas. Maize agriculture in the canyon (~220mm precipitation/year) depended on water-harvesting from runoff after summer monsoons. Tree-ring chronologies (Douglass's pioneering dendrochronology, 1929) document severe drought 1130-80. Chacoan populations migrated to the Rio Grande pueblos (Acoma, Zuni, Hopi) and the Mesa Verde region — modern Pueblo peoples are direct descendants. The collapse is a key Diamond Collapse (2005) case.

question: The Maasai of the East African savanna live as semi-nomadic pastoralists, moving cattle between wet and dry season pastures. The boma (enkang) is a circular thornbush kraal enclosing huts; cattle stay inside at night. How does this geography shape Maasai culture?
choices: Cattle wealth defines status, marriage, and ritual; mobility between seasonal pastures requires lightweight architecture and constant herd accounting via kinship
Maasai are descended from agriculturalist Cushitic populations; cattle pastoralism is a 19th-century adaptation to Rinderpest epidemics with no deeper basis
Maasai culture revolves around iron-smelting trades, not cattle; the pastoral image is a colonial-era stereotype and traditional economy was Swahili coast iron export
Maasai settlement is fully sedentary in highland villages; the boma is tourist reconstruction and Maasai historically lived in stone-walled towns like Engaruka
answer: Cattle wealth defines status, marriage, and ritual; mobility between seasonal pastures requires lightweight architecture and constant herd accounting via kinship
context: The Maasai (Maa-speaking, Nilotic) migrated south into the Great Rift Valley from the Nile region by ~17th century, displacing earlier populations and establishing pastoral dominance from central Kenya to central Tanzania. Cattle wealth (number of head) defines status; bride-wealth (cattle paid to bride's family) structures marriage; cattle-raiding from neighboring groups was traditional. The age-set system (moranism — young warriors, then elder councils) organizes male life-stages. The boma (enkang) is a thornbush-fenced circular kraal of huts (inkajijik) made by women from cattle dung, mud, and sticks. British and German colonial cattle policies, land alienation for Kenyan settler farming (1904, 1911 treaties), and Tanzanian ujamaa villagization (1973-76) all pressured the traditional geography. Maasai Mara and Serengeti national parks displaced traditional grazing.

question: A 2014 PNAS study (Pederson et al.) used Siberian-Mongolian tree-rings to reconstruct steppe climate during Genghis Khan's rise. It found 1211-1225 was the wettest 15-year stretch in 1,000+ years. What does the climate-window thesis claim?
choices: Unusual rainfall boosted steppe grass biomass and supported larger horse herds; Mongol military mobility scaled with horses that climate had transiently increased
Genghis Khan's empire was unrelated to climate; the conquest reflects political-organizational genius alone, and the 2014 tree-ring data correlates without causation
Drought drove Mongol conquest; armies moved south because steppe failed, contradicting the wet-window thesis and aligning with Ibn Khaldun's pastoral-pressure model
Tree-ring data from Mongolia is unreliable due to permafrost effects; the 2014 study has been retracted and steppe climate cannot be reliably reconstructed
answer: Unusual rainfall boosted steppe grass biomass and supported larger horse herds; Mongol military mobility scaled with horses that climate had transiently increased
context: Pederson, Hessl, Baatarbileg, Anchukaitis, and Di Cosmo (PNAS 2014) used Siberian pine and Mongolian larch tree-ring chronologies to reconstruct steppe climate from 900 to 2011 AD. Their finding: 1211-1225, the height of Mongol expansion under Genghis Khan, was the wettest 15-year period in the entire 1,100-year record. Mongol cavalry depended on 4-5 horses per warrior (rotated for endurance); horse availability scaled with grassland productivity, which scaled with rainfall. The argument: a transient climate window enabled the unprecedented scale of mobile cavalry the Mongol Empire deployed. Critics note correlation requires care; political organization (the yam relay system, the meritocratic military hierarchy, the Yassa law code) also mattered. The thesis fits a broader pattern of climate windows shaping pastoral expansion.

question: Pre-contact Hawaiian society divided each island into pie-slice districts running from mountain ridge to ocean reef. Each district contained the full ecological gradient: forest, midland taro fields, coastal fishponds. What was this land unit called?
choices: Ahupua'a — vertically-integrated districts giving each community access to all ecological zones; forest-agriculture-fishing economies without trade dependence
Moku — administrative districts grouped horizontally by elevation; coastal-fishing villages were separated from highland-agriculture, requiring elevation-band tribute
Heiau — sacred-precinct land grants to priestly families; the highland-to-reef pattern is a 19th-century missionary-era reconstruction unmatched in pre-contact
Konohiki — chiefly land grants of variable shape; the vertical pie-slice geography overstates regularity, and pre-contact Hawaiian land was distributed irregularly
answer: Ahupua'a — vertically-integrated districts giving each community access to all ecological zones; forest-agriculture-fishing economies without trade dependence
context: The ahupua'a (Hawaiian: 'pig altar,' from boundary markers) was the basic land-tenure unit in pre-contact Hawaii. Each ahupua'a ran from the mountain summit (mauka) to the outer reef (makai), containing the full vertical-ecological gradient: high forest for hardwoods and bird-feather collection, midland zones for sweet potato and dry taro, lowland wetlands for irrigated taro (lo'i kalo), coastal villages, and ocean fishponds (loko i'a). This vertical integration meant each community had independent access to timber, agricultural land, fresh water, and protein. Hawaiian fishponds (some still operating, like Heeia on Oahu) were sophisticated brackish-water aquaculture. The 1848 Mahele (land division under Kamehameha III) and the 1850 Kuleana Act restructured tenure under Western private-property law, breaking the ahupua'a system. Many modern Hawaiian land-management efforts try to restore the ahupua'a unit.

question: Traditional Korean houses (hanok) channeled kitchen-fire smoke through stone flues beneath the living-room floor before exiting via a chimney. The floor heated for hours and Koreans slept on it. What is this system called?
choices: Ondol — radiant under-floor heating using kitchen-fire waste smoke through stone flues; the floor warmed Korean homes through sub-zero Manchurian-cold winters
Maru — wooden raised-floor cooling for Korean summers; the ondol identification confuses winter and summer construction modes with no winter heating function
Daecheong — central courtyard heating drawing warm air upward in winter; the under-floor flue system is a 20th-century Japanese colonial introduction to Korea
Anbang — interior fire-pit heating in the principal room; the under-floor channeling is a misdescription and Korean houses used central fire-pits like Mongol gers
answer: Ondol — radiant under-floor heating using kitchen-fire waste smoke through stone flues; the floor warmed Korean homes through sub-zero Manchurian-cold winters
context: Ondol (Korean: 'warm stone') has been the traditional Korean floor-heating system since at least the Bronze Age and was fully developed by the Goryeo period (918-1392). The aagungi (firebox) outside or in the kitchen channels combustion gases through gorae (stone flues) under the bang (room) floor, then out a chimney. The floor stones (gudeul) retain heat for hours. This let Koreans sleep on heated floors through winters when Manchurian cold air sweeps the peninsula (Pyongyang January mean -6C). The maru (raised wooden floor) provided summer cooling in a separate room — the same house combined both. Modern Korean apartments retain the ondol concept as radiant heated floors (using hot water pipes rather than smoke). The system shaped Korean low-furniture culture: sitting and sleeping on warm floors, not on chairs or raised beds.

question: China's Loess Plateau is covered in fine wind-deposited silt up to 250m deep. Han and Yi farmers carved terraces into the slopes for millet and wheat. What geographic problem do the terraces solve, and what new one do they create?
choices: Terraces hold loess against erosion and gravity, enabling crops on steep slopes; but cleared terrace runoff sends silt to the Yellow River, worsening flood risk
Terraces capture monsoon rainfall otherwise lost as runoff; they create no new geographic problem and the Yellow River's silt load is unrelated to plateau cultivation
Terraces increase soil moisture by blocking evaporation; but they reduce groundwater recharge with no significant erosion contribution to Yellow River sediment
Terraces are a 20th-century Communist agricultural innovation; pre-modern Loess Plateau farmers used flat fields only and Yellow River silt is a Holocene-natural process
answer: Terraces hold loess against erosion and gravity, enabling crops on steep slopes; but cleared terrace runoff sends silt to the Yellow River, worsening flood risk
context: The Loess Plateau (Huangtu Gaoyuan) covers ~640,000 km2 of north-central China — loess up to 250m thick, wind-deposited from inner Asia during Pleistocene glacial periods. The soil is fertile but extremely erodible: rainfall cuts deep gullies in cleared land. Terracing dates to at least the Han dynasty and was systematic by the Ming-Qing. Terraces hold soil and enable wheat, millet, and (since 16th-c American crop exchange) maize and sweet potato cultivation. But cleared terraces yield runoff: the Yellow River (Huang He, 'Yellow River' for its silt color) carries ~1.6 billion tons of sediment annually — the highest sediment load of any major river. Aggradation has raised the river's bed above the surrounding plain in places (Kaifeng's river bed is meters above the city). Catastrophic floods (1931: ~1-4 million dead; 1887; 1855 course change) follow.

question: Cape Verde — 10 volcanic islands ~570 km off Senegal — sits in the Sahel rain-shadow. The islands receive ~150mm annual rainfall and have endured cyclic famine for 500 years. Yet a Creole population developed sophisticated adaptation. What did this involve?
choices: Banco terraces channeling rare rains; dragon-tree fog harvesting; emigration as remittance strategy; multi-island grain storage across drought-rotation patterns
Cape Verde Creoles abandoned agriculture entirely for fishing; the adaptation is purely maritime, and the inland terracing systems are post-1975 post-independence
Portuguese colonial irrigation solved the drought problem; pre-colonial Cape Verde was uninhabitable, and the Creole population required Portuguese water engineering
Cape Verde droughts are a modern climate-change problem; pre-19th-century islands received monsoon rainfall and supported continuous wet-agriculture without adaptation
answer: Banco terraces channeling rare rains; dragon-tree fog harvesting; emigration as remittance strategy; multi-island grain storage across drought-rotation patterns
context: Cape Verde (Cabo Verde) was uninhabited before Portuguese arrival ~1456 and was settled with Portuguese colonists and African slaves, producing a Creole (Crioulo-speaking) population. The Sahel rain-shadow leaves the islands with low and unreliable rainfall; major famines (~1773-75, ~1830-33, ~1864-65, ~1900-03, ~1941-43, ~1947-49) killed 30-50% of populations in worst episodes. Adaptation: banco terracing systems direct rare rainfall to fields; fog-collection from highland dragon trees (Dracaena draco); inter-island grain storage; and migration as economic strategy (~1 million Cape Verdeans live abroad — more than the resident population of ~550,000 — concentrated in New England, Netherlands, Portugal). The 1975 independence and subsequent agricultural-development projects reduced famine risk; tourism and remittances now dominate the economy.

question: In central Iran's desert cities (Yazd, Kashan), tall rectangular towers rise above flat rooftops. Shaft openings face all sides. Air is drawn down the shaft and across underground qanat water before reaching living rooms. What is this system?
choices: Badgir (windcatcher) — convection-and-evaporation cooling using prevailing-wind capture, qanat water for evaporative chill, and density-driven downdraft into rooms
Yakhchal — ice-storage chimney for winter ice; the cooling function applies only seasonally, and Yazd summer cooling uses underground cellars unrelated to the towers
Howz-khaneh — bath-house ventilation tower; the residential cooling identification is incorrect and Yazd badgirs functioned only for ceremonial bath complexes
Iwan — vaulted entrance hall facing prevailing breeze; the tower identification confuses two features and pre-modern Persian houses used only iwan-style cooling
answer: Badgir (windcatcher) — convection-and-evaporation cooling using prevailing-wind capture, qanat water for evaporative chill, and density-driven downdraft into rooms
context: The badgir (Persian: 'wind-catcher,' also called malqaf in Arabic) is a passive cooling system used across Iran, the Persian Gulf, Egypt, and parts of Pakistan and India. The tower rises above the roof to capture prevailing wind, with multiple opening orientations to catch wind from any direction. Air is drawn down the shaft; if the shaft passes over an underground qanat channel or a courtyard pool, evaporative cooling drops the air temperature 10-15C before it reaches the living spaces below. At night the system reverses: warm air rises and exits, drawing cool night air in. Yazd's old city (UNESCO 2017) preserves the densest concentration. The Dowlat Abad garden (Yazd, ~1750) has the tallest functioning badgir at 33m. Modern bioclimatic architects (Hassan Fathy in Egypt, contemporary Iranian designers) explicitly draw on the badgir tradition.

question: The Boran (Borana) of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya use the Ayaantu calendar — ritual experts (raagaa) read moon phases against fixed stars to coordinate camp movement, planting, and gada power-transition ritual. Why this complexity?
choices: Boran territory straddles the equator; without solstice markers, lunar-stellar timing was the only reliable way to coordinate movements across tropical seasons
The Ayaantu was imposed by Ethiopian Orthodox missionaries in the 19th century; pre-contact Boran used simple seasonal cues without astronomical calendars
Boran cycles match Coptic Christian holidays via Aksumite contact; the Ayaantu is a syncretic adaptation of Ethiopian Christianity to pastoral conditions
Boran timing reflects Islamic-Arabic mathematical knowledge via Somali trade; the system has no indigenous East African basis and is a 16th-century borrowing
answer: Boran territory straddles the equator; without solstice markers, lunar-stellar timing was the only reliable way to coordinate movements across tropical seasons
context: The Boran (Borana Oromo) calendar (Ayaantu) is one of the few documented African indigenous lunar-stellar calendars. Specialists called raagaa observe the relationship between the moon's position and certain bright stars (including Sirius and the Pleiades) to determine ritual and practical timing. The calendar tracks a 354-day lunar year with intercalations. Why? The Boran live at ~3-5 degrees north latitude, where solstice differences are minimal and seasons are governed not by sun-elevation but by the bimodal rainfall pattern (long rains March-May, short rains October-November) driven by the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone. Stellar-lunar timing gives better predictive timing than solar markers in equatorial conditions. Asmarom Legesse's Gada: Three Approaches to the Study of African Society (1973) documented the gada generational age-grade system within which the Ayaantu functions.

question: Andean villages in pre-Columbian Peru and Bolivia maintained scattered satellite settlements at multiple altitudes — potatoes at 3,500m, maize at 2,500m, peppers at 1,500m, fish at the coast. Anthropologist John Murra named this pattern. What was it?
choices: Vertical archipelago — ethnic groups holding non-contiguous lands at multiple Andean altitudes; spanned ecological zones from puna grasslands to coastal valleys
Encomienda — Spanish colonial labor grants; the vertical pattern was a 16th-century colonial adaptation and pre-Columbian Andean villages were single-zone only
Mit'a — Inca labor-tribute service; the multi-altitude land-holding is a misdescription and pre-Inca villages held only single-altitude territories from valley to ridge
Ayllu — kinship-based corporate village; the vertical archipelago confuses two concepts and ayllus held only single-altitude communal plots without satellites
answer: Vertical archipelago — ethnic groups holding non-contiguous lands at multiple Andean altitudes; spanned ecological zones from puna grasslands to coastal valleys
context: John V. Murra (Romanian-American Andean anthropologist, 1916-2006) developed the vertical archipelago (archipielago vertical) model in 'El control vertical de un maximo de pisos ecologicos en la economia de las sociedades andinas' (1972). Andean ecology stacks ecological zones (tierra caliente, tierra templada, tierra fria, puna, glacial) across short horizontal distances. Pre-Columbian communities (ayllus) maintained satellite colonies (chupachos) at different elevations to access maize (2,000-3,000m), potatoes (3,500-4,000m), tubers and llamas (4,000m+ puna), and chili peppers and coca (lower valleys).
